<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Reforestation efforts are often constrained by low seed survival under harsh environmental conditions due to seed displacement from suitable microsites. Myxospermous seeds produce mucilage that promotes post‐dispersal attachment and water retention, thereby enhancing seed establishment. Here, we investigated the biological factors governing mechanical attachment across four myxospermous species,
                    <jats:italic>Ocimum basilicum</jats:italic>
                    (basil),
                    <jats:italic>Salvia hispanica</jats:italic>
                    (chia),
                    <jats:italic>Plantago ovata</jats:italic>
                    (psyllium), and
                    <jats:italic>Linum usitatissimum</jats:italic>
                    (flax), which occupy diverse ecological environments. We used light‐sheet fluorescence microscopy, enzymatic treatments, physical characterization methods, and functional attachment assays to investigate the mechanisms underlying mucilage‐mediated seed attachment on heterogeneous surfaces. We found variation among mucilage‐mediated seed attachments under applied hydrostatic pressure. Enzymatic treatments revealed that pectin removal causes a marked loss of adhesion across all species. However, psyllium mucilage, which possesses hemicellulosic networks, showed stronger attachment than pectin‐rich flax mucilage on rough and porous substrates. Notably, mucilage could be transplanted to non‐myxospermous seeds, conferring functional attachment capabilities. Together, our results show that species‐specific mucilage properties generate distinct modes of attachment across diverse substrates, driven by differences in polysaccharide composition and fibrillar architecture. These findings link mucilage molecular structure to seed resilience and reveal an adaptive mechanism enabling seeds to persist in heterogeneous environments.
                  </jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>We introduce an end-to-end differentiable optimization framework for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) with fluid–rigid body coupling. The central difficulty is not only to obtain local derivatives of SPH operators, but also to propagate useful sensitivities through long rollouts whose particle neighborhoods, contacts, and pressure responses change rapidly over time. These effects make reverse-mode gradients noisy and often cause adjoint variables to explode in long-horizon control and inverse-design tasks. We formulate an SPH-specific reverse-mode pipeline for IISPH-based fluid–rigid simulation and implement the required vector–Jacobian products within checkpointed simulation segments. To make the resulting gradients usable for optimization, we introduce a self-adaptive adjoint correction sequence that acts as a descent-preserving preconditioner: it bounds pathological adjoint amplification while keeping the update direction aligned with the original reverse-mode sensitivity. Our experiments cover a sequence of increasingly demanding tasks, from low-dimensional impulse and shape optimization to scalar-amplitude water actuation, multi-object water-jet balancing, and neural fluid-mediated pendulum control. These results demonstrate that stabilized reverse-mode differentiation can support challenging SPH-based optimization problems involving indirect momentum transfer, long-horizon event timing, and high-dimensional control.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Formally open digital worlds can remain unevenly inhabited. This article examines Virtual Air Traffic Simulation Network, a global volunteer flight-simulation network, through postcolonial game studies and infrastructure scholarship, asking how infrastructural and historical conditions may shape participation and visibility. It combines Navigraph survey data, StatSim records from four matched 2025 routine-network windows and event geography, including Cross the Pond, and reflexive thematic analysis of asynchronous interviews with 15 participants across six regional contexts. Results show recurrent concentrations of simulated flight activity, volunteer air traffic control, and organized attention in Europe, while South Asia remains comparatively sparse; Dubai complicates a simple Global North/Global South binary. Survey comparisons caution against treating sparse activity as evidence of weak interest. Interviews identify recursive visibility, human infrastructure, route path dependence, and the costs of concentration as participant-reported mechanisms. The article conceptualizes these patterns as infrastructural inheritances: unevenly accumulated aviation resources translated into digital participation without implying direct historical determination.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We start with a brief introduction to the many faces of the Sun, the dynamic star that is the main source of space weather. We explain the need for spacecraft observations, the structure of the solar atmosphere, and the Sun’s magnetic cycle. Next, we focus on the Sun’s influence on Earth, define ‘space weather,’ and briefly discuss its effects on our technology and related socio-economic impacts. Then, we present data-driven, physics-based simulation models with predictive capabilities that enable forecasting and mitigation. We focus on models developed by my team at KU Leuven and the results and predictions they produce: the heliospheric wind and CME evolution models EUHFORIA and ICARUS, the global solar corona model COCONUT, and the solar energetic particle acceleration and transport model Particle Radiation Asset Directed at IP Space Exploration. We end with a few take-home messages.</jats:p>

title: A Progressive Instructional Paradigm for Physics-informed Neural Networks
abstract: <jats:p>Physics-informed neural networks as an interdisciplinary field combining deep learning and physical modeling, which needs high demands on student ability to transfer knowledge across disciplines. To address the cognitive gap students face when transitioning from traditional mathematical modeling to deep learning methods, this paper develops a three-stage progressive instructional paradigm. Taking the one-dimensional heat conduction equation as an example, teacher guides students through three successive cognitive stage, i.e., mechanistic modeling, data-driven modeling, and physics-informed modeling, corresponding respectively to the finite difference method, pure data-driven MLP fitting, and the PINNs approach. Rather than introducing PINNs directly as a new algorithm, the proposed design organizes their learning as a problem-driven cognitive progression. This can help students understand the paradigm shift from traditional numerical computation to data-driven learning and ultimately to physics-informed integration.</jats:p>

title: A physics-informed machine learning framework for high-resolution land subsidence prediction in the Greater Houston Area
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Land subsidence induced by groundwater extraction poses significant threats to urban infrastructure and flood resilience in rapidly urbanizing coastal regions worldwide. This study presents a novel physics-informed machine learning framework that integrates Persistent Scatterer Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PS-InSAR) observations, consolidation theory principles, and convolutional neural networks (CNN) for comprehensive land subsidence prediction in the Greater Houston Area. Processing 155 Sentinel-1 SAR images spanning January 2020 to March 2023 generated a high-resolution deformation dataset of 10,652 persistent scatterer points validated through comprehensive integration with 54 continuously operating GPS reference stations, achieving RMSE of 2.1 mm/year and correlation coefficient of 0.96. The hybrid framework integrates twelve mapped conditioning factors representing geological, hydrogeological, topographic, and anthropogenic domains, supplemented by clay-thickness and growth-fault inputs, within a physics-guided CNN architecture, achieving an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) of 0.9862, precision of 0.94, and recall of 0.92, which substantially exceed those of conventional machine learning approaches. Spatial analysis reveals that 18.66% of the study area (approximately 1,848 km
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    ) exhibits high to very high land subsidence susceptibility, with maximum observed rates reaching 24.3 mm/year in western Harris County near the Katy Prairie region. Unlike purely data-driven models that infer temporal dependence from empirical associations, the proposed framework embeds consolidation-derived temporal memory, allowing delayed aquitard response to influence subsidence susceptibility. Results indicate continued land subsidence despite significant regulatory interventions aimed at reducing groundwater extraction, with emerging subsidence hotspots identified in suburban areas experiencing rapid development. This framework provides critical insights for sustainable groundwater management, infrastructure planning, and flood risk mitigation in the Houston metropolitan region and offers a transferable methodology for similar coastal subsidence-prone areas worldwide.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present the first application of spectral nudging in a probabilistic ensemble forecasting framework, combining the physics‐based European Centre for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts' Integrated Forecasting System ensemble (IFS‐ENS) with forecasts from the probabilistic machine‐learned Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System Ensemble. Large scales of virtual temperature and vorticity are relaxed toward the machine‐learned forecasts, while mesoscale structures remain governed by the physics‐based model. This hybrid ensemble shows substantial improvements in large‐scale forecast skill, with gains in predictive skill extended by up to 2 days in the Tropics and by approximately half a day in the extratropics relative to IFS‐ENS. Despite nudging being applied only to upper‐air fields, improvements are also found in several near‐surface parameters. Tropical cyclone track forecasts improve significantly, consistent with improved representation of the large‐scale steering flow, without degrading storm intensity or ensemble spread. These results demonstrate that spectral nudging can be successfully extended to ensemble prediction and provide an attractive pathway for combining machine‐learned and physics‐based weather prediction systems.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Objective</jats:italic>
                    . Scintillation detectors with excellent timing resolution enable more precise localization of radiation sources in positron emission tomography, leading to substantial improvements in diagnostic capability for diseases such as cancer and dementia. At the timing precision required for such applications at the picosecond scale, detector performance is governed by the dynamics of scintillation photons generated within the detector and their subsequent detection processes. However, detector signals have conventionally been treated only as collective responses of many photons due to structural constraints inherent to photodetectors. In this study, we overcome this fundamental limitation using deep learning framework.
                    <jats:italic>Approach</jats:italic>
                    . The proposed method estimates photon-by-photon arrival times directly from detector waveforms without requiring any modification to the detector structure; the method operates on an event-by-event basis without ground-truth labels by integrating an unsupervised learning framework with a physically informed detector-response model.
                    <jats:italic>Main results</jats:italic>
                    . Through comprehensive validation combining Monte Carlo simulation and experimental measurements across various detector configurations, we experimentally demonstrate improved timing resolution, visualized depth-of-interaction-dependent photon transport, and classified Cherenkov and scintillation photons based on the estimated photon-level timing information using a unified deep learning-based framework.
                    <jats:italic>Significance</jats:italic>
                    . These results provide experimental access to photon dynamics, bridging the gap between theoretical modeling and experimental observation, and they open a new data-driven pathway for discovery in detector physics and optimization.

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Active colloidal matter provides a rich setting for the emergence of nonequilibrium patterns, dynamic aggregates, and self-assembled structures. Understanding how such organization arises from microscopic interactions, fluctuations, and sustained external driving remains a central challenge in soft-matter physics. This is largely because traditional theoretical and computational approaches often struggle with nonlinear dynamics, multiscale behavior, and high-dimensional parameter spaces. In this context, machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to identify relevant order parameters, classify dynamical regimes, predict emergent structures, infer assembly pathways, and guide the design and control of target states. This review examines how ML methods are incorporated into the study of pattern formation and self-assembly across both equilibrium and active colloidal systems. The discussion is organized around the analysis and representation of data pertaining to complex nonequilibrium systems, the prediction of dynamical and structural outcomes, the inference of latent variables and assembly pathways, and the design or control of target states through generative models and&#xD;reinforcement learning strategies. We also discuss hybrid approaches that incorporate physical constraints to improve interpretability, robustness, and generalization. By focusing on the interplay between machine learning and nonequilibrium soft-matter physics, we highlight both the opportunities and the open challenges of the field, including the connection between learned representations and physical variables, limited extrapolation capability across state space, and the need for reproducible benchmarks and high-quality datasets. Overall, we argue that ML is emerging as an important complement to theory and simulation in the study of active colloidal self-assembly, not as a replacement for physical modeling, but as a means to accelerate discovery and deepen understanding of emergent nonequilibrium organization.</jats:p>

title: Explainable breast cancer classification using machine learning deep learning and transfer learning across multiple data modalities
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A data-modality-driven cross-model classification using machine learning, deep learning, and transfer learning with transparency analysis for breast cancer binary classification across two different datasets is explored in this work. The ML track evaluates five models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Decision Tree. The Wisconsin Breast Cancer Diagnostic dataset, comprising 569 samples and 30 numerical features, is used for this evaluation. The DL track trains three convolutional architectures a baseline CNN, EfficientNetB0 with transfer learning, and DenseNet121 with two-phase fine-tuning on the IDC Regular Breast Histopathology Image dataset. The preprocessing pipeline for ML includes log transformation, stratified train/test splitting, and Standard-Scaler normalization to prevent data leakage. In addition, the DL pipeline incorporates balanced class sampling, a three-way 80/10/10 split; data augmentation; class weighting; and model-internal pixel rescaling. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving 98.24% accuracy on the WDBC dataset and 91.2% accuracy on the IDC histopathology image dataset. The findings indicate strong predictive capability across both tabular and image-based breast cancer classification tasks. Furthermore, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques, including SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM, were integrated to enhance model transparency and interpretability, enabling better understanding of feature importance and decision-making processes in breast cancer prediction. The study highlights that the adaptability of the paradigm should be guided by data modality rather than blanket assumptions about model superiority.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As a highly destructive geological hazard, landslides require accurate monitoring, and prediction for effective disaster mitigation. However, many current deep learning‐based methods for predicting landslide displacement still struggle to achieve high accuracy and to explain landslide behaviors. To address this long‐standing problem, we proposed a generative deep learning model with high accuracy and explainability for continuously predicting landslide displacement. Herein, we used 10‐day resolution and both displacement and pore pressure data. To enhance explainability, our model integrates the pore (water) pressure, which can modulate landslide displacement, by estimating the landslide acceleration probability. Furthermore, the structure of the generative model facilitates the identification of long‐term patterns and enables a more accurate prediction of landslide displacement. Experiments on two typical slow‐moving landslides in Oregon monitored with extensometers and piezometers show that compared with the best‐performing baseline models, MG‐DS reduces Root Mean Square Error and Mean Absolute Error by 11.8% and 16.1% for the Johnson Creek landslide and by 21.2% and 31.5% for the Carmel Knoll landslide, respectively. The model advantages manifest in three aspects: first, the generative model uses parallel prediction and iterative refinement to effectively enhance the accuracy; second, the model is able to identify and leverage pore pressure–displacement variations; and third, the use of a temporal decomposition architecture balances explainability and accuracy. Our study not only demonstrates that explicitly integrating pore pressure improves prediction performance but also shows that generative models provide a promising approach for landslide displacement prediction.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Identifying employees who may need additional professional-learning support could help organisations allocate training resources, but model comparisons in this area often omit trivial baselines and class-specific metrics. We compare seven classifiers (decision tree, random forest, logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) with a rule-based and a majority-class baseline under one protocol: stratified hold-out, the same tuning procedure, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, a descriptive repeated cross-validation check, and SHAP and LIME explanations. Experiment 1 predicts a KPI label of undocumented origin for 17,415 employees (35.9% positive); it is an illustrative comparison using the label as distributed, not validated evidence about KPI attainment. Experiment 2 predicts promotion for 54,808 employees (8.5% positive), a related task from the same public source and not an external validation. In Experiment 1, learning models reached macro-F1 of 0.628 to 0.663, against 0.590 for the rule-based baseline; a depth-5 decision tree was 0.005 below the reference random forest (95% bootstrap CI −0.016 to +0.005) but was not shown non-inferior at a 0.01 margin. In Experiment 2, boosting models were best (macro-F1 0.734 to 0.739), the decision tree was clearly worse (−0.030), and only about 35% of promoted employees were identified. Associations with training indicators are not causal, and no effect on decisions was tested.</jats:p>

title: Machine Learning-based Churn Customer Prediction

affiliation.name: Computer Science and Technology, Nanjing Normal University

abstract: <jats:p>This paper goes through and puts together earlier work on predicting customer churn, giving a structured look at the methods and approaches that appear in the literature. A large portion of studies still lean on traditional machine learning, though some treat churn as a special binary problem using a modified One-Class SVM, compare it with standard methods, and check how well it performs. Several studies step away from conventional machine learning by applying deep learning, running comparisons across different machine learning techniques, and using AdaBoost to lift classification performance, with Monte Carlo simulations doing the evaluation. Some teams have also turned to ensemble learning, pitting 11 machine learning algorithms against seven sampling methods. Using ensembles built on logistic regression (LR), XGBoost, and random forests (RF), together with various sampling strategies, the best pipeline was chosen based on AUC scores. These studies have not been free of trouble; they run into problems like weak interpretability or poor generalization in some models, and sometimes not enough attention is paid to customer privacy, raising privacy concerns. But these problems are not unsolvable: federated learning can block privacy leaks, and combining expert systems with transfer learning can fix limited interpretability and poor generalization.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>Soft drinks, often high in added sugars, have raised significant public health concerns due to
their association with adverse health effects such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, and
cardiovascular diseases. The aim of this study is to investigate the health impact of soft drink
consumption, particularly focusing on the implications of excessive sugar intake. To address
this concern, we employed four Ensemble Learning approaches to assess the health risks
associated with soft drink consumption, specific Ensemble Learning approaches such as
LightGBM, CatBoost, XGBoost, and Random Forest we adopted. Our findings indicate that
older individuals may not require as much soft drink consumption, and the general population
should limit their daily intake to a single bottle, approximately 35g per day. The study reveals
that using Ensemble Learning techniques, including LightGBM, CatBoost, XGBoost, and
Random Forest, yielded promising results, with CatBoost emerging as the top-performing
model with a model accuracy score of 97%, surpassing the performance of Random Forest and
XGBoost algorithms. The research reveals the importance of limiting the consumption of
sugary beverages and opting for healthier alternatives to mitigate the risk of adverse health
outcomes associated with excessive sugar consumption. Overall, our findings contribute
valuable insights into understanding the health implications of soft drink consumption and
highlight the efficacy of Ensemble Learning approaches in assessing and addressing public
health concerns. This study provides actionable recommendations for individuals and health
organizations to promote healthier dietary habits and mitigate the risk of sugar-related health
complications, emphasizing the importance of evidence-based interventions in safeguarding
public health.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Automated classification of canine dermatological images is challenging because visually overlapping lesions, uncertain repository labels, and repeated or transformed source photographs can influence performance estimates. This study evaluated fixed ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet201, ResNet50, and EfficientNetB0 features, alone and in fusion, with support vector machine (SVM), multilayer perceptron (MLP), and logistic regression classifiers for six repository-provided categories. Transformation-robust source auditing yielded 3088 images: 2862 development images from 864 source groups and a source-group-separated held-out internal test set of 226 images from 226 groups. Model selection used five-fold source-group-aware outer cross-validation with source-group-aware inner grid search. DenseNet201–EfficientNetB0 + SVM achieved the highest mean outer-fold balanced accuracy (0.9462 ± 0.0174), while triple fusion was comparable (0.9449 ± 0.0142) with a larger feature representation. On the held-out internal test set, accuracy was 0.8319 (95% CI 0.7832–0.8805), balanced accuracy was 0.7806 (0.7219–0.8384), and macro F1 was 0.7871 (0.7234–0.8432). Independent, clinically annotated external validation remains necessary to assess generalizability. These findings highlight the value of source-aware evaluation and parsimonious feature fusion when assessing multiclass canine dermatological image classification using repository-based datasets.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">The objective of this study was to predict the onset of high demand, the highest half-hourly average power, and the total duration of high demand over the next two hours using historical electricity consumption data from residential households. Half-hourly measurements from 2013 for 200 standard-tariff residential households selected from the Low Carbon London dataset were used. High demand was defined as exceeding the 90th percentile of each household’s average power values during the January–February period. The models were developed using data from 160 households; transfer performance was evaluated on the 40 households not included in model training. The process was divided into a training period (March–June), model selection in July, calibration of prediction intervals in August, and a testing period (September–December). The selected models were retrained using March–July data. Separate models were built for the three targets; Random Forest, histogram-based gradient boosting (HistGB), XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost were compared against a weekly seasonal reference. Model selection was initially based on average precision (AP) for the target and mean absolute error (MAE) for power and duration. For the residential units used in the training, the HistGB model selected during the testing period produced an AP of 0.4183; the CatBoost models produced an MAE of 0.2704 kW for power and 9.2361 minutes for duration. The contributions of historical consumption and calendar features to the model predictions were examined using the SHAP method. In the early warning evaluation, 78.81% of relevant events in known residential units were detected in advance; 60.93% of early warnings were identified as false alarms. The improvement in duration prediction relative to a reference that yields a duration of zero in every window remained limited. The findings indicate that the approach could contribute to monitoring residential demand; however, the burden of false alarms and the limited success in duration prediction must be taken into account from a practical standpoint.</jats:p>

title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of College Students’ Employment Status

affiliation.name: School of Information Science and Technology, Shanghai Sanda University

abstract: <jats:p>As the number of college graduates continues to increase, improving the accuracy of employment prediction has become an important research topic. This study uses public college students’ employment datasets and machine learning (ML) to investigate students’ employment outcomes. Key factors, including academic performance, technical skills, internship experience, project experience, and institutional background, were selected as predictive features. After data preprocessing, four ML models were developed for classification. Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 values were used for evaluation. In addition, the employment rate analysis, feature importance analysis, and correlation analysis were carried out to examine the factors related to the employment results. Among the four models, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) achieved the highest accuracy (69.67%), only 1.2 percentage points above the blind-guessing baseline (68.47%), while Decision Tree (DT) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) (both 68.48%) performed no differently from this baseline; Random Forest (RF) achieved the best overall balance across evaluation metrics. Correlation analysis further revealed moderate positive associations between employment outcomes and wage level with internship experience, technical competence, and academic performance. These findings suggest that feature-level analysis, rather than classification accuracy alone, offers practical value for universities in guiding students’ career development and planning.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>Lassa Fever, a severe hemorrhagic fever caused by the Lassa virus, is notably prevalent in
West Africa and can be fatal if not managed properly. Effective outbreak control and mitigation
rely heavily on early detection. This study introduces a predictive model for forecasting Lassa
Fever using machine learning techniques. The research employs an extensive dataset that
includes epidemiological and environmental data collected over multiple years to construct a
reliable predictive model. Several machine learning algorithms, such as Random Forest,
Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Gradient Boosting, are utilized to analyze historical data
and predict potential Lassa Fever outbreaks. To improve model accuracy and minimize false
positives, feature engineering and data preprocessing methods are applied. The dataset was
divided into 80% for training and 20% for testing, with various algorithms—including SVM,

recall, and F1 score. The SVM model demonstrated the highest performance, achieving
accuracy, precision, and F1 scores of 90%, 91%, and 96%, respectively. Consequently, SVM
was selected as the preferred algorithm for this research. The study recommends the use of this
model in Nigeria's medical industry to enhance diagnostic speed and reduce medical errors in
healthcare settings. Keywords: Lassa Fever, Predictive Model, Machine Learning, Support
Vector Machines (SVM), and Healthcare Diagnostics</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>As more and more activities are required in the new era market, the personalised marketing activities have been extended step-by-step. abstract: <jats:p>Plasma-based flow control has emerged as a promising approach for suppressing wake instabilities and reducing aerodynamic drag in bluff-body flows; however, its effectiveness depends on complex nonlinear interactions between actuation parameters and vortex dynamics. In this study, a surrogate-assisted evolutionary reinforcement learning (SA-ERL) framework is used to optimize duty-cycled plasma actuation over a square cylinder at Reynolds number Re=200. The control space consists of duty-cycle frequency f, duty-cycle ratio τ, and phase difference ϕ between symmetric trailing-edge actuators, forming a coupled, three-dimensional, multi-objective optimization problem. A hybrid Gaussian process-Transformer (GP-Transformer) surrogate is trained on computational fluid dynamics samples and refined through uncertainty-guided active learning, coupled with an evolutionary reinforcement learning (ERL) optimizer that combines a genetic algorithm (GA) for global search and proximal policy optimization for local refinement. The surrogate achieves high predictive accuracy, while the ERL optimizer outperforms standalone GA and deep reinforcement learning by converging to a higher and more stable terminal reward. Compared with the baseline, the optimized actuation (f=20 Hz, τ=0.9, ϕ=0) achieves about 52% reduction in mean drag and 97% suppression of lift oscillations, while reducing normalized actuation power nearly 10% relative to continuous forcing. Flow-field analysis shows the optimized frequency dominates over natural vortex shedding, reducing resonance risk, weakening coherent wake structures, and weakening the recirculation region. These results demonstrate that SA-ERL offers a computationally efficient, interpretable framework for multi-parameter plasma control, extendable to higher Reynolds numbers and three-dimensional flows.</jats:p>

title: Causal Machine Learning for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity: Interpretation, Benchmarking, Validation

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Causal machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach for predicting individualized treatment effects and advancing precision medicine, moving beyond the limitations of conventional one-variable-at-a-time subgroup analyses of randomized trials. A recent benchmarking study by Chen and colleagues evaluated several causal ML learners across two large trials and concluded that current methods do not yet demonstrate reliable performance for clinical application. While such applied methodological investigations are valuable, this conclusion warrants a more nuanced examination. Multiple independent research groups have successfully applied causal ML across respiratory medicine and critical care, identifying clinically meaningful treatment effect heterogeneity that prior subgroup analyses had not resolved, although these applications have methodological limitations and do not yet establish that the detected heterogeneity is robust across internal and external validation. We outline four sequential and iterative dimensions central to credible causal ML analyses: choice of learner, model training with cross-fitting, internal validation using calibration-for-benefit and rank-weighted metrics, and external validation aligned with the original causal question. With careful methodological execution, causal ML holds considerable promise for personalized treatment decisions and warrants continued development; dismissing the field prematurely risks overlooking a powerful tool for personalized treatment decisions.</jats:p>

title: Predicting Building Heating and Cooling Loads Using Hyperparameter Optimization and SHAP Based Explainable Machine Learning

affiliation.name: BATMAN ÜNİVERSİTESİ

abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">This study aimed to predict building heating and cooling loads from geometric and glazing characteristics and to explain the resulting model predictions. The UCI Energy Efficiency dataset was used, comprising 768 building configurations, eight input features, and two continuous targets. First, 14 regression algorithms were compared using test metrics and tenfold cross-validation. The hyperparameters of six algorithms were then optimized using RandomizedSearchCV with fivefold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and R². Histogram Gradient Boosting achieved the lowest test RMSE for both targets in the initial comparison, whereas Gradient Boosting performed best after optimization. For heating load, the optimized model achieved an RMSE of 0.34048, an MAE of 0.24123, a MAPE of 1.14%, and an R² of 0.99889. The corresponding cooling-load values were 0.81253, 0.51096, 1.84%, and 0.99287. SHAP analysis identified relative compactness, surface area, and overall height as the leading contributors to heating predictions, while roof area, surface area, and relative compactness were most prominent for cooling. The results indicate that optimized boosting models can predict thermal loads with low error within the simulated configurations examined. Strong dependence among geometric features requires their SHAP contributions to be interpreted jointly. By combining predictive performance and model explanations within a common evaluation framework, the study provides an application of explainable machine learning to building energy assessment.</jats:p>

title: PATH-63 Comparison of Feature-Based Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Grading Glioma Using Fractional Anisotropy

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fractional anisotropy (FA) has been explored as an imaging biomarker of diffuse glioma grade, but the relative performance of interpretable machine learning and image-based deep learning approaches remain uncertain. As part of a 2025 NeuroHackademy group project, we compared machine learning and deep learning models for FA-based classification of low-grade (WHO grade 2–3) versus high-grade (WHO grade 4) diffuse gliomas using the publicly available UCSF-PDGM dataset, a preoperative MRI resource containing 501 adults with grade II–IV diffuse gliomas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were split into training (80%) and test (20%) cohorts, with class imbalance handled by weighting in both pipelines. The machine learning model was a random forest using tabular imaging features derived from FA, including whole-brain, hemispheric asymmetry, and peritumoral distance-based measures, with and without clinical and molecular variables. The clinical model included age, sex, IDH status, and MGMT methylation status. The deep learning pipeline used FA images directly and employed a 10-layer residual neural network trained for 30 epochs with a learning rate of 0.0001.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The imaging-only machine learning model achieved test AUC 0.873 and 84% accuracy, with sensitivity 0.951, specificity 0.750, positive predictive value 0.939, and negative predictive value 0.789. The corresponding confusion matrix included 77 true positives and 15 true negatives. Adding clinical and molecular variables improved discrimination, with AUC increasing to approximately 0.94. Feature analysis showed that molecular variables accounted for 53.9% of total importance; the age-IDH interaction (13.6%) and IDH wildtype status (11.9%) were among the strongest predictors. In contrast, the deep learning model achieved 74.0% test accuracy, 84.5% sensitivity, and 30.0% specificity, with findings suggesting overfitting on training data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cohort, FA-based classification was more robust with interpretable tabular machine learning than with image-based deep learning. Performance improved further when clinical and molecular features were incorporated, supporting multimodal and explainable approaches for preoperative glioma grading.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-Based Spacecraft Health Monitoring System: A Machine Learning Approach for Telemetry-Based Health Classification

affiliation.name: Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Gaya College of Engineering, Bihar Engineering University, Gaya, Bihar, India.

abstract: <jats:p>Spacecraft continuously generate telemetry data from onboard sensors and subsystems to support monitoring of health, performance, and operational status. Manual observation of large volumes of telemetry can be difficult and may delay recognition of abnormal conditions. This paper presents an AI-Based Spacecraft Health Monitoring System developed during a research internship at Acceleron Aerospace. The proposed prototype combines ESP8266-based sensor acquisition, synthetic telemetry generation, Python-based data processing, a Random Forest machine learning classifier, and an interactive Streamlit dashboard. The dataset contains temperature, humidity, light, three-axis acceleration, and three-axis gyroscope measurements, with spacecraft health classified into HEALTHY, WARNING, and CRITICAL states. A balanced synthetic dataset of 3,000 samples was generated and divided into training and testing subsets. The trained model was integrated into the monitoring application to provide rapid health classification and graphical telemetry visualization. The work demonstrates a modular foundation for AI-assisted spacecraft monitoring and can be extended toward real telemetry, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, and intelligent alerting.</jats:p>

title: Anti-AI Infringement Methods for Image Data: A Machine Learning Lifecycle Perspective

affiliation.name: School of Computer and Electronic Information, Nanjing Normal University

abstract: <jats:p>The rapid development of the diffusion model has promoted the wide application of AI-generated images, and also brought serious copyright issues. For this reason, the anti-AI infringement methods in the image field came into being. However, the existing research involves multiple technical paths such as data poisoning, adversarial perturbation, machine unlearning, content detection, but lacks a unified classification framework. Starting from the lifecycle of machine learning, this paper constructs a five-level classification system covering data-level, input-level, model-level, output-level and system-level, systematically combs the mainstream methods and their technical characteristics, and summarizes the commonly used evaluation datasets and performance indicators. On this basis, the challenges of current methods in terms of robustness, transferability and engineering deployment are analyzed. This review aims to provide a structured reference for image copyright protection research. By mapping each anti-infringement strategy to a specific phase of the AI lifecycle, the proposed framework clarifies the logical relationships among different approaches and facilitates cross-method comparison and practical selection.</jats:p>

title: Spatial–temporal machine learning for traffic violation type prediction: a case study in Qatar
abstract: <jats:p>Although traffic violations are among the most significant factors contributing to road accidents, little research has focused on predicting specific types of traffic violations in Qatar and the Gulf region, where the number of vehicles has increased significantly in recent years. This work addresses this gap by proposing a machine-learning framework to solve fine-grained, multi-class prediction of traffic violation types on a large-scale dataset from Qatar. The dataset is extremely imbalanced and has a high-dimensional categorical space, with 97 original violation classes. We created a preprocessing pipeline to address these issues by filtering the 97 original codes to nine well-represented violation types while retaining 99.6% of the records. The final model uses 18 spatiotemporal features, including our zone violation entropy measure, which captures violation diversity in each enforcement zone. Five classifiers are evaluated with a strict temporal train–validation–test split, training-based encoding (to avoid temporal leakage), and balanced class weighting. Random forest's macro F1 score is 0.6184 and balanced accuracy is 0.7064, outperforming the linear and neural baselines. SHAP analysis shows that location-derived features account for ~74% of the model's predictive importance, while temporal features account for ~25%. The results indicate that violation type is more strongly associated with location than with time, and they provide implications for targeted enforcement by location. The suggested framework provides a reproducible way to predict violation types in a multi-class setting. It shows that enforcement information alone can support predictive analysis without using road topology or sensor data.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>This study evaluated whether a compact electronic nose could distinguish intact tomatoes treated with wood vinegar or neem oil from those without experimental biopesticide application. The dataset comprised 38 tomatoes and 228 technical runs, including six additional controls measured in triplicate initially and after 16 h: three untreated and three water-sprayed. Six commercial SnO2 sensors recorded voltages during a 180 s cycle. Six classifiers were compared using identical tomato-wise nested cross-validation with three outer folds, two inner folds, and five repetitions. With 54 full-cycle features, linear discriminant analysis (LDA) achieved 97.02% accuracy and 95.72% balanced accuracy; an artificial neural network (ANN) achieved 96.93% and 95.14%, respectively. Paired conditional intervals did not establish superiority of either model. Models trained on the original 32 fruits produced false biopesticide alarms in the new controls, including 17/36 ANN predictions. Incorporating eligible control fruit into training improved matched held-out performance, mainly under the new negative conditions. The separate two-treatment task included 32 fruits. These findings support exploratory recognition of patterns associated with application and show the value of procedural controls. Small control groups, unlogged chamber conditions, and missing chemical reference measurements limit chemical attribution and external screening claims.</jats:p>

affiliation.name: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Visakha Institute of Engineering & Technology (Autonomous), Visakhapatnam, affiliated with Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University, Gurajada, Vizianagaram, Andhra Pradesh, India.

abstract: <jats:p>Encrypted traffic classification is a key problem in network security because encryption and anonymity technologies limit access to packet contents used for monitoring and intrusion detection. This study compares six machine-learning and deep-learning models for classifying Layer 2 darknet traffic, distinguishing among Freenet, I2P, Tor, VPN, and ZeroNet traffic using the SafeSurf dataset. After removing duplicate records and observations with missing or infinite values, the final dataset comprised 75,201 flows described by 79 flow-level features, including port and protocol fields. Random Forest, XGBoost, Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and CNN-LSTM models were evaluated using identical stratified training, validation, and test partitions. Source and destination IP addresses and timestamps were excluded to avoid potential collection-specific information leakage. XGBoost achieved the highest test accuracy (94.78%), macro-F1 (0.9440), and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC; 0.9308), followed by Random Forest (93.50% accuracy, 0.9299 macro-F1, and 0.9136 MCC). MLP achieved 87.74% accuracy, followed by CNN-LSTM (84.84%), CNN (79.16%), and LSTM (77.13%). I2P and Tor were frequently confused, whereas tree-based models classified minority-class VPN traffic effectively. Removing the port fields lowered tree-model accuracy by 1.3 to 1.61 points without changing their ranking. McNemar’s tests on paired test-set predictions showed significant differences (all p < 0.001) for XGBoost versus Random Forest, XGBoost versus MLP, XGBoost versus CNN-LSTM, and MLP versus CNN-LSTM. These findings demonstrate the potential of flow-level features for five-class darknet technology classification, identify persistent classification challenges, and provide a baseline for evaluating generalisation to independent network environments.</jats:p>

abstract:

                    Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit extreme compute and memory demands, necessitating large-scale multi-chiplet systems to achieve high-performance and scalability. In such systems, frequent off-chip memory accesses for model parameters and intermediate activation exchanges induce substantial data movement between compute and storage chiplets, making inter-chiplet communication a critical performance and energy bottleneck. Silicon photonic (SiPh) Networks-on-Interposers (NoIs) offer high bandwidth and low latency communication, making them an attractive choice for the inter-chiplet communication backbone. However, conventional SiPh NoI designs require long-range multi-hop data exchanges, resulting in degraded performance and energy efficiency, and poor scalability. In this work, we present PHONON, a novel Silicon-
                    <jats:underline>Pho</jats:underline>
                    tonic
                    <jats:underline>N</jats:underline>
                    etwork-
                    <jats:underline>o</jats:underline>
                    n-I
                    <jats:underline>n</jats:underline>
                    terposer architecture, that jointly optimizes compute–compute and compute–storage inter-chiplet communication. PHONON employs structured waveguide placement, cluster-level connectivity to storage chiplets, and optimized mapping of compute kernels to chiplets. PHONON optimizes waveguide crossings and reduces waveguide propagation losses, insertion losses, and memory-access contention. Simulation results show that PHONON reduces NoI latency and energy consumption by up to 9.4× and 28.4×, respectively, compared to state-of-the-art SiPh NoI architectures, enabling scalable, high-performance, and energy-efficient LLM acceleration. title: Nanoscale Quantum‐State Mapping in the Scanning Electron Microscope Using Secondary Electron Energy Spectroscopy

affiliation.name: Department of Physics Politecnico di Milano  Milano Italy

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum technologies built on engineered nanostructures require their electronic states characterized at the scale on which they are made, which photoemission cannot reach. Secondary electron energy spectroscopy in a scanning electron microscope captures valence‐band density of states (DOS) information by subtracting two peak‐normalized spectra taken at 0.5 and 1 keV and differentiating the residual. This paper proposes a mechanism: interfacial Auger recombination at the boundary between the beam‐induced contamination layer and the specimen. Electrons injected by the primary beam occupy interface defect states as transient traps, in a steady state where the injected current balances recombination. A trapped electron drops into a metal valence‐band hole and transfers the released energy to an electron at the Fermi level, which escapes into vacuum. Only one valence electron takes part, and the trapped population has a sharp lower edge, so the emitted spectrum is a cumulative integral of the density of states and differentiation directly yields the valence‐band DOS distribution. The predicted one‐to‐one mapping between binding energy and secondary electron energy is confirmed across six elemental solids, with a fitted slope of 0.99 ± 0.02. The model presents the conditions a specimen must meet, each of which could be engineered.</jats:p>

title: RADT-50 FIRST STRIKE: Phase 1 trial of Neoadjuvant Radiotherapy in newly diagnosed High Grade Gliomas

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neoadjuvant radiotherapy (NART) in high-grade gliomas (HGG) holds potential to improve outcomes by capitalizing on pre-surgical tumor oxygenation for greater radiosensitivity, enabling precise target delineation before operative distortion of anatomy, and allowing treatment to begin during protracted surgical waiting periods. Pre-surgical radiation may additionally debulk tumor, facilitating resection and yielding more favorable pathological findings. To our knowledge, this represents the first clinical study of NART in HGG — a single-institute phase 1 trial.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aim</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the safety and feasibility of NART in newly diagnosed HGG.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methodology</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ten patients were enrolled for this pilot MD thesis study. Patient selection was based on Multiparametric CEMRI Brain review by a multidisciplinary tumor board comprising a Radiation Oncologist, Neuro-radiologist, and Neurosurgeon. NART was delivered to the primary lesion at 45 Gy in 15 fractions over 3 weeks, with concurrent Temozolomide (TMZ) at 75mg/m2. Following a 4-6 week interval, patients underwent Maximum Safe Resection. Adjuvant Temozolomide at 150-200 mg/m2 for 6-12 months was initiated 4 weeks post-surgery. The primary endpoint is Safety and Feasibility of NART in HGG. Secondary endpoints include surgical ease, Quality of Life (QoL), overall treatment time, radiation dosimetry, and progression-free and overall survival. Patients are followed up clinically, radiologically, and for QoL using EORTC QLQ-C30 and BN-20. Neurosurgeons are interviewed post-operatively via a self-designed questionnaire.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is an ongoing study#. All 10 patients completed NART without significant complications. abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (CIT) during concurrent temozolomide/radiotherapy (TMZ/RT) for high-grade glioma (HGG) can necessitate dose reductions, treatment delays, or discontinuation of treatment. Thrombocytopenia was noted in 15-20% underscoring the increasing burden of CIT during TMZ/RT treatment. Papaya leaf extract (PLE) has been reported to support the platelet counts, but clinical data of its use in TMZ/RT treatment are limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a single-institution retrospective cohort study of adults with HGG receiving concomitant TMZ/RT. PLE was recommended after noting its benefit. The cohorts were defined by electronic health record (EHR)–documented oral PLE use. Patients treated for HGG between 2016-2025 were screened; only patients with platelet counts on weeks 4-6 after TMZ/RT treatment were included. Platelet counts were categorized by degree of thrombocytopenia: absent (&gt;150 K/µL), mild (100 to &lt; 150), moderate (50 to &lt; 100), or severe (&lt;50). Weekly assessments were pooled across weeks 4-6 and compared between cohorts using two-sided Fisher’s exact tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sixty-two patients were evaluable (39 PLE-compliant; 23 non-PLE). Across pooled week 4-6 assessments, severe thrombocytopenia occurred in 0 PLE vs 8 non-PLE assessments (Fisher p = 0.000283). Moderate thrombocytopenia was numerically less frequent in the PLE compliant group (2 vs 5 assessments; Fisher p = 0.0952). Mild thrombocytopenia did not differ in the control vs PLE compliant groups (10 vs 4 assessments; Fisher p = 1.00). TMZ was held for a decrease in the platelet counts &lt;100 K/µL during RT, and TMZ holds occurred in 2 of 33 (6.1%) PLE vs 5 of 20 (25.0%) non-PLE patients. There were no reported adverse events associated with PLE.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this real-world retrospective cohort of HGG patients receiving concurrent TMZ/RT, PLE use was associated with no severe thrombocytopenia across pooled weeks 4-6 assessments and fewer required TMZ holds. Moderate thrombocytopenia trended lower and mild thrombocytopenia was unchanged, suggesting specificity of PLE for higher-grade CIT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:p>I define topological twists of supersymmetric field theories in the case when the supercharges involved obey an “open” algebra. Using the Batalin-Vilkovisky field-antifield formalism, I construct twisted theories algorithmically from the supersymmetry data, and explain supersymmetric localisation in terms of anticanonical transformations. I also treat equivariant topological twists and explain how BV observables contain the equivariant cohomology of the space of histories. Some results are generalised to theories with two topological supercharges — such as the “balanced” topological field theories of Dijkgraaf and Moore — using the geometry of “differential gorms” of Kochan and Ševera. Finally, I exhibit examples of these constructions, including a U(1)-equivariant topological B-model.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>
                    A
                    <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                  </jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Collisions of ultra-relativistic bubbles during cosmological phase transitions can produce particles much heavier than the transition scale. Previous analyses modelled this process as the off-shell decay of the scalar background. We show that its results parametrically overestimate hard particle production and depend on the gauge choice and the coordinate choice in field space. We propose an alternative formalism, analogous to the partonic description of high-energy collisions. In the ultra-relativistic limit, the colliding bubbles undergo nearly free passage and hard production arises from on-shell scatterings among the quanta constituting the Lorentz-contracted walls. We apply this approach to heavy scalar, fermion, and vector particle production, and study the implications for dark matter, leptogenesis, graviton production and primordial gravitational waves.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Increasing shares of variable renewable electricity (VRE) are creating more frequent periods of surplus electricity, increasing the need for flexible options that can absorb and use this excess generation. One option is to convert surplus electricity into heat, but its effective use requires storage when heat production and demand do not coincide. Because heat demand remains concentrated in the colder months, long-duration seasonal thermal storage is needed to bridge this temporal gap. High-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage (HT-ATES) is one technology capable of providing this seasonal storage function. This study develops a demand-oriented operational probability of success (PoS) framework for evaluating whether HT-ATES can convert historically observed surplus electricity into useful seasonal heat. The Neubrandenburg system in Germany was used as a physically grounded reference case. Historical German electricity data from 2015 to 2022 were represented through empirical four-week surplus distributions and coupled to a chronological Monte Carlo inventory model accounting for charging availability, well thermal throughput, adopted storage limit, and thermal recovery. The model first generated a distribution of achievable seasonal heat delivery, which was then evaluated against alternative heat-demand targets. PoS is therefore expressed as the probability that delivered heat meets or exceeds a specified thermal requirement, rather than as a fixed property of the aquifer. For the base configuration, with a thermal power of approximately 3.72 MW, an adopted storage limit of 12 GWh, and a recovery factor of 0.72, the 20,000 retained Monte Carlo cycles produced a mean seasonal delivery of 8.551 GWh. The upper modeled heat delivery of 8.640 GWh was reached in 94.63% of the cycles. Constraint diagnostics showed that well throughput was the unique limiting condition in 57.06% of injection decisions, remaining storage space in 28.82%, and zero-surplus charging windows in 10.90%, while positive-surplus magnitude alone did not limit any base-case injection decision. Sensitivity analyses further showed that increasing thermal power shifts the range of heat-demand targets that can be met with high probability, but the benefit diminishes as the modeled upper delivery limit is approached. Equivalent non-interacting doublet configurations exhibit the same throughput-storage-limit trade-off. The results demonstrate that nominal storage capacity alone is insufficient for assessing HT-ATES performance. Operational success depends jointly on charging opportunities, thermal power, storage capacity, thermal recovery, system configuration, and the thermal target used to define success. The proposed framework provides a transferable screening method for linking historical energy-system variability with subsurface storage constraints and explicit heat-delivery requirements.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The remarkable performance of fused‐ring electron acceptors (FREAs) in organic solar cells , along with their strong optical absorption and long‐lived excited states has stimulated high interest in the fundamental nature of photoexcited states in these materials. Whilst the excited‐state properties should be expressed via the materials’ spectroscopic response, it can be difficult to disentangle the different excited‐state parameters reliably by fitting models to spectra. In this work, we present a Bayesian inference framework to extract key excited‐state parameters, such as transition energies, reorganization energies, and vibrational couplings, from temperature‐dependent photoluminescence (PL) spectra and time‐resolved emission. We apply this approach to study different families of FREAs in different conditions (different solid‐state deposition conditions and in dilute solution). We find that Y‐series FREAs combine exceptionally low high‐frequency reorganization energies with pronounced energetic broadening, consistent with excited‐state delocalization driven by their rigid backbones and close intermolecular interactions. More broadly, the Bayesian workflow offers a reliable tool for linking molecular structure and processing conditions to excited‐state parameters, enabling rational design of new molecular optoelectronic materials.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant pediatric brain tumour that represents a leading cause of cancer-related mortality and long-term morbidity. It is a highly heterogeneous disease comprised of entities defined by distinct (epi)genomic, transcriptomic, demographic and clinical features. MYC amplified MB represents the most aggressive subtype that accounts for a majority of treatment failures despite intensive therapeutic regiments consisting of surgical resection, craniospinal irradiation and chemotherapy. Despite the vast genomic MB data that has been generated in recent years, it has not translated into biologically driven early phase clinical trials for this group. To address this urgent therapeutic need, we leveraged novel patient-derived spheroid models to identify vulnerable pathways via chemogenomic approaches. Using genome wide CRISPR/Cas9 essentiality screens, we identify homologous recombination and R-loop resolution as critical dependencies, which are highly enriched across multiple non-overlapping patient cohorts. To translate these genetic dependencies into potential therapeutic vulnerabilities, we performed a high-throughput drug screen which identified potent agents inhibiting enzymes involved in these pathways, namely TOP1 (topotecan) and PARP1 (talazoparib). Using genome wide Crispr-Cas9 screening with a sublethal dose of topotecan, we demonstrate significant genetic and pharmacological synergy between TOP1 and PARP1 inhibitors, that we show results in the persistence of R-loop structures and subsequent DNA damage. We leveraged isogenic MYC MB models to show that this vulnerability is generated exclusively through MYC dysregulation, likely representing transcriptional amplification generated DNA torsional stress. Lastly, we demonstrate striking clinical benefit of topotecan and AZD9574, a novel blood-brain-barrier permeable PARP1 selective inhibitor, across multiple patient-derived orthotopic models suggesting this combination should be prioritized for further clinical investigation. Together, these findings define MYC-driven transcriptional stress as a therapeutically exploitable liability in medulloblastoma and establish a mechanistically grounded combination strategy for clinical translation in this otherwise intractable disease.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: The objective of this study was to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, weight loss response, safety and preliminary clinical outcomes of a pragmatic 8-week food-based very-low-energy intervention in adults with obesity. Methods: In this prospective, single-arm study, 10 adults eligible for very-low-energy diet (VLED) therapy completed an 8-week food-based intervention targeting approximately 800 kcal/day with an accepted intake range up to 1000 kcal/day. Participants planned, purchased and prepared all foods, supported by dietary self-monitoring and fortnightly dietitian consultations. The primary feasibility outcomes were acceptability and weight loss response. The secondary outcomes included recruitment, retention and engagement. The exploratory outcomes included anthropometric measures, blood pressure, nutritional and biochemical markers, dietary quality, nutritional adequacy and adverse events. Results: All participants completed the intervention. Nine of 10 (90%) Food Acceptability Questionnaire (FAQ) scores met their prespecified item-level acceptability thresholds, while 90% (95%CI 55.5 to 99.7%) of participants achieved ≥5% weight loss. Mean weight loss was 10.8%. Attendance at study visits was 100% (95% CI 69.2 to 100%). Participants completed 93 ± 13% of expected food diary days with mean daily energy intakes of 842 ± 70 kcal/day. Statistically significant improvements were observed in anthropometric measures, blood pressure, total and LDL cholesterol and dietary quality. No clinically concerning changes in micronutrient or safety parameters were observed. Adverse events were predominantly mild to moderate. Conclusions: This pragmatic 8-week food-based very-low-energy intervention demonstrated encouraging feasibility outcomes, although challenges associated with eating out warrant further attention. Further evaluation in larger controlled trials is needed to assess its comparative effectiveness relative to traditional meal replacement VLEDs and longer-term outcomes.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Dual-energy X-ray transmission sorting of copper ores is often constrained by strong coupling between conventional features and particle thickness. To address this, we propose two decoupled features: R3, an improved R-value feature, and Zeff from basis material decomposition, which are designed to mitigate thickness interference and improve high-Z mineral identification. Copper and lead–zinc ore particles from the Yinshan Mine (Dexing, China), with particle thickness ranges of 8–60 mm for the copper ore and 8–25 mm for the lead–zinc ore, were tested on a laboratory DE-XRT sorter. A support vector machine regression model was trained on 314 phyllite copper ore particles (8–60 mm) to predict a weighted comprehensive grade (Cu+Fe+S), using R-value, R3, Zeff, and w3–w2 as inputs. The method showed favorable performance for porphyry copper ores (particle thickness: 8–60 mm): feed grades of 0.068%–0.109% Cu were upgraded to concentrates of 0.127%–0.244% Cu, with waste grades of 0.030%–0.051% and recoveries of 61.69%–79.67%. For phyllite copper ores (particle thickness: 8–60 mm), enrichment was observed through yield adjustment, with recoveries of 33.38%–71.69%. A plausible reason for the poor performance of the intermediate-grade Cu phyllite ore (Cu: 0.098%) is a combination of two factors: the chalcopyrite grain size (~0.1 mm) being below the detector resolution (0.8 mm), which causes mineral signals to be swamped by gangue, and the fundamental limitation of dual-energy XRT in distinguishing Cu from Fe. For lead–zinc ore (4.744% Pb+Zn feed), the sorter rejected 21.99% as waste while achieving 98.87% Pb+Zn recovery, with only 0.245% Pb+Zn in the waste. These results indicate that the proposed multi-feature fusion and SVM regression strategy provides a feasible approach for the preconcentration of low-grade copper ores and waste rejection for lead–zinc ores.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Efficiently harvesting thermal energy from human skin poses formidable challenges owing to its high‐entropy characteristics. While Seebeck‐effect wearable thermoelectric devices can convert skin heat flux into electrical voltage, prevailing generators remain constrained in delivering sustainable energy and multifunctionality. This limitation stems from a fundamental trade‐off where the output voltage falls below the effective charging threshold, leaving the ultra‐low skin heat flux underexplored for physiological sensing. In this study, we report a skin‐interfaced wearable thermoelectric sensor and generator that synchronously harvests body high‐entropy energy and monitors deep tissue temperature (< 0.2°C). This dual functionality is enabled by a thermal meta‐design that guides inherently dispersed cutaneous heat flux into a vertical, one‐dimensional path through geometric confinement, ensuring signal fidelity for both sensing and energy conversion. To overcome the limited skin‐ambient temperature gradient, we introduce a reusable cooling hydrogel patch based on a dual‐mode evaporation mechanism, boosting the electrical output to 120 mV and power density to 45.7 μW cm
                    <jats:sup>–2</jats:sup>
                    . Furthermore, during daily wear under an approximate 10 K skin‐environment temperature differential, the system achieved a sustained output of up to 34 mV. The integrated voltage boost‐storage circuit maintained the capacitor voltage at around 1.044 V, facilitating a sustainable power supply to electronic loads, and stabilized at approximately 5.2 V near full charge. The integrated system demonstrates continuous, multi‐parameter health monitoring powered solely by body heat. This research establishes a co‐design paradigm for concurrent deep body temperature monitoring and high‐entropy energy recovery, paving the way for self‐powered, multimodal integrated wearable devices.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Surgical resection of glioblastoma is never radical, and residual tumor cells remain untreated for several weeks within a post-surgical microenvironment that may impact treatment outcome. This untreated interval represents a critical opportunity to challenge the current treatment paradigm to achieve better outcomes. Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields), a non-invasive therapy with proven efficacy in the adjuvant setting, may offer an opportunity to target tumor cells earlier in the disease course. The PORTRAIT study investigates whether TTFields therapy can be administered preoperatively, followed by postoperative TTFields prior to radiotherapy. PORTRAIT is a safety and feasibility study that provides a unique opportunity to examine treatment-induced changes in the newly diagnosed setting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PORTRAIT is a prospective phase I cohort study (NCT06136611) enrolling 14 patients. Patients receive TTFields therapy in addition to standard-of-care. Serial MRI, blood, tear fluid, and tumor tissue are collected at five predefined timepoints. The primary endpoint is safety and feasibility; secondary endpoints include imaging biomarkers and molecular/translational changes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As of February 2026, 9 patients have been recruited. TTFields delivery in the preoperative and postoperative windows was feasible without delaying surgery, with high device usage being observed. Preoperative treatment duration ranged from 7 to 30 days (median = 15 days), with median device usage of 86%. Postoperative treatment duration ranged from 11 to 26 days (median = 19 days), with median usage of 83%. The usage calculation included days when patients underwent MRI and CT scans and were unable to wear the device. Comprehensive longitudinal data acquisition, including advanced MRI, liquid biopsies, and tissue sampling, was successfully achieved across all study time-points.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early findings support the feasibility of delivering TTFields therapy prior to surgery and radiotherapy, enabling initiation of oncological treatment from diagnosis. This approach provides unique access to treatment-exposed tumor biology in newly diagnosed glioblastoma. Ongoing analyses will determine the full safety profile and deliver unique scientific insights into TTFields treatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Gliomas are common adult brain tumours with diverse histologic and molecular subtypes, yet their management remains controversial. While radiotherapy (RT) remains standard treatment, adjuvant therapy with alkylating agents has shown promise. This GRADE-assessed, PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted using MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and SNO/ASCO proceedings (1986–2025). RCTs and observational studies reporting overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and grade ≥3 adverse events were included. Two independent researchers extracted data and pooled hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals for OS and PFS using the inverse-variance method. Subgroup analyses included tumour grade, chemotherapy type, and molecular markers (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT). Heterogeneity was assessed using I² and Cochran’s Q test, while sensitivity, trial sequential, and GRADE certainty analyses were also performed. Of 4,663 records identified, 25 RCTs and 8 cohort studies were included, with 3,740 patients reporting 1-year PFS data. Overall survival significantly improved with chemoradiotherapy compared to RT alone (RR 1.108, 95% CI) despite marked heterogeneity (I²=71.3%) and low GRADE certainty. No significant PFS benefit was observed (RR 1.151, 95% CI; I²=73.2%), and chemotherapy significantly increased grade ≥3 hematologic toxicities. TMZ-based regimens demonstrated significant OS benefit, whereas PCV did not, with greater effect in grade 4 gliomas. Sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness of OS findings, while trial sequential analysis suggested a trend toward improved survival despite insufficient information size. RoB2 assessment showed overall low risk among RCTs, while cohort studies were of good quality on NOS assessment. Chemotherapy with alkylating agents alongside RT improves overall survival but not PFS and is associated with increased toxicity. Despite encouraging trends, larger future trials are needed.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Neutral selective bond dissociation under low-energy electron irradiation is difficult to predict because the molecular states accessed by electron–molecule collisions do not, by themselves, reveal which chemical bond is locally activated. Here, we establish a natural bond orbital (NBO)-resolved antibonding-channel framework that connects electron-impact excitation to bond-specific neutral dissociation. Using 1-bromo-4-chlorobenzene as a model system containing competing C–Br and C–Cl cleavage pathways, we calculate state-resolved electron-impact excitation cross-sections with Quantemol-EC to quantify the accessibility of molecular excited states. Dissociative electron attachment analysis, incorporating bond dissociation energies, fragment electron affinities, and dissociative vibrational frequencies, predicts preferential C–Br cleavage in agreement with experimental trends. In contrast, potential energy curve-based neutral dissociation analysis along bond elongation coordinates shows configuration-dependent selectivity and does not directly identify the localized antibonding character responsible for bond weakening. We therefore project the same electron-impact-accessible excited states onto localized σ*(C–Br) and σ*(C–Cl) NBO channels. The resulting bond-resolved antibonding weights distinguish scattering accessibility from localized dissociation propensity, thereby revealing how an electronically accessed state is translated into selective neutral bond cleavage. Because the present postprocessing uses phase-insensitive excitation cross-sections rather than phase-resolved channel amplitudes, we adopt a diagonal-ensemble approximation in which no fixed relative-phase correlation is retained between distinct MO-pair channels; the channels are therefore combined incoherently at the probability level. This integrated DEA, PEC, and NBO analysis provides a chemically resolved framework for predicting electron-induced bond selectivity and identifies localized antibonding channels as the missing link between electron–molecule collision physics and neutral chemical reactivity.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this paper, using the original laboratory software and hardware systems, we investigate the structurally determined patterns of fracture stages in titanium alloy Ti‐6Al‐4V under consecutively applied short laser pulses (shock wave) and fatigue loads with the aim to predict the lifetime of advanced aircraft engine materials. It is shown that laser surface treatment followed by the grinding operation providing the desired roughness quality is a promising tool for increasing the fatigue resources of aircraft engine materials. Spatial structural scales associated with different stages of damage‐failure transition are determined by analyzing the roughness correlation and evaluating the power (Hurst) exponent and the corresponding structural lengths of characteristic fracture surfaces. These lengths and power exponents are incorporated into the constitutive laws as structure‐sensitive parameters that characterize different stages of the damage‐failure transition, which involve the initiation and growth of small cracks as well as the Paris crack propagation.</jats:p>
