abstract: <jats:p>Sinonasal malignancies are rare, biologically heterogeneous tumours arising in a confined anatomical space bounded by the orbit, skull base and brain. This combination of rarity, histological heterogeneity and anatomical constraint influences treatment selection and limits the evidence available to guide it. Radiotherapy is central to management in both the postoperative and definitive settings, and intensity-modulated radiotherapy is now the photon standard, with proton and carbon-ion therapy available in a small number of centres. This review appraises the evidence underlying current practice. Pooled outcome data derived from mixed-histology institutional series are difficult to interpret; definitive radiotherapy cohorts are subject to confounding by treatment allocation; the clinical evidence supporting particle therapy is weaker than the dosimetric evidence; and the evidence base for elective nodal irradiation is inadequate. The review identifies where the evidence supports firm recommendations and where it does not. Because most patients with these tumours are treated in settings without particle therapy, routine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or daily volumetric image guidance, it also describes resource-adapted alternatives and their limitations.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Standard of care (SoC) treatment for patients with IDH1-mutant astrocytoma typically includes maximal safe resection followed by RT/CRT and adjuvant TMZ. However, patients almost inevitably experience disease progression (PD) and salvage therapies provide inadequate benefit. Following SoC treatment, patients with high-risk IDH1-mutant astrocytoma tend to experience PD earlier than those without high-risk features. There is a clear unmet need for targeted treatments in IDH1-mutant astrocytoma that can delay PD after SoC, particularly in patients with high-grade disease or high-risk features. Safusidenib is an investigational oral mutant-IDH1 inhibitor with high potency, selectivity, and blood-brain barrier permeability. Safusidenib demonstrated antitumor activity and a favorable risk-benefit profile in Phase 1 (NCT03030066) and Phase 2 (NCT04458272) studies in patients with IDH1-mutant glioma, supporting its further development. In the Phase 1 study, safusidenib achieved durable responses in some patients with IDH1-mutant glioma across all grades and risk groups, including those with high-grade disease or tumor contrast enhancement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SIGMA is an ongoing Phase 3, randomized, double-blind study (NCT05303519) evaluating maintenance safusidenib vs placebo in adults with histologically confirmed IDH1-mutant astrocytoma with high-grade or high-risk features, per investigator (INV) assessment according to WHO CNS 2021 criteria. Patients must have received prior RT/CRT and 6–12 cycles of adjuvant TMZ, with no evidence of PD since the start of RT. Approximately 300 patients will be randomized 1:1 (within 75 days of adjuvant TMZ) to receive safusidenib 250 mg twice daily or placebo in 28-day continuous cycles as maintenance treatment, until PD or discontinuation. The primary endpoint is progression-free survival (PFS) by blinded independent central review (BICR) per RANO 2.0. Secondary endpoints include INV-assessed PFS, BICR- and INV-assessed objective response rate, duration of response, time to response, overall survival, safety, seizure activity, and health-related quality of life. The first participant was enrolled in October 2025.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Fast, stable, and low-cost solid electrolytes are essential for advancing all-solid-state sodium batteries. Here, we present a fast solid-state sodium ion conductor, which reaches an ionic conductivity of σ(Na+) = 2.8 × 10−3 S cm−1 at 60 °C with an activation energy of Ea = 0.393 eV, made by high-energy mechanochemical treatment of disodium dodecahydrido-closo-dodecaborate, Na2B12H12. The milling process facilitates a transition to the high-temperature dynamically disordered β-polymorph while also providing high stability toward thermal cycling in the range RT to 300 °C. The ionic and cationic transport numbers are both close to unity, and the electrolyte enables stable Na stripping/plating for over 100 cycles at 0.1 mA cm−2 and a critical current density of 0.55 mA cm−2. The onset of electrochemical decomposition of Na2B12H12 is found to be 3.7 V vs. Na+/Na, with the major decomposition at 4.1 V vs. Na+/Na. A Na9Sn4|Na2B12H12|Na3V2(PO4)3 cell is cycled at 0.1C, 0.2C, and 0.4C with a high coulombic efficiency of &gt;99.5% after the first 6 cycles. Long-term cycling shows acolumbic efficiency of &gt;99.5% across 100 cycles after the first five cycles. Therefore, shaker-milled Na2B12H12 stands out as a promising solid electrolyte for sodium battery development.</jats:p>

title: High-Pressure Grinding Rolls in Mineral Comminution Circuits: A Critical Review of Ore Competency, Circuit Integration, Energy Efficiency, Operational Performance, and Techno-Economic Sustainability

affiliation.name: Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG), Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil

container-title: Journal International Review of Research Studies
abstract: <jats:p>High-pressure grinding rolls (HPGR) offer a compression-based alternative or complement to conventional mineral comminution. However, their value depends on ore response and circuit context, not nominal specific energy alone. This critical review examines particle-bed breakage, mineralogical and mechanical applicability, circuit integration, energy normalization, roll wear, downstream liberation, predictive modeling, and techno-economic and environmental trade-offs. The evidence is organized by laboratory, pilot, and industrial scale, with particular attention to differences in feed and product specifications, recirculation, availability, and downstream processing boundaries. The synthesis indicates that improved particle breakage and microcracking do not automatically translate into higher metallurgical recovery, and that equipment-level efficiency cannot establish whole-plant superiority without a common functional basis. The paper proposes a conditional selection framework combining representative ore testing, validated mass–energy balances, downstream response, reliability, and uncertainty analysis. Gaps remain in public industrial datasets, wear-adjusted lifecycle comparisons, and transferability of numerical models across ore types. The review identifies the need for evidence-matched comparisons and explicit validation of source-specific quantitative claims; the methodology reports bibliographic verification status and limitations.</jats:p>

title: Molecular Semiconductor-Doped Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) Composite Dielectric Films for High-Temperature Capacitive Energy Storage
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Polymer dielectric capacitors are key components for high-power electrical energy storage, but their hightemperature performance is often restricted by low intrinsic permittivity, increased conduction loss and reduced breakdown strength. Here, poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) (PMP) was modified with the n-type molecular semiconductor 1,6,7,12-tetrachloro-N,N′-bis(octadecyl)perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic diimide (4Cl-C
                    <jats:sub>18</jats:sub>
                    PDI) through solution casting. The optimized 4Cl-C
                    <jats:sub>18</jats:sub>
                    PDI loading was 0.013 mmol/g. The dopant has a low LUMO level of -3.92 eV and introduces an estimated electron-trap depth of approximately 4.11 eV in PMP. Compared with pristine PMP, the composite film increased the low-frequency dielectric constant from 2.10 to 2.20 while maintaining low dielectric loss. The room-temperature DC breakdown strength increased from 475 MV/m to 512 MV/m, and the temperature at 5% weight loss increased from 367.5°C to 454.5°C. These improvements are attributed to the combined effects of conjugated-molecular polarization, deep-trap-assisted carrier restriction and enhanced thermal resistance. The composite film achieved discharge energy densities of 3.2 J/cm
                    <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                    at room temperature, 1.69 J/cm
                    <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                    at 120°C, and 1.37 J/cm
                    <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                    at 150°C. At 200 MV/m, both PMP and the composite films retained stable energy density and efficiencies above 95% after 10,000 cycles. This work links molecular energylevel design with high-temperature dielectric response. These results demonstrate that molecular-semiconductor doping is an effective all-organic route for improving high-temperature capacitive performance in PMP-based dielectric films.
                  </jats:p>

title: Cumulative Hyperglycemic Exposure and Intraventricular Hemorrhage in Very Preterm Infants
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Introduction: Current definitions of neonatal hyperglycemia rely on isolated glucose measurements and static thresholds, despite the dynamic evolution of glucose homeostasis in very preterm infants. Whether cumulative hyperglycemic exposure during the early postnatal period is associated with intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) remains uncertain. Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort study of very preterm infants (≤32 weeks’ gestation and/or ≤1500 g birth weight). Cumulative hyperglycemic exposure during the first 5 postnatal days was quantified using continuous glucose monitoring and evaluated using both conventional glucose thresholds and developmentally derived gestational age- and postnatal day-specific reference thresholds. The primary outcome was IVH, defined as grade II-III IVH or periventricular hemorrhagic infarction (PVHI). Results: Among 176 infants, 25 (14.2%) developed IVH. Infants with IVH experienced greater cumulative hyperglycemic exposure during the first 5 postnatal days. Cumulative exposure above the gestational age- and postnatal day-specific upper reference interval remained independently associated with IVH after adjustment for relevant clinical factors. Predicted risk increased progressively with increasing hyperglycemic burden, supporting an exposure-response relationship. Conclusions: Cumulative hyperglycemic exposure during the early postnatal period was independently associated with IVH in very preterm infants. Developmentally derived glucose thresholds incorporating gestational age and postnatal age may improve characterization of dysglycemia-related neurological risk.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Li−O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    batteries have attracted extensive attention due to their potential to achieve several times higher energy density than Li‐ion batteries. However, the actual discharge capacity and rate performance still fall short of practical requirements, as cathodes made of dense carbon black particles hinder the fast diffusion of O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    deep into the cathode during discharge, thus severely limiting cathode utilization. In this work, we introduce graphdiyne (GDY) into the cathode to accelerate O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>

                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    molecules to pass through. When incorporated into carbon‐black cathodes, GDY particles forms pathways of low diffusion resistance that facilitate O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>

                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>

                    . abstract: <jats:p>Cluster partitioning of distribution networks with distributed photovoltaic (PV) generation is a prerequisite for effective coordinated control, but the conventional K‐means algorithm is highly sensitive to initial cluster centers and easily disturbed by abnormal data, often converging to local optima. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an improved K‐means algorithm integrating isolation forest (IF), the K‐nearest neighbor (KNN) algorithm, and the whale optimization algorithm (WOA) and applies it to the dynamic cluster partitioning of high‐PV‐penetration distribution networks. The proposed method first removes outliers through a cascade model in which IF performs rapid global screening and KNN conducts fine‐grained local verification. WOA is then applied to optimize the initial cluster centers by minimizing the within‐cluster sum of squares, overcoming the local‐optimum problem caused by random initialization. On this basis, a partitioning framework is established, combining a clustering indicator system (active/reactive regulation capability and sensitivity‐based electrical distance) with an adaptive weighting mechanism driven by clustering‐quality‐oriented optimization. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. First, a two‐stage mechanism coupling cascaded anomaly detection with population‐based initial‐center optimization, which enhances the robustness and accuracy of K‐means. Second, its adaptation to PV‐integrated distribution networks through a dedicated indicator system and adaptive weighting scheme. Simulations on an IEEE 33‐node network show that, compared with genetic algorithm K‐means (GA‐K‐means), particle swarm optimization K‐means (PSO‐K‐means), conventional K‐means, and a fixed partitioning scheme, the proposed method improves voltage regulation capability by about 9.1% and load fluctuation suppression capability by about 65%, strengthening the operational stability of distribution networks under high PV penetration.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Context.</jats:italic>
                    The association of active galactic nuclei (AGN) with high-energy neutrinos has been investigated in both population studies and individual source analyses. However, whether individual associations are driven by physical processes or arise from chance coincidences remains an open question.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Aims.</jats:italic>
                    A sample of blazars, AGN with relativistic jets closely aligned with the line of sight, spatially consistent with IceCube high-energy events, provides a natural framework to address this question. By combining multifrequency observations with physically motivated emission models, it is possible to assess whether these sources can plausibly account for the detected neutrinos.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Methods.</jats:italic>
                    We studied six blazars with single gamma-ray counterparts to well-reconstructed IceCAT-1 high-energy events, accounting for the improved localization expected from IceCAT-2, and compiled their multifrequency spectral energy distributions. We modeled these sources within a lepto-hadronic framework, exploring their parameter space in order to reproduce the observed emission while preferentially selecting solutions that maximize neutrino production.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Results.</jats:italic>
                    We find that the spectral energy distributions can be reproduced with compact emission regions close to the broad-line region with moderately high Doppler factors. The overall emission is generally dominated by leptonic processes with subdominant contributions from hadronic cascades, except for one source where the hadronic components become dominant in gamma-rays. For four of the six sources, the energy density of the relativistic particles is close to equipartition with the magnetic field. The predicted neutrino-detection rates reach up to ∼5 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    per year, in most cases compatible with the observation of one IceCube high-energy event when accounting for Poisson statistics.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Conclusions.</jats:italic>
                    We conclude that, while the sources in the sample are not expected to significantly contribute to the diffuse neutrino flux, their properties are consistent with being possible counterparts to individual neutrino events. This is driven by a significant contribution of external photon fields to the hadronic interaction rate, even for sources where these fields have previously only been considered as nonsignificant.
                  </jats:p>

title: A simple model for evaporation-driven migration of liquid metal between plasma pulses in a fusion reactor with liquid metal plasma-facing components

affiliation.name: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Liquid metal plasma-facing components (PFCs) are being considered for a variety of fusion power plant designs, and careful control of the liquid metal inventory will be essential in these systems to mitigate challenges with liquid metal corrosion and hydrogen fuel retention. Since many power plant designs and existing test facilities rely on pulsed plasma sources, it is critical to understand how liquid metal evaporation leads to material migration within a reactor over the periods of time when no plasma is present. This work addresses this question by developing a simple particle balance model to efficiently calculate liquid metal vapor transport patterns over indefinitely long time periods, using a particle redistribution matrix to capture the vapor transport details. After developing the mathematical model, characteristics of a future Liquid Metal Core-Edge (LMCE) research facility with liquid lithium divertors are used as a reference to demonstrate how the particle balance model can be used. Examples of lithium migration during the cooldown period between plasma pulses show that the pattern of lithium deposition depends primarily on the system geometry. An important secondary effect in these scenarios is the relative cooldown rate of the lithium divertor with respect to other PFCs in the device. Examples are also provided to demonstrate how the particle balance model can be used to optimize the design of a cold finger to collect liquid metal condensation for extraction and reprocessing, with the results showing that a future LMCE facility may be capable of collecting all of the lithium evaporated between plasma pulses if the main chamber walls can be maintained above 350 C during operation.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Reliable identification of standard fetal ultrasound planes underpins prenatal biometry and screening, but manual identification depends on the operator. This study evaluates FetalSANet, a lightweight MobileNetV2 classifier with a 98-parameter spatial-attention module, against channel-attention, dual-attention and no-attention variants on FETAL_PLANES_DB. On the released split (five classes, one seed), spatial attention reached 93.70% accuracy, but its difference from the no-attention baseline was not significant (McNemar p=0.429), and a perceptual-hash audit found near-duplicate images across the training, validation and test partitions, mainly in Fetal Thorax and Maternal Cervix. We therefore re-evaluated the baseline and FetalSANet on a patient-disjoint, deduplicated split (six classes) with three seeds: accuracy was 88.13±0.37% and 88.29±0.79%, with no significant difference in paired tests (not evidence of equivalence). The module adds 9.6 KFLOPs to a 0.60 GFLOP network. In an external-domain evaluation without fine-tuning (two classes, two sources, N=2588), unrestricted five-class accuracy was about 87% (96.64% when restricted to the two present classes), and 11.51% of predictions fell into absent classes; class and data source are confounded. Grad-CAM++ maps are qualitative examples only. Spatial attention is therefore a nearly free but not demonstrably beneficial addition, and released-split accuracy should not be read as patient-level performance.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Synthetic haematocrit (HCT) permits cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) extracellular volume fraction (ECV) estimation without contemporaneous laboratory HCT. We evaluated four published equations in a clinical referral cohort. Methods: This retrospective audit included 67 adults scanned at 1.5 T (n = 34) or 3 T (n = 33), with laboratory HCT within 24 h. Two equations per field strength were assessed using correlation and Bland–Altman analysis with confidence intervals. Observer reproducibility of T1 and calculated synthetic ECV was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Post hoc exploratory analyses examined classification at ECV ≥ 30%, estimation-error associations and proportional bias. Results: Absolute mean ECV bias was below one percentage point for all equations, but model-specific limits of agreement extended from −4.47 to 4.19 percentage points. At the exploratory 30% threshold, classification agreement was 85.3% and 88.2% at 1.5 T and 75.8% for both equations at 3 T. Synthetic ECV intraobserver ICCs ranged from 0.853 to 0.949; interobserver ICCs were 0.936–0.944 at 1.5 T and 0.842–0.851 at 3 T. Shang HCT showed magnitude-dependent disagreement. Conclusions: Synthetic ECV may help assess myocardial tissue when timely laboratory haematocrit is unavailable, with low average differences from conventional ECV. However, the small groups limit precision and generalisability, and individual and observer differences prevent assuming interchangeability. Local validation is needed before using synthetic ECV for clinical decisions or monitoring changes over time.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) has no gold standard. Accuracy studies borrow one of several composite definitions instead, and these definitions do not label the same patients as infected. We asked how often accuracy studies say which definition they used, and how far the choice moves the numbers they report. Methods: In this systematic review, we searched PubMed on 20 October 2026 for primary accuracy studies of PJI tests and classified each abstract by the reference definition it named. Studies that applied two or more definitions (MSIS 2011/2013, ICM 2018, IDSA 2013, EBJIS proposed or 2021) to the same cohort were assessed further, and accuracy was extracted per definition. Ratios of PJI cases and the change in sensitivity of the alpha-defensin test were pooled with random-effects models. Results: Of 1744 accuracy studies, 437 (25%) named a reference definition in the abstract. The share rose from none before 2012 to 35% from 2021 onward. Seventeen studies reported accuracy under more than one definition in the same patients. EBJIS classified 1.47 times as many patients as infected as MSIS (95% CI 1.33–1.62; 6 cohorts; I2 = 4%) and 1.26 times as many as ICM 2018 (1.08–1.46; 6 cohorts; I2 = 58%). The pooled sensitivity of the alpha-defensin test was 85.6% (76.9–91.4) against MSIS and 56.3% (48.6–63.7) against EBJIS in the same three cohorts, while specificity stayed between 89% and 100%. Across 13 test–cohort pairs, the median change in sensitivity when the reference moved to EBJIS was −18.5 percentage points (IQR −29.0 to −4.9); sensitivity fell in 10 pairs and changed by less than 3 points in three. Conclusions: For several PJI tests, the reported sensitivity depends substantially on the reference definition chosen. A definition that labels more patients as infected is not, for that reason, a more accurate one. Accuracy figures obtained under different definitions should not be pooled or compared as if they measured the same thing, and every accuracy study should name its reference definition in the abstract.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: This study evaluates LQ-HybridNet, a parameter-compact classical architecture for skin-lesion classification. Methods: MobileNetV2 is augmented with amplitude–phase channel gating and a four-qubit variational circuit feature transformation. Crucially, all evaluations enforce a rigorous, leakage-resistant stratified lesion-level split to prevent data contamination. Here, quantum-inspired denotes a classical mathematical inductive bias, not quantum hardware execution or computational advantage. Results: On HAM10000, LQ-HybridNet achieved 90.80±0.25% accuracy, 0.7714 macro precision, 0.7257 macro recall, and 0.7428 macro F1-score, compared with 88.50±0.30% accuracy for MobileNetV2. The 2.30 percentage-point gain required 45.9K additional parameters. Across the evaluated backbones, accuracy gains ranged from 1.10 to 2.40 percentage points on HAM10000 and 1.77 to 4.00 points on ISIC 2018. Latency increased from 12.4 to 48.7 ms per batch of 32 images. Conclusions: The structured classical transformations yielded incremental benchmark improvements with small parameter overhead but approximately 3.9-fold higher latency. abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Cancer treatment can impair right ventricular (RV) systolic and diastolic function by altering cardiomyocyte metabolism and inducing cell death. The incidence and prognosis of cancer therapy-induced RV involvement remain uncertain. We assessed RV diastolic changes and their association with systolic RV and LV dysfunction in cancer patients. Methods: We prospectively observed 60 adults (91.7% female, aged 31 to 74 years) with breast or gastrointestinal cancer receiving chemotherapy for a median of 381 days (IQR 187, 464), excluding those with cardiovascular or pulmonary disease. RV diastolic function was assessed using the 2010 right heart echocardiographic guidelines. RV systolic dysfunction was defined by abnormal values in at least two of the following RV indices: fractional area change (RVFAC), systolic tissue Doppler velocity (RVS’), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, or myocardial performance index. LV dysfunction was defined by abnormal LV ejection fraction or average systolic LV tissue Doppler velocity. Results: RV systolic dysfunction was found in 7 patients (11.7%), RV diastolic dysfunction in 12 (30.7%), and LV dysfunction in 11 (18.3%). Generalised estimating equations showed early decreases in RVS’ and RVFAC at the first month (β = −0.68, p = 0.016; β = −2.2, p = 0.006), and later changes in RV early diastolic tissue velocity (RVe′) and the ratio of early RV filling velocity (RVE) to RVe′ (RVE/e′) at the third month (β = −1.03, p = 0.005; β = 0.35, p = 0.034). Higher RVFAC values were linked to lower odds of LV dysfunction (OR 0.88, p = 0.002). RVe′ was associated with RV systolic dysfunction (OR 0.61, p < 0.001), with a threshold of 10 cm/s (AUC 0.81; 95% CI: 0.69, 0.93). Conclusions: Conventional echocardiographic parameters may facilitate the detection of RV systolic and diastolic dysfunction during cancer therapy. Early alterations and the prognostic value of RV parameters support the necessity for their routine monitoring.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: The diagnostic value of oral microbiological testing in users of different nicotine products remains uncertain. We compared tongue-coating dysbiosis, salivary cultures, and chairside enzymatic activity across product groups and evaluated their discrimination of objective halitosis. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 225 adults: 60 never-users, 55 combustible cigarette users, 52 heated tobacco product users, and 58 e-cigarette users. Six tongue-coating taxa and total bacterial load were quantified by quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Salivary cultures and the benzoyl-DL-arginine-naphthylamide (BANA) test complemented organoleptic assessment and volatile sulfur compound measurement. Analyses included adjusted regression, compositional analysis, exploratory profiling and mediation, and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results: Adjusted dysbiosis-index differences versus never-users were 1.82, 1.50, and 2.08 units for combustible cigarette, heated tobacco product, and e-cigarette users, respectively (all p < 0.001). E-cigarette users had the highest Solobacterium moorei load and Candida carriage, whereas combustible cigarette users had the highest Porphyromonas gingivalis load and BANA positivity. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) R2 was 15.8%, with heterogeneous dispersions. Objective halitosis prevalence ranged from 10.8% to 66.7% across microbial profiles. The chairside/culture panel and dysbiosis index had areas under the curve of 0.72 and 0.71, respectively. Conclusions: Microbial differences were associated with product use, but exposure history and oral conditions may confound these associations. Moderate discrimination and absent external validation preclude diagnostic interchangeability or routine implementation of these adjunctive tests.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Objective: The study aims to evaluate the association of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) C677T and A1298C polymorphisms with cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), cerebral large vessel disease (CLVD), vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) and global and regional brain volumes. Methods: Clinical, laboratory, neuroimaging, volumetric, cognitive and MTHFR genotyping data were retrospectively collected from 62 patients with CSVD (n = 40) or CLVD (n = 22), all carriers of at least one MTHFR variant. Brain volumes were compared between patients with VCI carrying C677T (n = 30) and patients without VCI (n = 32). Analyses were repeated in the open-source platform jamovi and p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons with the Holm procedure. Results: The cohort comprised 41 women and 21 men (mean age 56.9 years). The CT and TT genotypes of C677T, the AC and CC genotypes of A1298C, blood pressure, total cholesterol and triglycerides differed between CSVD and CLVD at the unadjusted level (p < 0.05), but none of these differences remained significant after Holm correction. VCI carriers of C677T showed lower white matter (332.9 ± 25.5 vs. 437.9 ± 35.7 cm3) and gray matter volumes (626.0 ± 45.7 vs. 699.7 ± 51.5 cm3), higher cerebrospinal fluid volume (238.3 ± 42.2 vs. 197.1 ± 24.8 cm3) and reduced hippocampal, amygdalar, thalamic, superior frontal, middle temporal, entorhinal, parahippocampal and middle occipital volumes (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.05). Conclusions: Differences in MTHFR genotype distribution between CSVD and CLVD were not robust to correction for multiple testing, whereas VCI carriers of C677T showed global and selective regional volume loss that withstood correction. MTHFR variants are susceptibility markers rather than direct causes of vascular injury; these associations, which could not be adjusted for comorbid vascular risk factors or for concomitant neurodegenerative pathology, require confirmation in prospective, controlled studies with homocysteine measurements.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Background: Keratoconus causes characteristic spatial epithelial remodeling that may not be captured by conventional thickness measurements. Novel morphometric indices from MS-39 AS-OCT may better characterize these changes. Purpose: We aimed to evaluate novel MS-39 AS-OCT epithelial remodeling indices and compare their diagnostic accuracy with epithelial thickness and Pentacam tomography across the keratoconus spectrum, using an objective reference standard. Methods: This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study included 1319 eyes of 1286 patients with same-day Pentacam and MS-39 imaging at Noor Eye Hospital (2023–2025). Eyes were classified from the clinical records and Pentacam front-surface indices, without use of any epithelial data, as normal (n = 861), forme fruste keratoconus (FFKC; topographically normal fellow eye of very asymmetric ectasia; n = 40) or definite keratoconus (n = 418), graded mild, moderate or severe with the ABCD system. Generalized estimating equations, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis with DeLong confidence intervals and cross-validated cut-offs, and bootstrap-validated logistic models were used. Results: The central epithelial remodeling index (CERI) and central epithelial thickness range (CETR) increased with severity (+0.137 and +6.13 µm per severity grade; both p < 0.001). For definite keratoconus, CERI (AUC 0.932; 95% CI 0.913–0.948) and CETR (0.930) outperformed central minimum epithelial thickness (0.839; p < 0.001) but not BAD-D (0.972). Their AUCs rose from 0.666–0.677 in mild to 0.993–0.995 in severe keratoconus, a gradient that partly reflects the disease spectrum. For FFKC, the best epithelial AUC was 0.668 (6 mm epithelial thickness range) versus 0.728 for BAD-D, and adding five epithelial indices to tomography did not improve validated discrimination (out-of-bag AUC gain +0.000 for definite keratoconus and +0.012, 95% interval −0.080 to +0.083, for FFKC). Conclusions: CERI and CETR quantify epithelial remodeling and discriminate established keratoconus well, but they add little validated discrimination to Pentacam tomography; in FFKC, their discrimination was modest and any added value remains uncertain. They may complement, but not replace, tomography and biomechanics.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cold atmospheric plasma is applied to dental implants for surface activation, osseointegration, infection control and host modulation. This review reads those four uses as one reactive‐species mechanism with a separate exposure axis per target (an organizing interpretation, not a measured law) and audits what an illustrative sample of thirty‐three protocols reports about dose. Plasma medicine has a source‐characterization specification (DIN SPEC 91315) and candidate dose descriptors, delivered energy and equivalent total oxidation potential, whose inputs no audited protocol reports in full. Of twenty‐five atmospheric‐pressure protocols, working gas is stated in twenty‐four, flow in nineteen, power or voltage setting in eleven; across all thirty‐three, treated area and delivered dose in none, a measured output in two. Human endpoints are mostly surrogates.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We start with a brief introduction to the many faces of the Sun, the dynamic star that is the main source of space weather. We explain the need for spacecraft observations, the structure of the solar atmosphere, and the Sun’s magnetic cycle. Next, we focus on the Sun’s influence on Earth, define ‘space weather,’ and briefly discuss its effects on our technology and related socio-economic impacts. Then, we present data-driven, physics-based simulation models with predictive capabilities that enable forecasting and mitigation. We focus on models developed by my team at KU Leuven and the results and predictions they produce: the heliospheric wind and CME evolution models EUHFORIA and ICARUS, the global solar corona model COCONUT, and the solar energetic particle acceleration and transport model Particle Radiation Asset Directed at IP Space Exploration. We end with a few take-home messages.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>O envelhecimento cutâneo é um processo biológico multifatorial caracterizado pela degradação da integridade estrutural e da matriz extracelular (MEC). Para mitigar essas alterações morfológicas, a medicina regenerativa tem impulsionado terapias minimamente invasivas baseadas em hemoderivados. Este estudo tem como objetivo avaliar e comparar a eficácia clínica, a segurança e os mecanismos de ação tecidual das terapias autólogas de primeira e segunda geração, destacando a indispensabilidade da atuação técnica do biomédico na padronização pré-analítica. Trata-se de uma Revisão Integrativa da Literatura conduzida nas bases de dados PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science e BVS/LILACS. Após o rigoroso delineamento de elegibilidade, 15 artigos científicos (publicados entre 2020 e 2026) compuseram a amostra final. Os achados demonstram que, enquanto os concentrados de primeira geração apresentam uma liberação rápida de fatores de crescimento (bolus), a segunda geração forma uma rede tridimensional fisiológica, garantindo uma eluição sustentada e o aprisionamento funcional de leucócitos. Clinicamente, ambas as terapias induzem expressiva neocolagenogênese e aumento da espessura dérmica. Topograficamente, a segunda geração demonstra superioridade no preenchimento estrutural periorbital (textura e crepitação), enquanto a primeira se destaca no clareamento de hiperpigmentações infraorbitais. A acentuada heterogeneidade nos protocolos de centrifugação figura como o principal gargalo metodológico da literatura atual. Conclui-se que essas matrizes constituem estratégias altamente eficazes, contudo, o domínio sobre a fisiologia do processamento e a padronização operacional (força g e tempo) pelo biomédico são determinantes para a reprodutibilidade clínica e a segurança do paciente.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Mean-resource assessments miss days when wind and PV potential are simultaneously weak. Wind–solar resource indicators were reconstructed for the Al-Shahabi region in southeastern Iraq using 227,928 hourly ERA5 time steps across 12 grid cells during 1995–2020. Conditional resource responses were subsequently assessed using five CMIP6 models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5.WPD is calculated from hourly 100 m wind vectors and air density; a temperature-adjusted PV proxy is derived from hourly horizontal irradiation. Historical 20th-percentile (P20) thresholdsdefine comparable low resource days. The mean wind power density was 296.74 W m⁻², while the mean daily temperature-adjusted PV resource indicator was 0.7508 kWh m⁻² d⁻¹. Simultaneous deficiencies occur on 643/9497 (6.77%) days, mostly in boreal winter. For four future scenario–horizon combinations, the equal-weight five-model mean WPD changes −3.19% to −6.98% (all five models are reduced under transfer assumptions), while concurrent low-resource frequency changes range from −0.20 to +0.63 percentage points (pp) in the ensemble mean and are not signed consistently among individual models. Sensitivity analyses show strong seasonality dependence of thresholds and wind change amplitude transferred. These results separate a relatively coherent mean wind-resource response from much less robust compound-deficitbehaviour. Because monthly change signals are imposed on historical sequences, the adjusted daily episodes are conditional threshold outcomes but not predictions for weather persistence or operational electricity system reliability.</jats:p>

title: Governing Cross-Border Nuclear Partnerships: A Q-NPT Framework Analysis of the Egypt–Russia El Dabaa Nuclear Power Project

affiliation.name: Faculty of Liberal Arts & Professional Studies, School of Administrative Studies, Atkinson College, York University, Toronto, ON M3J 1P3, Canada

abstract: <jats:p>Large-scale nuclear energy projects depend on credible governance arrangements to support international cooperation and address institutional and societal concerns surrounding nuclear energy development. This study applies the Qudrat-Ullah Nuclear Peace and Trust (Q-NPT) framework to examine the governance of the Egypt–Russia El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant (ERENPP). The framework comprises four pillars—Trust, Equity, Transparency, and Inclusion—with institutional alignment treated as a cross-cutting dimension. Using a qualitative single-case study design and deductive content analysis, the study examines documentary evidence from intergovernmental agreements, financing arrangements, regulatory and international review documents, official project statements, media reports, civil-society publications, and relevant academic literature. The analysis distinguishes formal commitments and reported activities from implementation, stakeholder perceptions, and demonstrated outcomes. The findings identify formal bilateral and institutional arrangements relevant to trust and coordination, alongside governance questions concerning the disclosure of project information, the distribution of costs and benefits, and the scope and influence of stakeholder participation. Although documented consultation activities and regulatory milestones provide evidence of governance processes, they do not independently establish public confidence, equitable outcomes, or the effectiveness of stakeholder engagement. The study demonstrates how Q-NPT can structure documentary evidence across the four pillars, identify cross-pillar relationships, and make evidence gaps explicit without assigning an unsupported overall governance rating or inferring causal effects. It contributes a context-sensitive application of Q-NPT to cross-border nuclear energy governance and identifies priorities for further assessment, including accessible information disclosure, meaningful stakeholder engagement, institutional coordination, and transparent evaluation of project costs and benefits. The framework offers a complementary analytical approach for examining governance in nuclear energy partnerships and informing comparative research on energy-system development.</jats:p>

title: On increasing the resolution of diagnostics of food layered media by the method of resonance scattering

affiliation.name: Russian Biotechnological University (ROSBIOTECH)

abstract: <jats:p>The problem of early electromagnetic diagnostics of the appearance of unwanted layers in food-grade layered media is considered. The specific features of these challenges include, on the one hand, the thin layer thickness (from 20 μm), and, on the other hand, the high contrast between the main layer of the medium and the unwanted peeling layer. Standard electromagnetic diagnostic methods are unable to detect layers 20 μm thick. The method is based on determining the frequency dependence of the incident field reflectivity. Selecting antireflection layers allows for a low reflectivity at the resonant frequency, while the addition of an additional layer changes the reflectivity by an order of magnitude. For 20 μm, the qualitative form of the frequency dependence of the reflectivity changes, resulting in the appearance of two dips in the reflectivity rather than a single one. The reflectivity pattern allows for the determination of the thickness of the unwanted layer in the 20-50 μm range of interest. The key principle of the method under consideration is the use of the high sensitivity of the reflectivity at the resonant frequency to changes in the complex permittivity of the layered medium, in order to increase the ability to detect the unwanted layer.</jats:p>

AI-driven intelligent vibration monitoring for predictive maintenance in chemical process plants: Signal processing, diagnostics, and industrial integration
container-title: Journal of AI-Driven Engineering Innovation and Applications
abstract: <jats:p>Intelligent vibration monitoring is increasingly important for predictive maintenance (PdM) in chemical process plants, where machinery faults may appear as weak, mixed, nonstationary, or process-dependent signatures. This review examines how vibration measurements can be converted into reliable maintenance intelligence using signal processing, artificial intelligence (AI), and plant-level integration. A structured critical narrative review was conducted using literature identified from Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and IEEE Xplore, focusing mainly on studies published from 2016 to September 2026. It compares fault signature complexity across pumps, compressors, agitators, turbines, fans, gear-driven systems, and rolling-element bearings and evaluates time- and frequency-domain analysis, wavelet methods, empirical mode decomposition, cepstral enhancement, and time–frequency approaches. AI-based classification, anomaly detection, deep learning, and prognostic modelling were assessed in relation to interpretability, generalisation, benchmark data limitations, uncertainty, and industrial trust. Particular emphasis is placed on process-aware interpretation because vibration responses can be affected by the flow, pressure, hydraulic instability, operating duty, structural transmission, and maintenance constraints. This review proposes a deployment-oriented, tiered PdM framework that aligns analytical depth, AI support, asset criticality, process context, and maintenance workflow integration. A standards-informed distinction between condition monitoring, diagnostic advisories, and machinery protection functions was also introduced. Future studies should prioritise explainability, field robustness, cross-condition validation, and traceable linkages between diagnostic outputs, plant information systems, and maintenance decisions.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>In this paper, we investigate the thermodynamic behavior and extremal configurations of magnetically charged black holes in nonminimal Einstein–Yang–Mills theory, focusing on the interplay between nonminimal interactions, local stability, and thermodynamic topology. The derived mass and Hawking temperature recover the Reissner–Nordström–anti-de Sitter results in the minimally coupled limit. However, integrating the first law leaves an entropy-normalization ambiguity, so conclusions based on entropy positivity remain conditional on the prescription adopted here. Our stability analysis distinguishes the extremal boundary from divergences in the heat capacity, which indicate singular local responses but do not independently establish a first-order phase transition. The topological analysis further shows that the winding number depends on both magnetic charge and pressure. Restricting the thermodynamic domain to positive entropy can alter the endpoint contribution, making a separate evaluation necessary. Regarding extremality, the asymptotically flat solution admits a positive extremal branch throughout the considered nonnegative coupling range, while the AdS case possesses a unique positive extremal radius under the stated conditions. The extremal mass increases with the nonminimal coupling, and its response remains finite at finite positive coupling but grows without bound in the large-coupling limit. These findings clarify the geometric and thermodynamic consequences of the nonminimal interaction without overstating their implications for quantum gravity. In particular, the extremality results alone neither establish nor rule out the magnetic Weak Gravity Conjecture, whose assessment requires a consistently normalized gauge sector and information about the spectrum of charged states.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>Based on the energy confinement time scaling law of stellarator in the low-confinement mode, combined with energy balance equation and the plasma propagation and power deposition equations of the electron cyclotron wave in the three-dimensional magnetic field, a stellarator plasma start-up model including electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) and impurity radiation power loss is established. Validation against W7-X experimental data demonstrates good agreement in the temporal evolution of electron temperature and radiation losses, which verified that the model can correctly give the plasma start-up results of the stellarator under ECRH. This model is applied to predict the results of plasma start-up under 28 GHz ECRH for China Helical Device 1 (CN-H1) stellarator. The effects of the initial electron-to-ion temperature ratio (Te/Ti), ECRH injection power (Pinj), deposition position and effective charge number Z_{\text{eff}} on start-up are systematically studied and analyzed. The results show that the initial Te/Ti ratio affects only the ramp-up rate, while the final steady-state electron and ion temperature remain unaffected. Higher Pinj accelerates electron temperature rise and increases flat-top electron temperature, whereas the ion temperature exhibits the opposite trend, decreasing with increasing Pinj. The deposition location has a decisive impact on the start-up outcome: only core deposition on the low-field side leads to a successful start-up, while high-field side and off-axis low-field side depositions fail owing to refractive deviation of the ray trajectory and insufficient absorption, respectively. The steady-state electron and ion temperatures are insensitive to {\mathrm{Z}}_{\text{eff}} within a reasonable range.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Sepsis remains a major cause of mortality and healthcare burden worldwide, and delays in identifying infectious etiologies and clinically actionable diagnostic signals continue to compromise the timely initiation of appropriate antimicrobial therapy and patient outcomes. Conventional blood culture methods are limited by prolonged turnaround times, while recent advances in molecular diagnostic technologies have significantly improved the speed and sensitivity of pathogen detection. These advances highlight the potential of rapid and accurate molecular diagnostics to support timely diagnosis and targeted treatment. However, as analytical performance continues to improve, the major bottlenecks have increasingly extended beyond individual assay performance to workflow integration, operational complexity, and clinical implementation. Current platforms still face inherent trade-offs among diagnostic performance, cost, automation, and usability, limiting their widespread clinical adoption. To address these challenges, we propose the SPICE framework, encompassing Speed, Precision, Intelligence, Cost, and Ease of Use, as a unified perspective for evaluating existing technologies and guiding the design of next-generation molecular diagnostic systems. Based on these five interconnected dimensions, this review synthesizes recent advances in nucleic acid amplification, sequencing, multiplex detection, data-driven analysis, and sample-to-answer diagnostic platforms within a unified system-level framework, and compares representative approaches according to their SPICE-based capability profiles, major strengths, and limitations. These analyses further identify key barriers to clinical translation and the system-level requirements for the development and clinical implementation of intelligent, integrated sample-to-answer molecular diagnostic platforms for sepsis.</jats:p>

title: Impacto da inteligência artificial na melhoria da qualidade de imagem em diagnóstico por imagem
Impact of artificial intelligence on image quality improvement inimage diagnostics
abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to analyze the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare, highlighting its main contributions, limitations, and implications for healthcare practice and the organization of health services. This is an integrative literature review with an exploratory and descriptive approach, in which searches were conducted in the SciELO, LILACS, and PubMed databases. Studies were selected according to previously established inclusion criteria, followed by the analysis, synthesis, and organization of the findings in a comparative table. The results showed that AI has been widely applied in diagnostic imaging and in different medical and dental specialties, demonstrating good performance in the identification and classification of clinical findings, as well as contributing to the optimization of workflows and supporting decision-making. However, its performance may vary according to the clinical context, and in certain situations, AI does not outperform conventional methods or achieves better results when used in combination with human assessment. It is concluded that AI represents a promising tool for healthcare, with the potential to improve diagnostic quality and the efficiency of health services. Nevertheless, its application should be carried out carefully, with continuous validation and integration with clinical judgment to ensure safety and effectiveness in healthcare practice.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Background: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects approximately 10% of the global population, and it is a critical challenge for public health worldwide. The integration of metabolomics with machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach to enhancing disease diagnosis and prognosis. Objective: This study characterized the urinary metabolomic profiles of individuals with intermediate-to-advanced CKD and developed predictive models for disease diagnosis and prognosis. Methods: Urine samples from 129 participants, including healthy individuals and patients with CKD, were analyzed using liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Multivariate analysis was performed to identify differences between groups. ML algorithms were the best for developing predictive models for the diagnosis, prognosis, and progression of CKD. Results: The results show the identities of 1499 metabolites. They also indicate that ML models effectively differentiated between healthy individuals and CKD patients, demonstrating high accuracy and specificity. The RF model was effective for diagnostic purposes, while the SVM showed superior performance in prognostic and disease progression predictions. The differentially expressed metabolites found, predominantly lipids, may serve as potential biomarkers for the detection and progression of CKD. Conclusions: The combination of urinary metabolomics with ML algorithms represents a promising, non-invasive approach for CKD diagnosis and follow-up, offering an alternative that may improve both the precision and personalization of disease management.</jats:p>

title: Perturbative analysis of planar quantum electrodynamics in the Heisenberg picture
abstract: <jats:p>We investigate quantum electrodynamics in (2 + 1) dimensions within a covariant quantization scheme formulated in the Heisenberg picture. To avoid the conceptual difficulties associated with Haag’s theorem, we construct a perturbative framework based on the physical requirement of unitarily equivalent representations, rather than relying on the conventional Feynman diagram expansion. Within this approach, radiative corrections are evaluated up to one-loop order using a perturbative operator formalism in which the canonical commutation relations guarantee a consistent Fock representation for the interacting fields. The Heisenberg picture provides a clear advantage over the standard Interaction picture by offering an unambiguous regularization framework for the treatment of radiative effects. As a final result, we demonstrate that the infrared divergence in the electron’s anomalous magnetic moment correction can be removed without the introduction of the Chern–Simons term.</jats:p>

<jats:p>Newton’s gravitational constant G is measured but has never been derived from more fundamental quantities. Within the
baryonic expansion framework developed by the author since 1990, we examine how G is related to the proton’s mass,
radius and internal pressure. The principal findings are three. (i) Applying the author’s 1993 expansion equation to the
proton and comparing the result with the acceleration its internal pressure (≈1035 Pa) would produce in the absence of
confi nement defines a confinement leakage factor k ≈ 3 × 10-40.
(ii) G is then bound to proton quantities by the exact relation G = 4π k Pp rp

leakage factor equals the proton’s gravitational coupling αG ≈ 6 × 10-39 divided by a geometric factor of about 20. As
defi ned here, k contains G, so these relations are consistency relations and not yet a derivation of G. We state the condition
under which they become one, an independent determination of k or of the proton surface expansion rate from confinement

title: Quantum annealing through a first-order phase transition: Field theory approach
A Toy Model for Topological Entanglement Features in 1 + 1D Integrable Quantum Field Theory
container-title: International Journal of Modern Physics D
abstract: <jats:p>In this paper we investigate an entanglement measure, the Rényi entropy, in a 1+1D integrable quantum field theory known as the Federbush model. This is a deformation of the theory of two massive Dirac fermions by means of a bilinear term in the U(1) currents that couples the two fermion species. This deformation gives rise to S-matrix elements which are coupling-dependent phases, distinct from –1. These non-trivial phases can be seen as encoding anyon-like statistics. From this viewpoint, the Federbush model is a toy model for topological features of entanglement in one space dimension. In this paper we show that, a standard computation based on form factors of branch point twist fields leads to the conclusion that these topological features play no role when computing most known measures of entanglement at equilibrium in the ground state. This conclusion applies also to the post-quench dynamics at first order in perturbation theory, after a small quench of the topological parameter.</jats:p>

title: Bridging disciplines for quantum futures: homologation and professional skills in an interdisciplinary MSc in quantum information science & technology (QIST)
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum technologies increasingly require professionals who can work fluently across physics, computer science, electrical engineering and mathematics. A persistent challenge for quantum master’s programmes is the heterogeneity of incoming students’ preparation, which can slow early progress and impede collaboration. Building on prior calls for dedicated quantum engineering education, we describe two curricular pillars implemented in the MSc in Quantum Information Science & Technology (QIST), jointly offered by Delft University of Technology and Leiden University: (i) a structured 10 ECTS homologation module that aligns foundational competencies via tailored submodules spanning quantum physics, mathematics, computer science, information theory, electronics, and computer engineering; and (ii) a credit-bearing professional skills module that integrates career orientation, ethics and reflection early on in the curriculum. Together with multi-stage team projects and diverse thesis pathways, these elements provide a practical model for interdisciplinary quantum education aimed at inclusive participation, shared vocabulary and workforce readiness. Presented as an educational innovation report, we propose homologation and early professional formation as transferable curricular design patterns, adaptable to other quantum graduate programmes facing similar challenges of cohort heterogeneity and interdisciplinary breadth.</jats:p>

title: Cyclic universe and uniform rate inflation from polymerized scalar field in loop quantum cosmology

affiliation.name: Department of Physics, University of North Bengal, Siliguri, Darjeeling 734 013, West Bengal, India
Department of Physics, Guru Jambheshwar University of Science and Technology, Hisar 125001, Haryana, India

container-title: International Journal of Modern Physics D
abstract: <jats:p>We investigate the uniform rate inflationary universe in the framework of Loop Quantum Cosmology (LQC) and find that this seemingly simple inflationary model is interlinked with various concepts such as cyclic evolution, HNI inflation, and polymer-quantized scalar fields when the background spacetime is loop-quantized. The potential for an exactly uniform rate inflation in a loop-quantized FRW spacetime turns out to be a polymerized version of the corresponding potential in general relativity, which mimics the potentials for a polymerized scalar field and Hybrid Natural Inflation (HNI). There is also a radical modification of the background spacetime, leading to a cyclic universe with identical epochs separated by quantum bounces that replace the classical singularity. The energy density and Hubble rate are bounded. Polymerization of the scalar field is found to be intimately tied to the polymerization of the background geometry in LQC. Remarkably, a single polymerized scalar field simultaneously governs the cyclic evolution of the universe and drives the inflationary phase. Preliminary predictions for cosmological perturbations are worked out and are found to depend on the value of the field at the end of inflation. The parameter space is explored to compare the results for the spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio with observational constraints.</jats:p>

title: Hybrid Quantum Secret‐Sharing Subprotocols for a Class of Non‐Maximal Quantum Access Structures

affiliation.name: School of Mechano‐Electronic Engineering Xidian University Xi'an China

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum secret sharing (QSS) over non‐maximal quantum access structures (QASs) remains challenging because direct constructions may require complex quantum resources. This paper investigates a class of non‐maximal QASs, particularly hyperstar QASs containing three hyperedges. We give information‐theoretic definitions of authorized, forbidden, and intermediate sets and introduce a representative‐element QAS as a reduced substructure of the original hyperstar QAS. For each minimal authorized set of the representative‐element structure, we construct an entangled‐state‐based quantum secret‐sharing component. By incorporating a corresponding classical secret‐sharing scheme as an auxiliary component, we obtain a family of classical–quantum hybrid secret‐sharing subprotocols for the minimal authorized sets of the considered class of non‐maximal hyperstar QAS and prove exact correctness and information‐theoretic perfect secrecy under the stated security model. In particular, the joint classical–quantum reduced state available to every subset unauthorized with respect to the corresponding subprotocol is completely independent of the quantum secret. The representative‐element reduction restricts the quantum part of each authorized‐set‐specific subprotocol to a smaller auxiliary access structure. A complete resource comparison with global QSS schemes under a unified operational model is left for future research.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Many complex quantum phenomena require a description that goes beyond the standard paradigm of state preparations, evolutions, and measurements. A suitable framework for tackling such scenarios is that of , i.e., quantum operations that transform quantum operations. These objects are fundamental to modern quantum theory, and recent years have seen a proliferation of technical and conceptual results that fundamentally rely on them; they naturally emerge in quantum circuit architectures, correlated open dynamics, and investigations of quantum causality, to name but a few fields of application. In this tutorial, we provide a pedagogical introduction to higher-order quantum operations: we offer the tools to work with them in various contexts and firmly embed them within the current research landscape. Through this approach, our intent is to enable multiple points of access to the field, highlight the interconnectedness of  distinct areas, and provide the means to meaningfully engage with state-of-the-art research developments. We conclude by identifying open problems and future research directions in this rapidly evolving field.</jats:p>

affiliation.name: Department of Physics Politecnico di Milano  Milano Italy

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum technologies built on engineered nanostructures require their electronic states characterized at the scale on which they are made, which photoemission cannot reach. Secondary electron energy spectroscopy in a scanning electron microscope captures valence‐band density of states (DOS) information by subtracting two peak‐normalized spectra taken at 0.5 and 1 keV and differentiating the residual. This paper proposes a mechanism: interfacial Auger recombination at the boundary between the beam‐induced contamination layer and the specimen. Electrons injected by the primary beam occupy interface defect states as transient traps, in a steady state where the injected current balances recombination. A trapped electron drops into a metal valence‐band hole and transfers the released energy to an electron at the Fermi level, which escapes into vacuum. Only one valence electron takes part, and the trapped population has a sharp lower edge, so the emitted spectrum is a cumulative integral of the density of states and differentiation directly yields the valence‐band DOS distribution. The predicted one‐to‐one mapping between binding energy and secondary electron energy is confirmed across six elemental solids, with a fitted slope of 0.99 ± 0.02. The model presents the conditions a specimen must meet, each of which could be engineered.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Valleytronics and valley photonics exploit the valley degree of freedom to encode and manipulate information. Here we show that photonic valleys can be selectively addressed in quantum optics using a simple two-level emitter, provided it is coupled nonlocally to the field, thereby realizing a so-called giant atom. Specifically, we consider a qubit coupled at multiple points to an engineered honeycomb lattice of resonators with detuned sublattice frequencies. By tailoring the geometry and phases of the coupling points, the giant atom can be made to emit selectively into a single valley. The emitted photons thereby acquire a well-defined valley character and effectively nonzero Berry curvature. By placing the qubit near a domain wall between regions of opposite sublattice detuning, whose interface supports valley-polarized edge modes, emission becomes chiral along the domain wall. This provides a promising route toward implementation of single-photon disorder-robust chiral emission without breaking time-reversal symmetry of the electromagnetic medium in platforms such as circuit QED.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum illumination exploits quantum correlations to improve weak‐target detection in noisy, lossy environments. Infrared radiation is widely used in spectroscopy, imaging, and environmental monitoring, yet quantum illumination in this spectral region remains comparatively unexplored. Here, we propose an infrared QI protocol based on a molecular optomechanical platform. The infrared field serves as the target‐probing signal, while the weak return is converted to the visible domain, where mature detection technologies enable joint readout with the retained idler. Within experimentally relevant parameter regimes, the driven molecular optomechanical system generates infrared–visible quantum resources and achieves a lower target‐detection error probability than an equal‐energy coherent‐state benchmark. The proposed protocol may find applications in low‐reflectivity target detection and weak infrared sensing under severe background noise.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical investigation of quantum information storage via the Higgs amplitude mode in superconductors. We propose a novel quantum memory mechanism based on coherent excitation and echo retrieval of the Higgs mode, exploiting the collective nature of the superconducting condensate. Through rigorous theoretical analysis combining time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory with quantum master equations, we demonstrate that Higgs mode excitations can store quantum information with coherence times exceeding 100 ns. We derive analytical expressions for storage fidelity as a function of temperature, gap anisotropy, and disorder, achieving theoretical fidelities above 95% for storage times up to 100 ns in clean s-wave superconductors below. Numerical simulations validate our theoretical predictions and reveal optimal parameter regimes for NbN thin films. Our findings establish fundamental bounds on Higgs-based quantum memory and propose experimental protocols compatible with current THz spectroscopy capabilities. This work opens new directions for exploiting collective modes in quantum technologies.</jats:p>

To address this gap, we investigated how upper-secondary students and pre-service teachers understand quantum teleportation when taught with a simplified diagrammatic formalism based on the ZX-calculus, which represents quantum processes as diagrams of wires and boxes. Through phenomenographic analysis of video-recorded group work sessions, written responses to exercises, and a group interview, with a total of

Our findings indicate that while a simplified diagrammatic formalism for teaching quantum physics can provide an accessible entry point at the upper-secondary level, it does not automatically resolve fundamental conceptual challenges, and requires careful consideration in terms of developing teaching and learning sequences.                       </mml:math>

                    . We derive the most general solution of Einstein’s field equations for this class of sources and identify a broad family of geometries, including black holes, naked singularities, and traversable wormholes, parametrized by the integration constants and the equation of state parameter
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>

                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mi>ω</mml:mi>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    . We determine the conditions for traversability and show that only two classes of matter can support traversable wormholes: Casimir-type matter with
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>

                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , whereas quintessence and conventional dark energy are excluded by the flare–out condition at the throat. For the Casimir value
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mi>ω</mml:mi>

                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , we find that the transverse pressure approaches
                    <jats:inline-formula>

                      </jats:tex-math>

                          <mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    near the central naked singularity at
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">

                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , implying that the complete algebraic structure of the Casimir stress–energy tensor, characterized by
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>

                          <mml:mo>∝</mml:mo>
                          <mml:mo>−</mml:mo>
                          <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mo>/</mml:mo>
                          </mml:mrow>
                          <mml:msup>

                    <jats:inline-formula>

                      </jats:tex-math>

                            <mml:mi>p</mml:mi>

                          </mml:msub>
                          <mml:mo>=</mml:mo>
                          <mml:mn>3</mml:mn>
                          <mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:msub>
                            <mml:mi>p</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>

                          <mml:mo>=</mml:mo>
                          <mml:mo>−</mml:mo>
                          <mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , is dynamically recovered in the vicinity of the origin. This behavior is not imposed
                    <jats:italic>a priori</jats:italic>
                    but emerges directly from Einstein’s field equations. Adopting a purely classical framework in which the amplitude of the energy density is treated as a free parameter, we obtain traversable wormhole solutions with throat radii ranging from microscopic to astrophysical scales. These Casimir-like configurations share the functional structure of the Casimir stress–energy tensor,
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>

                            </mml:mrow>

                    <jats:inline-formula>

                      </jats:tex-math>

                          </mml:msub>
                          <mml:mo>=</mml:mo>
                          <mml:mn>3</mml:mn>
                          <mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , but are not generated by the physical Casimir effect. Within this setting, Garattini’s Planck–scale Casimir wormhole is recovered as a particular case when the quantum Casimir energy scale is imposed. We further show that the total amount of exotic matter required is finite for arbitrary
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">

                    </jats:inline-formula>

                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">

title: Electron-phonon coupling and electronic transport at the moiré scale in twisted bilayer graphene
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    First-principles calculations can accurately describe electron-phonon (e-ph) interactions and electronic transport in a wide range of materials, but are currently limited to unit cells with up to ~100 atoms due to computational cost. Here, we develop an atomistic electronic potential with Holstein- and Peierls-like terms for modeling e-ph interactions and phonon-limited electronic transport that enables the study of moiré systems with thousands of atoms per unit cell. This method can accurately reproduce first-principles e-ph coupling and resistivity in graphene and large-angle twisted bilayer graphene (TBG). Using this approach, we study TBG over a range of twist angles down to 1.6
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    (5044-atom unit cell), and report the evolution of e-ph interactions and phonon-limited resistivity with twist angle. The predicted resistivity increases by two orders of magnitude between 13.2
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    and 1.6
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    , driven by the progressive reduction of the electronic energy scale. Our calculations can predict key experimental trends in 2.0
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    and 1.6
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    TBG, including the resistivity and its dependence on temperature and band filling. Our work establishes a scalable approach for quantitative studies of e-ph interactions and transport in moiré materials and other systems with previously inaccessible length scales.
                  </jats:p>

                  <jats:p>
                    Using a robust photon loss model for photonic quantum experiments, we derive
                    <jats:inline-formula>

                        </mml:mrow>

                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    th order parameter-shift rules (PSRs) for computing gradients of Fock boson sampling transition probabilities where
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">

                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    photons are sent into a lossy interferometer. We also show that one cannot naturally generalize this gradient recipe to the case of Gaussian boson sampling. Only in the specific case where the transmission matrix of the interferometer can be factorized as a diagonal loss matrix premultiplied by a pure unitary it is possible to obtain PSRs with a finite order given by twice the total number of photons detected. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method by comparing its performance against finite differences on real hardware.

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum batteries constitute a promising energy storage platform that harnesses inherent quantum resources to improve charging performance, which has garnered widespread research attention. In this work, we explore the charging dynamics of a quantum battery consisting of an atomic ensemble coupled to an optical charging medium with Kerr nonlinearity. Adopting the truncated Wigner phase‐space formalism, we verify the generation of intrinsic non‐Gaussian Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen (EPR) steering between atomic and optical modes, and systematically characterize how this steering relies on the Kerr nonlinear strength. Our numerical results reveal that forward EPR steering originating from the atomic ensemble toward the optical field markedly elevates battery charging efficiency, accelerating energy accumulation, raising the average charging power, and increasing the extractable ergotropy. Conversely, reverse EPR steering propagating from the optical field to the atomic ensemble degrades the overall charging performance of the quantum battery.</jats:p>
