abstract:
<jats:title>SUMMARY</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ground-shaking site effects, which are anomalous earthquake ground motions at the Earth’s surface, are caused by the generation of specific wavefields in specific near-surface structures. The best known are effects in surface sedimentary layers, sedimentary basins and valleys, which are related to wave trapping in softer materials. To a lesser degree, topographic effects, associated with irregular surface geometry and often also with collocated softer or cracked material, have also received much attention and gave rise to specific provisions in some building codes (e.g., EC8). By contrast, site effects related to sharp lateral boundaries between media with very different stiffness have been much less investigated, despite consistent macroseismic observations of a significant increase in damage intensity on “stripes” located along strong lateral discontinuities. In this study we consider a semi-infinite layer as a canonical model for many real situations with sediments relatively sharply laterally bounded or with abrupt change of sediment thickness. We investigate numerically simulated particle velocity, rate of rotational motion and rate of axial strain for the vertically incident SH, SV and P waves. We use a novel type of characterization of transfer properties – time-frequency transfer functions for the particle velocity and rates of rotational motion and axial strain. We found that the rates of rotational motion and axial strain display sharp peaks at the lateral discontinuity mainly in the case of the incident SV and P waves. Particle-velocity components exhibit a maximum close to the discontinuity, but at variable distances depending on central frequency and incident wave type (“basin-edge” effect). At larger distances from the discontinuity, the decay of rotational motion and axial strain is controlled by the attenuation in sediments. The sharp peaks of the rates of rotational motion and axial strain across the lateral discontinuity, together with the well-known basin-edge effects for translational motion, are found to be the key site effects of the laterally bounded sedimentary layer.</jats:p>

title: Flat band excitons and quantum metric
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We discuss the excitons in flat band systems. Quantum metric plays a central role in determining the properties of single exciton excitations as well as the exciton condensate. While the electrons and holes are supposed to be extremely heavy in flat bands, the excitons (the bound state of an electron-hole pair) could be light and mobile. In particular, we show that the inverse of the effective mass tensor of excitons is proportional to the quantum metric tensor. Meanwhile, the flat band excitons have a finite size, lower bounded by the trace of the quantum metric tensor. Given the properties of single exciton excitation, one can argue for the formation of exciton condensate. Because of the quantum metric, the exciton condensate can support dissipationless counterflow supercurrent, implying the stability of exciton condensate.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Helium shows great promise in radiotherapy due to improved dose conformality and higher biological effectiveness compared to protons, but limited data on its physical and biological properties hinder its clinical potential.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to characterize the microdosimetric distributions of 160 MeV/u helium ions in‐field and out‐of‐field, benchmark the measurements against Monte Carlo simulations, and investigate how the measured radiation quality propagates into radiobiological predictions from mathematical models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Microdosimetric measurements were performed using a Tissue Equivalent Proportional Counter (TEPC) in a water phantom at various depths along the beam direction and lateral positions. The experimental data were compared with OpenTOPAS Monte Carlo simulations. The measured microdosimetric spectra and derived microdosimetric quantities were then used as physical input for two microdosimetry‐based radiobiological models, the modified Microdosimetric Kinetic Model (mMKM) and the Generalized Stochastic Microdosimetric Model (GSM
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      ), to calculate the Relative Biological Effectiveness (RBE) at each measured location.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The microdosimetric characterization revealed increasing radiation quality parameters ,  and  along the
                      <jats:italic>in‐field</jats:italic>
                      direction up to the Bragg peak, followed by a decrease in the distal region. The values of  range from 2.43 ± 0.19 keV/µm at 50 mm depth to 21.8 ± 1.1 keV/µm at the Bragg peak, and decreasing to 2.39 ± 0.12 keV/µm at 250 mm depth. All microdosimetric parameters declined with depth at the
                      <jats:italic>field‐edge</jats:italic>
                      , while remaining approximately constant
                      <jats:italic>close</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic>far out‐of‐field</jats:italic>
                      . OpenTOPAS reproduced the measured spectra with primary helium ions contributing predominantly to the higher‐
                      <jats:italic>y</jats:italic>
                      region and secondary protons to the lower‐
                      <jats:italic>y</jats:italic>
                      region. Although mMKM and GSM
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      predicted similar trends, the RBE(0.1) values differed, with the largest variations of up to 37% relative to the mMKM occurring in the distal
                      <jats:italic>in‐field</jats:italic>
                      region. The lack of corresponding in vitro measurements prevents validation of the model predictions and assessment of their accuracy.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This study provides the first comprehensive experimental microdosimetric characterization of a helium beam at clinically relevant energy across
                      <jats:italic>in‐field</jats:italic>
                      and out‐of‐field regions. The observed discrepancies with Monte Carlo simulations highlight the need for improved characterization and modeling of secondary‐particle production in helium beams. The RBE calculations further illustrate how differences in the physical description and interpretation of heterogeneous radiation fields propagate into biological predictions from different models. Dedicated radiobiological measurements under these irradiation conditions are needed to validate these predictions.

abstract: <jats:p>Diffuse laser cooling (DLC) provides a compact, robust, and scalable approach to generating cold-atom ensembles, offering significant potential for ground-based and spaceborne microwave atomic clocks. However, the performance of DLC systems remains limited by the weak atom-light interaction arising from their relatively low atomic density. This limitation is characterized by the optical density (OD), which quantifies the effective interaction strength between the atomic ensemble and the probe light and strongly influences the achievable signal-to-noise ratio. Although quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) DLC extends the probe interaction length and improves atomic utilization, increasing the local atomic density within the interrogation region remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a magnetically enhanced quasi-1D DLC system that simultaneously maintains the extended interaction length and increases the atomic density through a two-dimensional magnetic-field gradient. By spatially compressing and accumulating atoms near the probe axis, we enhance the OD of a 70-cm-long cold rubidium ensemble from 2.49 to 3.94, representing a 58% enhancement and an equivalent increase in the local atomic density. The dependence of the OD on the magnetic-field gradient, probe intensity, beam size, and cooling-light polarization is systematically investigated. This work establishes a practical pathway for enhancing optical interrogation efficiency and could pave the way for the development of high-performance DLC-based cold-atom clocks and quantum sensing systems.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Based on the energy confinement time scaling law of stellarator in the low-confinement mode, combined with energy balance equation and the plasma propagation and power deposition equations of the electron cyclotron wave in the three-dimensional magnetic field, a stellarator plasma start-up model including electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) and impurity radiation power loss is established. Validation against W7-X experimental data demonstrates good agreement in the temporal evolution of electron temperature and radiation losses, which verified that the model can correctly give the plasma start-up results of the stellarator under ECRH. This model is applied to predict the results of plasma start-up under 28 GHz ECRH for China Helical Device 1 (CN-H1) stellarator. The effects of the initial electron-to-ion temperature ratio (Te/Ti), ECRH injection power (Pinj), deposition position and effective charge number Z_{\text{eff}} on start-up are systematically studied and analyzed. The results show that the initial Te/Ti ratio affects only the ramp-up rate, while the final steady-state electron and ion temperature remain unaffected. Higher Pinj accelerates electron temperature rise and increases flat-top electron temperature, whereas the ion temperature exhibits the opposite trend, decreasing with increasing Pinj. The deposition location has a decisive impact on the start-up outcome: only core deposition on the low-field side leads to a successful start-up, while high-field side and off-axis low-field side depositions fail owing to refractive deviation of the ray trajectory and insufficient absorption, respectively. The steady-state electron and ion temperatures are insensitive to {\mathrm{Z}}_{\text{eff}} within a reasonable range.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Dual-energy X-ray transmission sorting of copper ores is often constrained by strong coupling between conventional features and particle thickness. To address this, we propose two decoupled features: R3, an improved R-value feature, and Zeff from basis material decomposition, which are designed to mitigate thickness interference and improve high-Z mineral identification. Copper and lead–zinc ore particles from the Yinshan Mine (Dexing, China), with particle thickness ranges of 8–60 mm for the copper ore and 8–25 mm for the lead–zinc ore, were tested on a laboratory DE-XRT sorter. A support vector machine regression model was trained on 314 phyllite copper ore particles (8–60 mm) to predict a weighted comprehensive grade (Cu+Fe+S), using R-value, R3, Zeff, and w3–w2 as inputs. The method showed favorable performance for porphyry copper ores (particle thickness: 8–60 mm): feed grades of 0.068%–0.109% Cu were upgraded to concentrates of 0.127%–0.244% Cu, with waste grades of 0.030%–0.051% and recoveries of 61.69%–79.67%. For phyllite copper ores (particle thickness: 8–60 mm), enrichment was observed through yield adjustment, with recoveries of 33.38%–71.69%. A plausible reason for the poor performance of the intermediate-grade Cu phyllite ore (Cu: 0.098%) is a combination of two factors: the chalcopyrite grain size (~0.1 mm) being below the detector resolution (0.8 mm), which causes mineral signals to be swamped by gangue, and the fundamental limitation of dual-energy XRT in distinguishing Cu from Fe. For lead–zinc ore (4.744% Pb+Zn feed), the sorter rejected 21.99% as waste while achieving 98.87% Pb+Zn recovery, with only 0.245% Pb+Zn in the waste. These results indicate that the proposed multi-feature fusion and SVM regression strategy provides a feasible approach for the preconcentration of low-grade copper ores and waste rejection for lead–zinc ores.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Liquid metal plasma-facing components (PFCs) are being considered for a variety of fusion power plant designs, and careful control of the liquid metal inventory will be essential in these systems to mitigate challenges with liquid metal corrosion and hydrogen fuel retention. Since many power plant designs and existing test facilities rely on pulsed plasma sources, it is critical to understand how liquid metal evaporation leads to material migration within a reactor over the periods of time when no plasma is present. This work addresses this question by developing a simple particle balance model to efficiently calculate liquid metal vapor transport patterns over indefinitely long time periods, using a particle redistribution matrix to capture the vapor transport details. After developing the mathematical model, characteristics of a future Liquid Metal Core-Edge (LMCE) research facility with liquid lithium divertors are used as a reference to demonstrate how the particle balance model can be used. Examples of lithium migration during the cooldown period between plasma pulses show that the pattern of lithium deposition depends primarily on the system geometry. An important secondary effect in these scenarios is the relative cooldown rate of the lithium divertor with respect to other PFCs in the device. Examples are also provided to demonstrate how the particle balance model can be used to optimize the design of a cold finger to collect liquid metal condensation for extraction and reprocessing, with the results showing that a future LMCE facility may be capable of collecting all of the lithium evaporated between plasma pulses if the main chamber walls can be maintained above 350 C during operation.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>Collisions of ultra-relativistic bubbles during cosmological phase transitions can produce particles much heavier than the transition scale. Previous analyses modelled this process as the off-shell decay of the scalar background. We show that its results parametrically overestimate hard particle production and depend on the gauge choice and the coordinate choice in field space. We propose an alternative formalism, analogous to the partonic description of high-energy collisions. In the ultra-relativistic limit, the colliding bubbles undergo nearly free passage and hard production arises from on-shell scatterings among the quanta constituting the Lorentz-contracted walls. We apply this approach to heavy scalar, fermion, and vector particle production, and study the implications for dark matter, leptogenesis, graviton production and primordial gravitational waves.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>To address the problem of forecasting abnormal passenger flow at urban rail transit stations caused by large-scale events, holidays, and weather changes, this paper proposes a multi-source big data abnormal spatio-temporal prediction framework, MBDASPF. Based on historical entry and exit passenger flow, the model incorporates external disturbance factors such as day of week, holidays, weather, official event website information, and Weibo super topic data, and adopts a “branch-transform-fuse” strategy to extract the historical passenger flow correlation and the abnormal disturbance correlation, respectively. The historical branch employs GRU to capture recent proximity, daily periodicity, and weekly tendency, while the disturbance branch employs LSTM to model the influence of external events. Finally, through two-stage fusion and an attention-based output layer, multi-step forecasting for the next 10, 20, and 30 min are realized. Experiments on data from the Olympic Sports Center Station of Nanjing Rail Transit Line 10 show that MBDASPF outperforms ARIMA, SVR, BPNN, and GRU overall in terms of MAE, RMSE, and MAPE, and can more effectively characterize abnormal passenger flow fluctuations during large-scale events.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>To improve the accuracy of short-term passenger flow prediction at urban rail transit transfer stations, this paper proposes a Multi-Scale Dual-Graph Spatial-Temporal Fusion Network (MS-DSTGFN).                   <jats:p>The additional‐ionization environment induced by a high‐altitude nuclear explosion (HANE) substantially alters the ionospheric electron density distribution, thereby disturbing the radio propagation channel and directly degrading the quality of high frequency (HF) communication links. This study investigates the propagation characteristics and communication availability of a representative single‐hop, point‐to‐point HF link in an additional‐ionization environment 5 min after a HANE. An additional‐ionization environment is constructed by superposing HANE‐induced ionization onto the International Reference Ionosphere 2020 (IRI‐2020) natural ionosphere. Three‐dimensional magnetoionic point‐to‐point ray tracing is used to perform frequency sweeps and identify geometrically accessible paths and multipath structures. Link‐budget calculations are further integrated with signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR) and bit‐error rate (BER) evaluations to establish a three‐tier framework consisting of geometrical accessibility, analog‐link availability, and digital‐link availability. The results show that additional ionization substantially contracts the frequency bands available for HF communication. For the prescribed link configuration, the available bands are restricted to 3.6–7.8 MHz for the ordinary (O) mode and 4.4–8.0 MHz for the extraordinary (X) mode. Although some high frequency paths exhibit geometrically resolvable multipath, enhanced absorption reduces the received SNR below the communication availability threshold.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are fatal cancers of the central nervous system with a median survival of less than 18 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 20%. Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) fusions represent major oncogenic driver alterations in pHGGs and have been identified in up to 40% of cases. These fusions result in constitutive activation of RTK signaling through ligand-independent oligomerization and engagement of downstream pathways to promote tumor initiation and progression. Of these RTK fusion driven pHGGs, MET fusions have been identified in approximately 10% of cases and offer a potential therapeutic target for specific tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Clinical testing of TKIs in RTK fusion driven pHGGs have shown mixed results, often with initial clinical responses followed by tumor progression or recurrence. Such clinical reporting necessitates investigating the mechanisms of RTK fusion driven pHGG responses and resistance to TKI treatment. We and others have previously identified cytoplasmic MET fusions in patient pHGGs and have shown that these MET fusions in combination with loss of tumor suppressors TP53 or CDNK2A are sufficient to transform neuro-glial progenitor cells and induce lethal pHGG tumors in vivo. Ongoing work focuses on the development of immunocompetent murine models of MET fusion driven pHGGs to investigate tumor cell intrinsic and tumor cell extrinsic responses in the tumor microenvironment as well as potential mechanisms of resistance to MET TKI treatments, with a focus on comparing between MET targeted TKIs and their mechanisms of action. Together, this work aims to gain insight into the dynamics of TKI treatments of RTK fusion driven pHGGs in order to inform the development of new and improved treatment strategies for these tumors.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Increasing shares of variable renewable electricity (VRE) are creating more frequent periods of surplus electricity, increasing the need for flexible options that can absorb and use this excess generation. One option is to convert surplus electricity into heat, but its effective use requires storage when heat production and demand do not coincide. Because heat demand remains concentrated in the colder months, long-duration seasonal thermal storage is needed to bridge this temporal gap. High-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage (HT-ATES) is one technology capable of providing this seasonal storage function. This study develops a demand-oriented operational probability of success (PoS) framework for evaluating whether HT-ATES can convert historically observed surplus electricity into useful seasonal heat. The Neubrandenburg system in Germany was used as a physically grounded reference case. Historical German electricity data from 2015 to 2022 were represented through empirical four-week surplus distributions and coupled to a chronological Monte Carlo inventory model accounting for charging availability, well thermal throughput, adopted storage limit, and thermal recovery. The model first generated a distribution of achievable seasonal heat delivery, which was then evaluated against alternative heat-demand targets. PoS is therefore expressed as the probability that delivered heat meets or exceeds a specified thermal requirement, rather than as a fixed property of the aquifer. For the base configuration, with a thermal power of approximately 3.72 MW, an adopted storage limit of 12 GWh, and a recovery factor of 0.72, the 20,000 retained Monte Carlo cycles produced a mean seasonal delivery of 8.551 GWh. The upper modeled heat delivery of 8.640 GWh was reached in 94.63% of the cycles. Constraint diagnostics showed that well throughput was the unique limiting condition in 57.06% of injection decisions, remaining storage space in 28.82%, and zero-surplus charging windows in 10.90%, while positive-surplus magnitude alone did not limit any base-case injection decision. Sensitivity analyses further showed that increasing thermal power shifts the range of heat-demand targets that can be met with high probability, but the benefit diminishes as the modeled upper delivery limit is approached. Equivalent non-interacting doublet configurations exhibit the same throughput-storage-limit trade-off. The results demonstrate that nominal storage capacity alone is insufficient for assessing HT-ATES performance. Operational success depends jointly on charging opportunities, thermal power, storage capacity, thermal recovery, system configuration, and the thermal target used to define success. The proposed framework provides a transferable screening method for linking historical energy-system variability with subsurface storage constraints and explicit heat-delivery requirements.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) productivity is influenced by planting geometry, plant population, crop growth and rainfall distribution. The high-density planting system (HDPS) has emerged as an alternative to conventional cotton cultivation because it can improve productivity per unit area despite lower boll production per plant on light soils. A field-based comparative evaluation was undertaken to assess the growth and yield performance of cotton under three planting methods: high-density planting system (T1), closer spacing (T2) and conventional planting (T3), under the agroclimatic conditions of Mancherial District, Telangana, India. The observations included plant height and the number of functional leaves at 30, 60, 90 and 120 days after sowing (DAS), sympodial branches per plant, dry matter accumulation, bolls per plant and seed cotton yield (q/acre). The reported monthly rainfall from June to November totalled 1,193.99 mm, with the highest rainfall in August (372 mm), followed by September (336 mm) and July (239.22 mm). Conventional planting recorded the highest plant height (120 cm), number of sympodial branches (18 per plant), dry matter accumulation (142 g per plant) and number of bolls per plant (32). In contrast, HDPS recorded the highest reported seed cotton yield (12.50 quintals per acre), followed by closer spacing (11.00 q/acre) and conventional planting (8.50 q/acre). The yield under HDPS was 13.64% higher than that under closer spacing and 47.06% higher than that under conventional planting.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>
                    Efficiently harvesting thermal energy from human skin poses formidable challenges owing to its high‐entropy characteristics. While Seebeck‐effect wearable thermoelectric devices can convert skin heat flux into electrical voltage, prevailing generators remain constrained in delivering sustainable energy and multifunctionality. This limitation stems from a fundamental trade‐off where the output voltage falls below the effective charging threshold, leaving the ultra‐low skin heat flux underexplored for physiological sensing. In this study, we report a skin‐interfaced wearable thermoelectric sensor and generator that synchronously harvests body high‐entropy energy and monitors deep tissue temperature (< 0.2°C). This dual functionality is enabled by a thermal meta‐design that guides inherently dispersed cutaneous heat flux into a vertical, one‐dimensional path through geometric confinement, ensuring signal fidelity for both sensing and energy conversion. To overcome the limited skin‐ambient temperature gradient, we introduce a reusable cooling hydrogel patch based on a dual‐mode evaporation mechanism, boosting the electrical output to 120 mV and power density to 45.7 μW cm
                    <jats:sup>–2</jats:sup>
                    . Furthermore, during daily wear under an approximate 10 K skin‐environment temperature differential, the system achieved a sustained output of up to 34 mV. The integrated voltage boost‐storage circuit maintained the capacitor voltage at around 1.044 V, facilitating a sustainable power supply to electronic loads, and stabilized at approximately 5.2 V near full charge. The integrated system demonstrates continuous, multi‐parameter health monitoring powered solely by body heat. This research establishes a co‐design paradigm for concurrent deep body temperature monitoring and high‐entropy energy recovery, paving the way for self‐powered, multimodal integrated wearable devices.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We introduce a systematic analysis of density functional approximation errors in solids by separating functional-driven from density-driven contributions using quantum Monte Carlo densities of silicon, sodium chloride, and copper as reference. Typically, functional errors dominate, but we identify important exceptions where the xc component of the density-driven error exceeds the functional error, notably for SOGGA11 in the semiconductor and the insulator. Material dependence is striking: 61% of functionals show error cancellation in silicon versus 16% in copper, and only five functionals surpass LDA accuracy for metallic copper even with exact densities. For silicon and sodium chloride, GILL or BECKE exchange combined with PBE, PW91, or P86 correlation achieves near-exact xc energies on QMC densities, while copper requires specialized functionals like PBEsol or PBELYP. High-quality densities consistently reduce density-driven errors across all systems. Historical analysis reveals that 1990s GGA functionals outperform many modern meta-GGAs, contradicting expectations of systematic improvement along Jacob’s ladder. These results provide practical guidance for functional selection and highlight implications for machine learning potential development, where material-dependent error cancellation may compromise transferability.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>We start with a brief introduction to the many faces of the Sun, the dynamic star that is the main source of space weather. We explain the need for spacecraft observations, the structure of the solar atmosphere, and the Sun’s magnetic cycle. Next, we focus on the Sun’s influence on Earth, define ‘space weather,’ and briefly discuss its effects on our technology and related socio-economic impacts. Then, we present data-driven, physics-based simulation models with predictive capabilities that enable forecasting and mitigation. We focus on models developed by my team at KU Leuven and the results and predictions they produce: the heliospheric wind and CME evolution models EUHFORIA and ICARUS, the global solar corona model COCONUT, and the solar energetic particle acceleration and transport model Particle Radiation Asset Directed at IP Space Exploration.                     <jats:p>Although neuroimaging has identified network abnormalities in panic disorder (PD), the rapid and transient nature of panic symptoms highlights the need for methods with high temporal resolution. This study used high‐density electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate cortical network alterations in PD and explore their potential as translational biomarkers.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This longitudinal study enrolled 52 drug‐naïve PD patients and 43 healthy controls. High‐density (128‐channel) resting‐state EEG was collected from both groups at baseline, with repeat assessments performed in PD patients after 6 weeks of venlafaxine treatment. Source‐level functional connectivity and network topology were analyzed to characterize cortical network features. Support vector machine (SVM) was used to evaluate the discriminative potential of baseline network features.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At baseline, PD patients showed frequency‐specific network disruptions, with enhanced connectivity within and between the default mode network, frontoparietal network, and dorsal attention network in the α band, but reduced connectivity across multiple networks in the θ and δ bands. Graph theory analysis revealed decreased global efficiency and increased characteristic path length in the α and δ bands. The SVM classifier achieved 86.32% accuracy in distinguishing PD patients from controls. Following treatment, clinical improvement was accompanied by network reorganization, including increased global efficiency and small‐worldness in the α band, and enhanced fronto‐temporal connectivity in the δ band. Exploratory brain–behavior associations did not survive FDR correction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PD is characterized by frequency‐specific cortical network disruptions that show dynamic reorganization following treatment. These findings highlight the potential of EEG‐derived network features as candidate markers for PD identification and treatment monitoring.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>We develop a kinetic model of electron–ion inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas that extends the conventional constant-Coulomb-logarithm treatment. The model incorporates the velocity dependence of the Coulomb logarithm and plasma screening directly into the electron–ion collision frequency, while a super-Gaussian electron distribution is used to account for non-Maxwellian distortions. The formulation explicitly retains magnetization and circular-polarization effects and yields asymptotic scaling laws for magneto-inertial fusion (MIF) plasmas and microwave-heated magnetically confined plasmas. The results show that the velocity-dependent Coulomb logarithm can either reduce or enhance absorption depending on the electron distribution, whereas plasma screening systematically suppresses it. Under the conditions studied, the complete collisional model changes the MIF absorption rate by about 19% relative to the thermal-logarithm approximation. In the microwave-heated regime, the corresponding reduction is about 6% over the whole density range considered. These results highlight the need to treat non-Maxwellianity, velocity-dependent collisions, and plasma screening self-consistently when modeling inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in magnetized fusion plasmas.</jats:p>

title: Luminescent Molecular Logic: Fundamentals, Implementation Strategies, and Emerging Architectures

affiliation.name: Departamento de Física and IUdEA Universidad de La Laguna  San Cristóbal de La Laguna Santa Cruz de Tenerife Spain

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The increasing demand for energy‐efficient, adaptable, and environment‐responsive information processing is motivating the exploration of computing paradigms that complement conventional silicon electronics. Among these, luminescent molecular logic offers a versatile approach in which chemical, physical, or optical stimuli are converted into measurable photophysical outputs and interpreted according to Boolean operations. This Review critically examines the principles, implementation, and validation of luminescent molecular logic, with particular emphasis on the methodological transition from continuous optical signals to reproducible digital outputs. A systematic framework is discussed encompassing photophysical measurements, response‐function selection, uncertainty propagation, signal digitization, threshold definition, truth‐table construction, and logic‐gate assignment. Particular attention is also given to the distinction between independent optical channels and mathematically derived response functions, as well as to interrogation‐level reconfiguration, data‐analysis‐level reassignment, and material‐level reprogramming. Quantitative figures of merit are introduced to assess state discrimination, reproducibility, stability, crosstalk, and scalability beyond qualitative gate assignment. Representative supramolecular, photochromic, DNA‐based, carbon‐dot, and trivalent‐lanthanide platforms are critically compared in terms of their capabilities, limitations, and prospects for integration. Finally, current bottlenecks and emerging opportunities in multidimensional luminescence, adaptive architectures, and hybrid molecular–photonic and molecular–electronic systems are discussed.</jats:p>

title: Neural architecture of the jhānas: a gamma-infraslow duet with quantum overtones

affiliation.name: Independent Researcher

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Building on previous electrophysiological investigations that posited meditative absorption (jhāna) as a radical disruption of sensory default consciousness (DCs), this study explores the underlying non-linear neural architectures and state transitions. Re-analysis of long-duration (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 18) DC-stabilized records reveals that alpha spindles index three distinct developmental stages of the first jhāna, reflecting attentional mastery through
                    <jats:italic>vitakka</jats:italic>
                    (directed attention) and
                    <jats:italic>vicāra</jats:italic>
                    (sustained attention). A broadband (0.005–150 Hz) 3D eLoreta source analysis of a major 4,000 µV relaxation-oscillation (R-O) transition into the second jhāna, confirms the active silencing of fronto-temporal linguistic networks, leading to the profound mental stillness characteristic of higher absorption states. This macro state transition is driven by a near-absolute variance concentration of infraslow rhythms localized to the midline vertex (
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                     = 70) supplementary motor area (SMA), supported by a lateralized left-hemisphere temporal and visual-gating gamma network. As the jhāna hierarchy deepens, the brain recruits an unprecedented electrophysiological dynamic range. Spanning four orders of magnitude in time (10
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    –10
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    s) bridging the absolute physical boundaries of human neurobiology, this architecture couples high-amplitude infraslow carriers (2,000–4,000 µV) to ultra-fast gamma microbursts (100–200 µV). This coordinated gamma–infraslow duet constructs an impenetrable, low-entropy Markov blanket, actively insulating the internal cognitive field from sensory perturbation while maintaining waking alertness. Concurrently, the 600-fold deceleration of cortical rhythms at the vertex facilitates heightened synchrony with visceral neurovascular systems. At critical R-O inflection thresholds, brief (1–2 s) global high-gamma microbursts function as inhibitory sweeps across left-lateralized hubs (BA 47, BA 21/22/38), dismantling emerging inner speech to protect absorptive stability. The study further demonstrates that the jhāna hierarchy follows a scale-free trajectory distinct from the θ, α, β frequency bands of default sensory consciousness (DCs), bypassing the 1 Hz deep-sleep transition, replacing nested sensory Markov blankets with a singular global boundary at the fourth-jhāna limit—a system with intriguing similarities to noise-shielded quantum “superposition.” We conclude that jhāna consciousness (JCs) constitutes an autonomous and previously unrecognized, highly structured second-tier of human consciousness, rather than an altered state of (sensory) consciousness (ASC).
                  </jats:p>

title: From Static Structural Coloration to Dynamic Photonics in Metal–Organic and Covalent–Organic Frameworks

affiliation.name: Department of Functional Materials and Catalysis University of Vienna  Vienna Austria

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent–organic frameworks (COFs) combine structural tunability, accessible porosity, and chemically responsive interiors, making them attractive photonic building blocks. Yet in framework‐dominated static architectures, porosity can reduce dielectric contrast and increase the structural coherence required for strong macroscopic optical responses, while disorder, scattering, and processing‐induced defects can further weaken color saturation. This Review examines how refractive‐index contrast, optical interaction depth, positional correlation, scattering, and mechanical integrity collectively govern static MOF‐ and COF‐based photonic platforms. It then discusses dynamic strategies in which pore occupancy, framework dimensions, particle organization, and competing optical pathways become externally addressable through chemical, thermal, mechanical, electric, or magnetic stimuli. Rather than treating porosity and disorder solely as limitations, this Review highlights their potential as functional degrees of freedom. A central design principle therefore emerges, in which photonic performance should be optimized by controlling the type and length scale of order required for a targeted optical function.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Multilevel (ML) neutral-point-clamped (NPC) dual-active-bridge (DAB) topologies have emerged as a promising solution for multiport dc-dc power conversion systems. In particular, the 4L NPC DAB is a promising solution for the auxiliary power module (APM) in electric vehicles (EVs) featuring a multiple-voltage architecture in their auxiliary system (AS). By connecting three low-voltage (LV) battery modules between the 4L dc-link nodes, multiple dc ports with different operating voltages are obtained. Then, EV auxiliary loads can be grouped according to their optimum voltage ratings and supplied from three distinct-voltage dc ports. In this configuration, the main challenge is to regulate the state of charge (SoC) of the LV-battery modules. For this purpose, this paper proposes a moving-discretized-control-set model predictive control (MDCS-MPC) for a 2L–4L NPC DAB in the EV APM application. The proposed control strategy combines the adjustment of modulation angles with the use of redundant switching patterns to regulate the LV-battery modules SoC in a wide operating range, including no-load conditions in the partial-voltage dc ports. Hardware-in-the-loop experiments verify the real-time performance of the proposed control.</jats:p>

title: Non‐Hermitian Induced Unidirectional Guided Resonance

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We propose a method to realize unidirectional guided resonance (UGR) by modulating non‐Hermitian parameters. Owing to the flexible tunability of these parameters, we further merge an exceptional point (EP) with a UGR to form an EP‐UGR point. Our scheme is based on a three‐band system analytically described by a tight‐binding model and implemented in a photonic crystal. Introducing gain and loss induces the UGR: parameter variations split a bound state in the continuum (BIC) into two ‐points. Because the ‐points associated with upward radiation and downward radiation evolve differently, only the downward radiation ‐points re‐merge as the non‐Hermitian parameter varies, thereby forming the UGR. Introducing an additional asymmetry parameter produces an EP. Temporal coupled‐mode theory predicts the existence of the EP‐UGR point, which is realized by precise multi‐parameter tuning that merges the UGR and EP. This work deepens the understanding of UGR formation and provides new insights into light–matter interactions, laser design, and on‐chip photonic devices.</jats:p>

title: A narrow-bandwidth resonance-gated Kuramoto model of individualized gamma entrainment

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Objective. &#xD;We examined whether frequency mismatch between fixed 40 Hz Gamma ENtrainment Using Sensory Stimulation (GENUS) and an assigned local resonance centre reduces simulated entrainment, and what this implies for individualized stimulation.&#xD;Approach. &#xD;A forced Kuramoto population received stimulation through an assumed Gaussian resonance gate. Unforced and ungated controls separated gate effects from oscillator dynamics. We tested bandwidth (BW), coupling, amplitude, gate shape, swept stimulation and a delayed modular network. BW denotes the input gate's standard deviation. Existing event-related synchronization (ERS) and within-visual connectivity-strength data were analyzed with separate observation templates.&#xD;Main results.&#xD;Predictions were conditional on the imposed gate. At BW=0.5 Hz, a 2 Hz mismatch reduced stimulus-referenced phase-locking value (PLV_stim) by 95.0%, from 0.508 to 0.026. At BW=2–3 Hz, reductions were 31.0–46.9% at default coupling and 29.9–51.9% across couplings. Narrow-gate attenuation persisted under tested supercritical coupling. Compensation depended on gate tails and amplitude; finite Gaussian gain permitted compensation at sufficiently large internal drive. Among 200 simulated subjects, matched stimulation yielded 13.71-fold higher PLV_stim than fixed 40 Hz. Sweeps produced transient resonance capture with little subsequent locking. In the delayed network, collective frequencies fell below nodal frequencies, while raw selectivity depended on gate placement and unforced reference locking. Empirical ERS and connectivity strength did not uniquely identify physiological gate BW or validate 0.5 Hz.&#xD;Significance. &#xD;The model quantifies consequences of a narrow-gate hypothesis rather than establishing narrow biological tuning. Results motivate measuring individual stimulation–response curves, including network outcomes, but do not establish an optimal individualized GENUS protocol or support frequency prescription from a resting gamma peak alone.&#xD;</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Precise modulation of carrier dynamics in two‐dimensional (2D) materials is pivotal for the advancement of ultrafast optoelectronics and terahertz (THz) technologies. THz spectroscopy, with its ability to probe photoconductivity on ultrashort timescales without contact effects, serves as a typical tool for this purpose. With particular emphasis on terahertz time‐domain spectroscopy (THz‐TDS) and optical pump–THz probe (OPTP) spectroscopy, this article reviews carrier transport and ultrafast dynamics in representative 2D material systems, including graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), MXenes, and other material classes with extensive THz studies. Special attention is devoted to the regulation of carrier dynamics, interfacial charge‐transfer mechanisms in heterostructures, and their correlations with device performance. Rather than attempting an exhaustive survey of all 2D material families or all THz spectroscopic methodologies, this review adopts a focused perspective on how THz spectroscopy can connect microscopic carrier processes with tunable optoelectronic properties and device functionalities. By synthesizing these insights, this review aims to provide a focused framework for understanding and exploiting the THz optoelectronic properties of 2D materials.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This review surveys the development of uncooled and thermoelectrically cooled photon‐counting detectors capable of single‐photon detection. It introduces photon‐counting principles and key performance metrics, including quantum efficiency (QE), photon detection efficiency (PDE), dark count rate (DCR), afterpulsing, dead time, timing jitter, spectral range, and fill factor. Major detector classes include photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), microchannel plate photomultipliers (MCP‐PMTs), hybrid photon detectors (HPDs), single‐photon avalanche diodes (SPADs), silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), III–V and germanium‐on‐silicon (Ge‐on‐Si) SPADs, and CMOS‐integrated SPAD arrays. Charge‐integration technologies, including EMCCDs, sCMOS/qCMOS sensors, and quanta image sensors (QIS), are also considered in the context of single‐photon sensitivity. The review examines trade‐offs between sensitivity, timing resolution, noise, spectral coverage, scalability, and system integration. Tolerance to excessive optical power is discussed for field‐deployed quantum communication and LiDAR systems. Emerging low‐dimensional and novel semiconductor detectors are critically assessed, distinguishing Geiger‐mode operation from alternative high‐gain approaches. Frequency‐upconversion detection is considered as a complementary approach to room‐temperature photon counting beyond the near‐infrared. Finally, representative detector systems are compared in terms of spectral range, PDE/QE, timing jitter, DCR, operating temperature, and applications.</jats:p>

title: Nanoscale Quantum‐State Mapping in the Scanning Electron Microscope Using Secondary Electron Energy Spectroscopy

affiliation.name: Department of Physics Politecnico di Milano  Milano Italy

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum technologies built on engineered nanostructures require their electronic states characterized at the scale on which they are made, which photoemission cannot reach. Secondary electron energy spectroscopy in a scanning electron microscope captures valence‐band density of states (DOS) information by subtracting two peak‐normalized spectra taken at 0.5 and 1 keV and differentiating the residual. This paper proposes a mechanism: interfacial Auger recombination at the boundary between the beam‐induced contamination layer and the specimen. Electrons injected by the primary beam occupy interface defect states as transient traps, in a steady state where the injected current balances recombination. A trapped electron drops into a metal valence‐band hole and transfers the released energy to an electron at the Fermi level, which escapes into vacuum. Only one valence electron takes part, and the trapped population has a sharp lower edge, so the emitted spectrum is a cumulative integral of the density of states and differentiation directly yields the valence‐band DOS distribution. The predicted one‐to‐one mapping between binding energy and secondary electron energy is confirmed across six elemental solids, with a fitted slope of 0.99 ± 0.02. The model presents the conditions a specimen must meet, each of which could be engineered.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Optical neural networks (ONNs), particularly diffractive neural networks (DNNs), offer a promising computational paradigm owing to their high speed, intrinsic parallelism, and low energy consumption. However, most demonstrated DNNs are static, with their functionalities fixed after fabrication. Although several reconfigurable architectures such as spatial light modulators (SLMs) and electrically controlled digital‐coding metasurfaces have been demonstrated, they often suffer from high power consumption and limited scalability. Here, we introduce an electrochemically reconfigurable diffractive neural network (ECDNN) based on a PANI‐functionalized Pancharatnam‐Berry (PB) phase metasurface, whose optical response is reversibly controlled through electrochemical redox reactions. Using a simultaneous multi‐objective optimization (SMOO) strategy, different computational tasks can be mapped to distinct state configurations. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate a single‐layer ECDNN capable of performing two classification tasks. The system exhibits response times of 30–40 ms for optical transmission under sub‐volt driving voltages, enabling low‐power operation and facilitating compatibility with low‐voltage driving electronics. Numerical studies further extend the state‐conditioned framework to a two‐layer architecture with four predefined state combinations. This work provides a fast, energy‐efficient, and high‐neuron‐density hardware platform for brain‐inspired optical computing.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Separating thermal and laser intensity effects in plasmonic photocatalysis has proven challenging because the two are frequently intertwined. Higher laser intensities will increase any laser-induced heating, making it difficult to isolate the influence of laser intensity and complicating efforts to disentangle thermal versus nonthermal contributions to plasmonic photocatalysis. Here, we decouple laser intensity and laser heating effects by fabricating plasmonic nanostructures with nearly identical optical properties but divergent thermal properties, allowing us to modulate and even eliminate laser heating while applying the same range of laser intensities. We simultaneously perform upconverting nanoparticle (UCNP)-based microscale thermometry and monitor the photocatalyzed dimerization of 4-nitrothiophenol (4-NTP) to 4,4′-dimercaptoazobenzene (DMAB) with Raman spectroscopy. We show that larger temperature rises enhance the reaction and, even more importantly, the temperature rise alone dictates the degree of 4-NTP to DMAB conversion, independent of the applied laser intensity. These results are consistent across two different plasmonic nanostructures. External heating combined with a threshold laser intensity can also drive the reaction, with the degree of conversion again determined solely by the temperature rise. However, despite the critical influence of the temperature rise, external heating alone fails to catalyze the reaction. Leveraging ultrahigh thermal conductivity diamond substrates, which let us increase the laser intensity without inducing heating, we further demonstrate that higher laser intensities increase the reaction rate yet have no effect on the degree of conversion. Thus, although temperature plays an outsize role, the plasmonic photocatalysis process nonetheless cannot be explained by a purely thermal mechanism.</jats:p>

abstract:

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nod-like receptors (NLRs) are intracellular sensors acting as major regulators of cytokine secretion, gene expression and various signaling pathways, modulating immune responses, metabolism and cell fate. Beyond leukocytes, NLRs are also expressed in various non-immune competent cells, however, their expression and function in skeletal muscle, the largest tissue in the human body, are largely unknown.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We studied NLR expression in response to IFN-γ treatment in
                      <jats:italic>ex vivo Tibialis anterior</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      C2C12 myoblast (MB) and myotube (MT) with RT-qPCR and Western blot. We focused on the assessment of gene expression changes and cytokine production in MT following IFN-γ priming and activation of NOD1, a key NLR identified, using RNA-seq, RT-qPCR and ELISA, followed by functional studies to understand its immunomodulatory roles. NOD1 function in the context of differentiation of MT was studied with scratch assay, while lipid droplet accumulation was determined with Oil Red O staining.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found that the expression of regulatory NLRs (NOD1, NOD2, NLRX1, NLRC3) dynamically changed during MB to MT differentiation, and identified NOD1, as a key immunomodulatory NLR in skeletal muscle. IFN-γ treatment in MT highly induced NOD1 expression, and NOD1 activation following IFN-γ priming resulted in global gene expression changes. We found that most myokines are induced in a NOD1-dependent manner, while a cluster of genes related to migration and differentiation were strongly downregulated. In particular, upon IFN-γ priming NOD1 regulates IL-6 production via NF-kB. In addition, IFN-γ-induced NOD1 strongly reduces the differentiation of MT, while enhances lipid accumulation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results show that while NLRs are expressed in MB and dynamically change during MT differentiation, NOD1 has important, so far uncharacterized function in skeletal muscle. Our results suggest that NOD1 and tentatively other NLRs in the skeletal muscle are connected to diverse physiological and pathological processes, implying their potential roles in myopathies or as therapeutic targets in other disease states.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract: <jats:p>Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a rapidly growing neurological disorder characterized by motor and non-motor symptoms associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Photobiomodulation (PBM) may modulate mitochondrial pathways. This randomized, controlled, single-blind pilot trial investigated intranasal and transpalatal PBM, individually or combined, in 48 individuals with idiopathic PD allocated to TP + IN (intranasal + transpalatal PBM), IN (intranasal PBM), TP (transpalatal PBM), or Sham. Participants underwent 24 sessions over 12 weeks using near-infrared light (808 nm, 100 mW, 60 J, or 120 J per point). Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T1), 1 week after the intervention (T2), and 1-month follow-up (T3) using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS). Forty participants completed the study. IN significantly improved MoCA and MDS-UPDRS scores, with benefits persisting at follow-up. Sham showed a decline in MoCA. These findings suggest that intranasal PBM may be a promising adjunctive therapy for PD; further studies are needed to elucidate mechanisms and optimize treatment protocols.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hollow‐core anti‐resonant fibers (HC‐ARFs) have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional solid‐core fibers (SCFs) by combining low loss, broad transmission bandwidth, ultra‐low nonlinearity, low dispersion, and reduced latency. This review critically examines advances in HC‐ARFs from structural evolution and guiding physics to applications and deployment. We trace the progression from Kagome and single‐ring designs to nested and double‐nested architectures, and discuss anti‐resonant reflection, inhibited coupling, cladding density of photonic states, major loss mechanisms, and machine‐learning‐assisted prediction and design. We further review applications in ultrafast and nonlinear optics, gas and mid‐infrared lasers, ultraviolet guidance, high‐power delivery and extreme photonics, as well as high‐capacity, ultra‐wideband, long‐haul, quantum, and advanced optical communications. Particular attention is given to fabrication tolerances, reproducibility, bending sensitivity, interconnection, environmental stability, scalability, cost, and system‐level integration. Finally, we identify remaining bottlenecks and prospects for beyond‐fifth‐generation and sixth‐generation networks, artificial‐intelligence data interconnection, next‐generation optical networks, quantum technologies, high‐power laser delivery, and extreme photonics.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Stokes parameters are three real parameters that completely characterize partially coherent light spanned by two modes – whether a pair of polarization or spatial modes – whose use is ubiquitous in optics. Whereas the Stokes parameters are defined through an expansion of the  coherence matrix in terms of Pauli matrices, it has been theorized that the  Gell–Mann matrices – developed in high‐energy particle physics – can serve as a basis for  coherence matrices for three‐mode light. This entails eight Stokes–Gell–Mann (SGM) parameters required for the polarization of non‐paraxial fields (spanned by three polarization modes), and fields comprising three spatial or temporal modes. Here we present the first measurements of the SGM parameters for partially coherent three‐mode light in a photonic integrated platform comprising a hexagonal mesh of Mach–Zehnder interferometers. Measuring the SGM parameters on chip, from which we reconstruct the  coherence matrix, facilitates exploring the full space of iso‐entropy fields that can be inter‐converted into each other unitarily and those that cannot. These results pave the way to utilizing multimode partially coherent light in applications involving optical communications, sensing, and information processing.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>
                    Polarization control is essential for modern optical systems. Recently, 2D materials featuring highly anisotropic absorption across broad wavelength regions have emerged as a promising solution for realizing optical polarizers with operation bandwidths far exceeding those achievable using bulk materials. Despite this, existing 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers face critical limitations in simultaneously delivering high polarizer figures of merit (FOMs), robust power endurance, and scalable fabrication, hindering their practical deployment beyond the laboratory. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by demonstrating optical polarizers through integrating 2D MXene films onto silicon photonic devices and subsequently converting them in situ into 2D titanium dioxide (TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ). The 2D TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    exhibits significantly improved anisotropic absorption and thermal/chemical stability compared with MXene, enabling the hybrid polarizers that achieve high polarizer FOMs of up to ∼19.3 (a record among 2D‐material‐coated devices) and excellent power tolerance (stable under > 2 W coupled average power), together with a broad operation bandwidth (> 140 nm) and a high fabrication yield (∼98%). We also demonstrate microring resonator polarizers achieving high polarization extinction ratios of up to ∼12 dB. With outstanding overall performance and strong potential for large‐scale manufacturing, these devices represent a solid step toward industrial implementation of 2D‐material‐based optical polarizers.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Periodically driven coupled waveguides provide an ideal platform for exploring nonlinear Floquet dynamics. While nonlinear states matching the driving period are well‐understood, multi‐period Floquet states—which break discrete time‐translation symmetry and are closely related to discrete time crystals—remain largely unexplored, especially beyond the period‐doubling regime and in their connection to T‐periodic states. Here, we reveal multi‐period nonlinear states that bifurcate from their T‐periodic counterparts in a waveguide‐based Floquet system. By utilizing the phase angle of the Floquet multiplier governing T‐periodic state stability, we establish a general rule to identify the bifurcation point. In the weak nonlinearity regime, stable and unstable branches of multi‐period nonlinear states bifurcate precisely at this point, whereas a slight shift occurs under strong nonlinearity. Using this framework, we discover multi‐period Floquet states beyond the period‐doubling regime. Our work uncovers a fundamental link between T‐periodic and multi‐period nonlinear solutions, opening new avenues for designing discrete‐time‐crystal‐inspired photonic devices.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Scar formation is a physiological tissue repair process that may lead to structural and functional changes affecting tissue mobility, elasticity, and overall tissue quality. In this context, low-level laser therapy has been investigated as a complementary physiotherapeutic approach for scar management. This study aimed to analyze the effects of low-level laser therapy in the treatment of scars, considering its potential benefits for tissue repair and scar characteristics. This literature review was conducted through the analysis of scientific studies addressing the use of laser therapy and photobiomodulation in different types of scars. A total of 16 articles were selected, eight of which were considered more closely related to the research objective and were included in the discussion. The analyzed studies reported favorable outcomes regarding scar thickness, elasticity, pigmentation, pliability, pain, and pruritus, although differences were observed according to scar type, therapeutic modality, treatment parameters, and intervals between sessions. It was concluded that low-level laser therapy has potential as a complementary resource in physiotherapeutic scar management, requiring individualized treatment and continuous assessment of clinical response. Further studies with greater methodological standardization are needed to establish more consistent therapeutic parameters.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Introdução: O pé diabético é uma das complicações do diabetes mellitus e pode ocasionar úlceras de difícil cicatrização, infecções e amputações de membros inferiores. Nesse contexto, a laserterapia tem sido investigada como recurso complementar para favorecer a reparação tecidual e contribuir para o tratamento dessas lesões. Objetivo: avaliar a utilização da laserterapia como recurso fisioterapêutico no tratamento de pacientes com úlceras do pé diabético.  Materiais e Método: Trata-se de uma revisão integrativa da literatura, realizada a partir da análise de 15 estudos científicos publicados entre 2022 e 2026, incluindo ensaios clínicos, estudos de caso, revisão bibliográfica, estudo observacional e pesquisas exploratórias. Os trabalhos selecionados abordaram diferentes modalidades de laserterapia aplicadas ao tratamento de úlceras do pé diabético. Resultados e discussão: Os estudos analisados apontam resultados promissores quanto ao uso da laserterapia como recurso complementar no tratamento de úlceras do pé diabético, com potencial para favorecer a cicatrização e a recuperação dos tecidos. Contribuição Científica: O estudo contribui para ampliar o conhecimento sobre a aplicação da laserterapia no tratamento do pé diabético, destacando suas possibilidades terapêuticas e a importância de sua associação aos cuidados convencionais e às medidas de autocuidado. Conclusão: A laserterapia pode auxiliar na cicatrização das úlceras do pé diabético, como complemento ao tratamento convencional, sendo a Fisioterapia importante em sua aplicação e acompanhamento.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is commonly served as a sealing element for oil-tight seals in ultra-high voltage converter stations. Due to the harsh environmental conditions in these stations, NBR is frequently exposed to thermal oxidation, ultraviolet radiation, and low temperatures, as well as the effects of the sealed medium. This work focuses on evaluating the impacts of various environmental conditions on the mechanical characteristics of NBR and analyzes the underlying mechanisms. Stress distribution under the combined action of force, heat and hypothetical electric field is analyzed with the aid of ABAQUS simulation; the aging test only investigates single factors without verifying the multi-field coupling mechanism, and the conclusions are only for qualitative reference of the simulation. The service life of NBR is effectively predicted based on the compression set decay curve. Analysis of TGA measurements reveals the gradual loss of incorporated additives upon aging, accompanied by a reduction in the thermal stability of aged NBR. Results from crosslinking density tests, FTIR, and XPS analyses demonstrate that oxidation crosslinking progressively increases as thermal-oxidative aging proceeds, the rise in C–C and C–H content is associated with the degradation of C=C bonds, oxygen-containing functional groups (carboxyl, hydroxyl, and carbonyl) are generated during the thermal-oxidative aging of NBR, and the cleavage of C–S bonds leads to the formation of S=O species.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>The exploration of topological states has emerged as a vibrant frontier across diverse physical systems. Among these, the Möbius strip stands out as a canonical structure that has recently inspired intriguing optical physics. In this work, we extend this concept into the high‐dimensional realm by using an optical analogue—the optical Möbius snail. Specifically, employing a skyrmionic beam as the input field, tight focusing yields a continuous family of Möbius strips that exist in three‐dimensional space, giving rise to a snail‐like polarization topological texture. Furthermore, we demonstrate full‐field polarization tomography and achieve switchable control of this optical snail texture by tuning the Skyrme number of the incident skyrmionic beam. Our findings establish a direct bridge between low‐ and high‐dimensional Möbius geometries, opening a new platform for exploring complex spatial topology and tailored light‐matter interactions.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pediatric central nervous system lesions represent a unique clinical challenge, with brain tumors being the most common solid neoplasms in children and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) carrying significant hemorrhagic risk. Gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) has emerged as a promising minimally or non-invasive treatment modality for pediatric patients when conventional surgical options are limited, lesions are surgically inaccessible, or in cases of recurrence or residual disease; however, GKRS data for pediatric patients remains limited, and long-term toxicity data are lacking. We retrospectively reviewed all patients ≤ 18 years of age who underwent GKRS at our institution from an IRB approved database. Patients were stratified by indication (AVMs vs. neoplastic lesions), and dosimetric parameters were analyzed. Primary outcomes included local control and AVM obliteration, assessed using Kaplan-Meier methodology, with obliteration confirmed by MRA or digital subtraction angiography. Secondary outcomes included CNS toxicity. From 1997 to 2024, 61 patients with 111 lesions were identified (median age 13.7 years). Median follow-up was 80.7 months for AVMs and 40.3 months for neoplastic lesions. AVMs accounted for 59% of cases and neoplasms accounted for 41%, which included benign (48%), malignant (32%), and metastatic (20%) tumors. For neoplastic lesions, median tumor volume was 0.86 cc and median margin dose was 18.5 Gy; local control at median follow up was 91.8%. For AVMs, median nidus volume was 5.55 cc with a median margin dose of 20 Gy; obliteration occurred in 44.4% of patients at median follow up, with a median time to obliteration of 2.9 years (range 1.5 – 10 years). Of all GKRS patients, grade 3 or higher toxicity was seen in 3.1% of patients. No second malignant neoplasms were seen. GKRS demonstrates favorable outcomes in pediatric CNS lesions with low rates of high-grade toxicity, supporting its role as a safe and effective treatment option in carefully selected patients, though further evaluation of long-term effects and treatment interactions is warranted.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) remains a lethal pediatric malignancy, with a median overall survival of &lt; 12 months and no curative therapeutic options. B7-H3 and HER2 represent compelling therapeutic targets in pediatric DIPG, given their frequent co-expression across patient-derived tumor specimens and limited expression in normal CNS tissue. Yet current chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T strategies using alpha-beta T cells have not yet performed adequately against CNS tumors with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Gamma delta (γδ) T cells are an intriguing allogeneic effector cell therapy platform by virtue of their MHC-unrestricted cytotoxicity, innate stress-ligand sensing, and negligible alloreactive potential. We recently published a scalable, non-viral engineering platform to generate polyclonal γδ chimeric antigen receptor T cells that is amenable to simultaneous high-fidelity Cas9 base editing for gene knockout or modification.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>We sought to preclinically test a novel dual-CAR γδ T cell product that recognizes both B7-H3 and HER2. The dual-CAR architecture pairs a B7-H3 scFv/CD28 CAR with a HER2 scFv/4-1BB CAR, forming disulfide-bonded heterodimers that share a single CD3ζ signaling domain to reduce tonic signaling and exhaustion. Our pipeline achieved 60–67% dual-CAR transgene expression and 10,000-fold outgrowth. Critically, our dual-CAR γδ T cells demonstrated in vitro cytotoxicity as measured through effector cytokine production and functional killing across multiple patient-derived DIPG lines (SU-DIPG13, SU-DIPG36), underscoring their therapeutic potential against clinically relevant tumor models.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Ongoing work with this dual-CAR γδ platform includes evaluating base editor-driven KO of four independent negative immune regulators (CBL-b, CISH, SOCS1, and HPK1), assessing whether individual gene disruption enhances effector cytokine production and maintains cytotoxic function under immunosuppressive conditions in suppressive 2D and 3D tumor killing assays.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Collectively, these findings provide early preclinical proof-of-concept for a modular, non-viral dual-CAR γδ T cell platform, motivating further in vivo validation toward clinical translation for DIPG.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Geometric phases have long been confined to the cross‐polarized channel under circularly polarized incidence. Their manipulation in the co‐polarized channel remains challenging. Exceptional points (EPs), where eigenvalues and eigenvectors simultaneously coalesce in non‐Hermitian systems, provide topological degrees of freedom for field manipulation. Using temporal coupled‐mode theory (TCMT), we demonstrate EPs in the co‐polarized transmission channel of broadband high‐transmission metasurfaces. The metasurfaces comprise a multilayer metal‐dielectric structure with top and bottom patches connected by metallized vias. Counter‐rotation of the metallic layers breaks out‐of‐plane mirror symmetry and introduces structural chirality. This produces direction‐asymmetric effective coupling in a selected circular‐polarization channel while the full electromagnetic system remains Lorentz reciprocal. By tailoring the projected input and output coupling parameters, the scattering operator is brought to Jordan form, thereby constructing EPs in the co‐polarized channel. The EPs introduce phase singularities and branch cuts that reconstruct the winding behavior and phase evolution of the complex transmission trajectory in parameter space, thereby reshaping the conventional geometric‐phase accumulation. Using the reconstructed phase response, we realize broadband, high‐efficiency, large‐angle wavefront decoupling of orthogonal circularly polarized channels. This work extends EP‐based topological phase manipulation to the co‐polarized channel and provides a platform for broadband, direction‐asymmetric, polarization‐stable transmissive wavefront shaping.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate prediction of isotope distributions is essential for high-resolution mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of biomolecules. We present Pointless 2.0, an updated and unified framework extending our previous Pointless4DNA and Pointless4Peptides models. Pointless 2.0 overcomes key limitations of earlier implementations by introducing a data transformation that enables the use of simple linear models in place of more complex statistical approaches, substantially improving computational efficiency and addressing statistical drawbacks without compromising accuracy. In contrast to prior versions, the framework includes dedicated models for predicting isotope distributions from experimentally measured average mass, in addition to the traditional monoisotopic mass−based approach. Benchmarking against earlier models demonstrates comparable predictive performance while achieving substantial reductions in computational time. Pointless 2.0 further introduces a convolution-based strategy, called IsoSwap, to account for sulphur contributions and post-translational modifications in peptides and oligonucleotides. This modular convolution framework eliminates the need for separate sulphur-specific peptide models and enables flexible post hoc adjustment of isotope distributions. Finally, we present a method to reconstruct monoisotopic and centroid masses from predicted isotope probabilities and experimentally observed average mass, thereby removing dependence on directly observable monoisotopic peaks. The framework further offers an optional intensity-weighted mass-drift correction that estimates and removes a constant calibration offset between predicted and observed isotope masses, validated on experimental DNA spectra spanning seven charge states. Collectively, Pointless 2.0 provides a unified, extensible, and computationally efficient platform for isotope distribution modelling in mass spectrometry. Pointless 2.0 is available at https://github.com/VilenneFrederique/pointless.</jats:p>

                    <jats:italic>Porites</jats:italic>

                    <jats:sup>208</jats:sup>

                    <jats:sup>208</jats:sup>

                    Pb composition than Dongsha, whereas the middle-to-late change within Lutao itself was not statistically resolved. This contrast shows that inter-site isotopic differences need not imply an equivalent temporal shift at an individual site. Published Pb isotope reference fields are compatible with multiple possible source combinations but do not uniquely identify historical sources or marine transport mechanisms. Together, these results reveal spatial heterogeneity in coral Pb isotope histories, with smaller inter-site differences during 1964–1984, and highlight the need to evaluate the spatial representativeness of individual coral Pb isotope records before extrapolating site-specific signatures to regional historical interpretations.

                    <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) with isotope-based approaches has demonstrated a strong potential for enhancing the analysis of hydrological processes, tracer dynamics, system responses, and strengthening water resource management under increasing environmental pressures.                     <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To fill this knowledge gap, this paper conceptualizes perspectives on the application of AI/ML tools in isotope hydrology to promote sustainable water management. Results were developed based on the expert consultations and group work following the modified Delphi and Nominal Group Technique method. Fourteen international experts with diverse background worked together during the technical meeting coordinated by International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) (Vienna, Austria, 2025).</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diverse applications of AI/ML methods to enhance interpretation of isotope data, improve isotope-enabled modeling accuracy, and support decision-making were conceptualized in this paper. The results showed the need for developing interoperable data platforms, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and hybrid physical-AI modeling, ensuring ethical AI/ML practices and the advancement of IAEA Global Water Analysis Laboratory (GloWAL) Network. The approach presented here has broader applicability and could be implemented across other networks and related programmes to support resilient and sustainable water resource management.</jats:p>
