title: Stable Isotope Analysis Reveals Group-Specific Reliance on Elasmobranch Prey by Killer Whales in the Gulf of California
abstract: <jats:p>Killer whales (Orcinus orca) globally exhibit a broad dietary spectrum, ranging from cartilaginous and teleost fish to large marine mammals. However, discrete populations often show prey specialization, which is commonly associated with the evolution of distinct foraging strategies and behavioral adaptations. In the Gulf of California, killer whales have been observed utilizing specialized hunting techniques on a wide range of prey, including different elasmobranch species. To quantify this dietary specialization, we analyzed δ13C and δ15N stable isotope ratios from skin biopsies of eight individuals from two different groups (n = 7 from the group designated as “Moctezuma pod” and n = 1 from a second distinct pod) of killer whales alongside isotopic profiles of six sympatric potential prey species (Mobula munkiana, Delphinus delphis bairdii, Balaenoptera physalus, Carcharodon carcharias, Isurus oxyrinchus, and Tursiops truncatus), as well as estimated trophic position, isotopic niche, and prey contribution by Bayesian mixing models. Killer whales exhibited mean (± SD) isotopic values of -17.04 ± 0.54‰ for δ13C and 19.59 ± 0.69‰ for δ15N, resulting in an estimated trophic position of 4.3. Elasmobranchs, specifically shortfin mako sharks (I. oxyrinchus) and white sharks (C. carcharias), collectively accounted for over 50% of the median estimated dietary contribution. Together with independent observations of elasmobranch predation in the Gulf of California, these results indicate substantial reliance on elasmobranch prey by the sampled killer whales during the dietary period integrated by the sampled tissue and suggest potential trophic specialization, possibly complemented by dietary plasticity. Additional temporal and individual sampling will be necessary to determine the persistence and broader prevalence of this dietary pattern.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diffuse midline gliomas (DMG) primarily rely on glycolysis but exhibit a critical dependence on glutamine (Gln) to fuel the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, maintain epigenetic landscapes, and support proliferation. Consequently, amino acid transporters (AATs), particularly the primary Gln transporter ASCT2, are promising theranostic targets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To characterize the interplay of glucose (Glc), Gln, and AAT metabolism in DMG using in silico, in vitro, and in vivo models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RNA-sequencing data from 505 high-grade tumor patients (CBTN) underwent pathway enrichment and survival modeling. Three patient-derived DMG cell lines were cultured under varying Glc/Gln gradients to evaluate survival and SLC1A5 expression. 13C-isotope tracing was performed on the line with lowest baseline SLC1A5 expression. An orthotopic murine tumor model growth was monitored via bioluminescence, 7T MRI, dynamic [18F]F-Gln, and static [18F]FDG PET/CT. Explanted brains underwent immunohistochemistry (IHC) for metabolic transporters.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analysis of 1,190 metabolic genes revealed significant amino acid pathway enrichment in DMG. Elevated SLC1A5 transcription correlated with poorer event-free and overall survival (p = 0.02, p = 0.003). In vitro, SLC1A5 expression dynamically increased under Gln deprivation and extreme Glc concentrations. While cells were highly Glc-dependent, only 30% survived Gln deprivation. Isotope tracing confirmed Glc primarily drives glycolysis, whereas Gln supplements the TCA cycle (Glc:Gln contribution—lactate 65.83%:4.47%; succinate 7.2%:44.4%; malate 11.6%:59.8%). In vivo, F-Gln tumor uptake was modest compared to FDG (SUVmax 0.5±0.2 vs 2.86±1.2) but demonstrated a higher tumor-to-background ratio (2.37±0.46 vs 1.07±0.01, p = 0.02). IHC confirmed reduced Glut1 and slightly elevated SLC1A5 expression relative to healthy brain tissue.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DMGs exhibit a targetable partial metabolic reliance on Gln for tumor growth. SLC1A5 expression is dynamically regulated by nutrient availability, serving as a strong prognostic indicator. Targeting SLC1A5 and utilizing F-Gln PET as a biomarker warrant further investigation for metabolic and epigenetic interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydrogen governs virtually every stage of heterogeneous catalytic reactions, yet its chemical identity, location, mobility, and mechanistic role are often difficult to establish by experiments. Recent advances in neutron spectroscopy have enabled direct observation of hydrogen species across increasingly complex catalytic systems, generating a rapidly growing body of mechanism insights. However, general principles of hydrogen behaviour have not been fully extracted. In this mini‐review, we present a hydrogen‐centred framework that reorganises recent neutron‐spectroscopic studies around four fundamental questions: what hydrogen species exist, where hydrogen resides, how it moves, and how it participates in catalytic reactions. This mini‐review integrates hydrogen species, spatial distribution, dynamics, and reactivity into understanding across diverse systems, and emphasises how neutron spectroscopy provides direct mechanism insights into the chemistry of hydrogen and enables discrimination between competing catalytic pathways. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future opportunities for combining neutron spectroscopy with complementary experimental and theoretical approaches to establish a more comprehensive understanding of hydrogen‐controlled catalysis.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    This study provides a preliminary assessment of the subsistence base and possible dietary patterns of communities along the lower Syr-Darya River (modern-day Kazakhstan) in Central Asia from the fourth century BCE to the eighteenth century CE, with a deep focus on the medieval period, particularly attention to the Antiquity and Mongol periods. Stable carbon and nitrogen isotope analyses of animal bone collagen (fourth-second centuries BCE and twelfth-fifteenth centuries CE) and human bone collagen (twelfth-fifteenth centuries CE) were combined with archaeobotanical evidence (fourth century BCE to eighteenth century CE) and published palaeoenvironmental data to examine subsistence strategies in these desert-oasis settings. This research challenges several hypotheses previously proposed by scholars, including Aral regressions in Antiquity due to intensive agriculture and irrigation (the second half of the first millennium BCE) and the shift to pastoralism after the Mongol Conquest (the thirteenth to fifteenth century CE). The isotope data further suggest that livestock diets were predominantly based on C
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    resources, while elevated herbivore
                    <jats:italic>δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N values may reflect aridity, soil salinization, or grazing and foddering in nitrogen-enriched environments. Human
                    <jats:italic>δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N values from Kyshkala are consistent with substantial animal-protein consumption, although the specific dietary sources of this enrichment remain uncertain. By providing some of the first isotope data for fish remains from the Syr Darya region, this study establishes a preliminary ecological baseline for future reconstructions of human diet in Mongol and post-Mongol Central Asia. Overall, this pilot study demonstrates the potential of integrating archaeobotanical and stable isotope evidence to critically evaluate existing models of subsistence change. Future research should apply this approach to larger, systematically sampled datasets to test these preliminary interpretations at a regional scale.

abstract:
<jats:sec id="sec001">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rodents (order Rodentia) are the most diverse and geographically widespread order of mammals, occupying virtually all terrestrial ecosystems and playing key ecological roles in food webs and ecosystem functioning. Stable isotope analysis has become a tool for investigating trophic ecology, resource use, habitat use, and movement across spatial and temporal scales. Although isotope applications in rodent ecology have expanded in recent decades, the literature remains diverse, and no comprehensive synthesis currently maps this evidence. This scoping review aims to systematically map and synthesize how stable isotope analysis has been applied in ecological studies of the order Rodentia across diverse ecosystems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="sec002">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This protocol follows the methodology of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), Adelaide, South Australia for scoping reviews and will be reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches will be conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, SciELO, and Google Scholar (first 200 results sorted by relevance), covering studies from database inception to January 2026. Eligible sources will include peer-reviewed articles, master’s theses, and doctoral dissertations published in any language, searches will be conducted in ProQuest, BTDT (Biblioteca digital brasileira de teses e dissertações) and CAPES Theses and Dissertations. Nine reviewers will screen randomized titles and abstracts in pairs, with a pilot-test of 100 random articles to ensure reviewers consistency. Full-text assessment and data charting will be conducted by the reviewer pairs using a standardized form, with a pilot-test verification of a subset of included studies to ensure consistency. No critical appraisal will be performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="sec003">
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This review will provide a structured overview of stable isotope applications in rodent ecology, identifying methodological patterns, ecosystem and geographic coverage, and knowledge gaps to inform future research and evidence syntheses.</jats:p>

                    100 cm) per panel, mounted on wheeled castors for bedside deployment. The two units were deployed together, one along each lateral side of the bed. Scatter dose rates were measured using an radiation survey meter and a portable X-ray unit during phantom radiography across common orthopedic projections at eight angular positions (0°–315° in 45° increments) and five distances (50–250 cm). The two-unit configuration achieved a median scatter dose reduction of 94.1% (IQR: 88.0%–97.7%; Wilcoxon W = 51,360,
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 320,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>

Reductions were broadly consistent across tube voltages (65–85 kVp) and remained substantial across all measurement distances (84.3%–89.6% across 50–250 cm), but varied significantly by angular position, with the highest reduction at 90° (mean 96.91%) and the lowest reductions recorded at 0° (mean 54.02%) and 180° (mean 75.69%). These two directions represented the open axial ends of the setup and were not directly covered by the side-mounted shielding panels. Under a representative high-workload scenario, the two-unit configuration reduced estimated annual occupational doses across all projections, with all post-shielding means remaining well below the average annual occupational dose limit of 20 mSv/year. User feedback was more favorable among radiologic technologists (mean 4.80/5) than among orthopedic ward nurses (mean 3.67/5). The two-unit configuration showed substantial scatter reduction and may serve as an additional protective measure during portable radiography in orthopedic ward settings, with positioning guidance required to maximize protection at clinically relevant angular locations.

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumour showing low survival and characterised by poor therapeutic opportunities. We have recently described the expression of Acid Sensing Ion Channel 3 (ASIC3), a proton gated ion channel, in GBM cancer stem cell (CSC) derived from human biopsies, while low ASIC3 levels in the healthy human brain tissue. We have demonstrated that the chronic activation of ASIC3 by 2-guanidine-4-methylquinazoline (GMQ) selectively induces GBM CSC death while being virtually safe for neurons. To investigate the therapeutic potential of ASIC3 modulation, we virtually designed and synthesized a library of GMQ like compounds. We developed an automated imaging platform to screen compounds affecting CSC-derived neurospheres growth, and we selected a promising lead. ASIC3 specificity was validated using the selective toxin APETx2, as well as the lentiviral shRNA mediated downregulation of ASIC3. The pharmacokinetic of our putative lead was assessed following intravenous administration in mice. ASIC3 modulation by GMQ demonstrated to be more effective than Temozolomide (TMZ), the standard drug used in clinic against GBM, in controlling GBM CSCs growth in vitro. Based on this evidence, a virtual screening of GMQ analogues was performed, enabling the design of novel ASIC3 agonists with enhanced potency and improved predicted pharmacokinetic properties. Subsequent synthesis and a preliminary structure activity relationship (SAR) on GMQ-inspired analogues led to the identification of a new, patentable ASIC3 activator more potent than TMZ and GMQ itself. The efficacy of our lead across GBM CSCs subtypes strongly correlated with ASIC3 expression levels and account for its potential use as a therapeutic opportunity in controlling GBM CSCs growth. Our findings identify chronic ASIC3 activation as a meaningful strategy for the control of GBM CSCs growth. We identified a novel highly selective ASIC3 modulator as an innovative approach for GBM treatment.</jats:p>

                    <jats:italic>The Peony Pavilion — The Youth
						Version</jats:italic>

title: Plasma Immersion Ion Implantation of AISI 316L Stainless Steel Parts Manufactured by Laser Powder Bed Fusion
container-title: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Austenitic stainless steel (SS) AISI 316L is highly compatible with laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), an advanced additive manufacturing (AM) technique for producing high-quality near-net-shape parts with complex geometries, especially for aerospace and medical applications. To further enhance its surface properties, temperature-controlled nitrogen plasma immersion ion implantation (TC-NPIII) was applied to LPBF-manufactured AISI 316L to obtain an expanded austenite (
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N) layer, thereby enhancing surface performance and expanding the applicability of this material in demanding environments. The present work investigates the influence of TC-NPIII treatment temperature and duration on the microstructural evolution and mechanical performance of LPBF-manufactured AISI 316L. Samples were produced by LPBF in a laser-adapted powder bed system and subsequently treated by TC-NPIII, varying treatment duration for 1 and 3 h at controlled temperatures (450-520 °C). Microstructural analysis after treatment revealed a modified layer with a thickness that ranged from approximately 18.30 to 28.40 µm, superimposed on the characteristic LPBF microstructure. Grazing Incidence x-ray Diffraction (GI-XRD) analysis confirmed the formation of the desired
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N phase, while no diffraction peaks associated with chromium nitrides were detected within the investigated processing window. Cross-sectional nanoindentation measurements of the treated samples yielded hardness values of approximately 386-751 HV, representing a substantial increase compared with the untreated LPBF sample (238 HV). These results indicate that, among the treatment temperatures and durations investigated, 450 °C for 3 h represents the optimal processing condition, promoting
                    <jats:italic>γ</jats:italic>
                    N formation while preventing chromium nitride precipitation. The present work demonstrates that TC-NPIII can effectively produce expanded austenite and achieve significant surface hardening within treatment durations as short as 1-3 h. Moreover, these findings confirm the effectiveness of the TC-NPIII treatment in modifying the surface of LPBF-produced AISI 316L stainless steel, thereby enhancing its mechanical performance while preserving the characteristic hierarchical microstructure generated during LPBF.
                  </jats:p>

title: Luminescent Molecular Logic: Fundamentals, Implementation Strategies, and Emerging Architectures

affiliation.name: Departamento de Física and IUdEA Universidad de La Laguna  San Cristóbal de La Laguna Santa Cruz de Tenerife Spain

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The increasing demand for energy‐efficient, adaptable, and environment‐responsive information processing is motivating the exploration of computing paradigms that complement conventional silicon electronics. Among these, luminescent molecular logic offers a versatile approach in which chemical, physical, or optical stimuli are converted into measurable photophysical outputs and interpreted according to Boolean operations. This Review critically examines the principles, implementation, and validation of luminescent molecular logic, with particular emphasis on the methodological transition from continuous optical signals to reproducible digital outputs. A systematic framework is discussed encompassing photophysical measurements, response‐function selection, uncertainty propagation, signal digitization, threshold definition, truth‐table construction, and logic‐gate assignment. Particular attention is also given to the distinction between independent optical channels and mathematically derived response functions, as well as to interrogation‐level reconfiguration, data‐analysis‐level reassignment, and material‐level reprogramming. Quantitative figures of merit are introduced to assess state discrimination, reproducibility, stability, crosstalk, and scalability beyond qualitative gate assignment. Representative supramolecular, photochromic, DNA‐based, carbon‐dot, and trivalent‐lanthanide platforms are critically compared in terms of their capabilities, limitations, and prospects for integration. Finally, current bottlenecks and emerging opportunities in multidimensional luminescence, adaptive architectures, and hybrid molecular–photonic and molecular–electronic systems are discussed.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>The study file presents the activity of the doctoral supervisor, Prof. Ion Buzași, within the Doctoral School of Philology of IOSUD-Alba Iulia. The twenty doctoral theses defended under his coordination during the period 14.07.2009-20.04.2021 are listed in chronological order, and the seven volumes authored by former doctoral students resulting later from the publication of some of these theses are also identified. For each doctoral student, the occupation and current place of work are indicated, as well as the email address. The fifteen academics who have acted as referees within the thesis defense committees are also listed, with their professional affiliation and number of participations. The statistical distribution of former doctoral students by occupation and geographical location is conclusively and succinctly presented, and the number of citations in Google Academic of two of the published volumes of theses is recorded. Finally, three of the doctoral supervisor’s reviews are reproduced, later published as prefaces. In the second part, nineteen other doctoral theses are presented, with the same structural approach, for which Professor Ion Buzași acted as a referent between 10.06.2008 and 15.09.2020, theses coordinated by his colleagues from the Doctoral School.</jats:p>

title: From Static Structural Coloration to Dynamic Photonics in Metal–Organic and Covalent–Organic Frameworks

affiliation.name: Department of Functional Materials and Catalysis University of Vienna  Vienna Austria

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent–organic frameworks (COFs) combine structural tunability, accessible porosity, and chemically responsive interiors, making them attractive photonic building blocks. Yet in framework‐dominated static architectures, porosity can reduce dielectric contrast and increase the structural coherence required for strong macroscopic optical responses, while disorder, scattering, and processing‐induced defects can further weaken color saturation. This Review examines how refractive‐index contrast, optical interaction depth, positional correlation, scattering, and mechanical integrity collectively govern static MOF‐ and COF‐based photonic platforms. It then discusses dynamic strategies in which pore occupancy, framework dimensions, particle organization, and competing optical pathways become externally addressable through chemical, thermal, mechanical, electric, or magnetic stimuli. Rather than treating porosity and disorder solely as limitations, this Review highlights their potential as functional degrees of freedom. A central design principle therefore emerges, in which photonic performance should be optimized by controlling the type and length scale of order required for a targeted optical function.</jats:p>

title: Non‐Hermitian Induced Unidirectional Guided Resonance

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We propose a method to realize unidirectional guided resonance (UGR) by modulating non‐Hermitian parameters. Owing to the flexible tunability of these parameters, we further merge an exceptional point (EP) with a UGR to form an EP‐UGR point. Our scheme is based on a three‐band system analytically described by a tight‐binding model and implemented in a photonic crystal. Introducing gain and loss induces the UGR: parameter variations split a bound state in the continuum (BIC) into two ‐points. Because the ‐points associated with upward radiation and downward radiation evolve differently, only the downward radiation ‐points re‐merge as the non‐Hermitian parameter varies, thereby forming the UGR. Introducing an additional asymmetry parameter produces an EP. Temporal coupled‐mode theory predicts the existence of the EP‐UGR point, which is realized by precise multi‐parameter tuning that merges the UGR and EP. This work deepens the understanding of UGR formation and provides new insights into light–matter interactions, laser design, and on‐chip photonic devices.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Precise modulation of carrier dynamics in two‐dimensional (2D) materials is pivotal for the advancement of ultrafast optoelectronics and terahertz (THz) technologies. THz spectroscopy, with its ability to probe photoconductivity on ultrashort timescales without contact effects, serves as a typical tool for this purpose. With particular emphasis on terahertz time‐domain spectroscopy (THz‐TDS) and optical pump–THz probe (OPTP) spectroscopy, this article reviews carrier transport and ultrafast dynamics in representative 2D material systems, including graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), MXenes, and other material classes with extensive THz studies. Special attention is devoted to the regulation of carrier dynamics, interfacial charge‐transfer mechanisms in heterostructures, and their correlations with device performance. Rather than attempting an exhaustive survey of all 2D material families or all THz spectroscopic methodologies, this review adopts a focused perspective on how THz spectroscopy can connect microscopic carrier processes with tunable optoelectronic properties and device functionalities. By synthesizing these insights, this review aims to provide a focused framework for understanding and exploiting the THz optoelectronic properties of 2D materials.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This review surveys the development of uncooled and thermoelectrically cooled photon‐counting detectors capable of single‐photon detection. It introduces photon‐counting principles and key performance metrics, including quantum efficiency (QE), photon detection efficiency (PDE), dark count rate (DCR), afterpulsing, dead time, timing jitter, spectral range, and fill factor. Major detector classes include photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), microchannel plate photomultipliers (MCP‐PMTs), hybrid photon detectors (HPDs), single‐photon avalanche diodes (SPADs), silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), III–V and germanium‐on‐silicon (Ge‐on‐Si) SPADs, and CMOS‐integrated SPAD arrays. Charge‐integration technologies, including EMCCDs, sCMOS/qCMOS sensors, and quanta image sensors (QIS), are also considered in the context of single‐photon sensitivity. The review examines trade‐offs between sensitivity, timing resolution, noise, spectral coverage, scalability, and system integration. Tolerance to excessive optical power is discussed for field‐deployed quantum communication and LiDAR systems. Emerging low‐dimensional and novel semiconductor detectors are critically assessed, distinguishing Geiger‐mode operation from alternative high‐gain approaches. Frequency‐upconversion detection is considered as a complementary approach to room‐temperature photon counting beyond the near‐infrared. Finally, representative detector systems are compared in terms of spectral range, PDE/QE, timing jitter, DCR, operating temperature, and applications.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Optical neural networks (ONNs), particularly diffractive neural networks (DNNs), offer a promising computational paradigm owing to their high speed, intrinsic parallelism, and low energy consumption. However, most demonstrated DNNs are static, with their functionalities fixed after fabrication. Although several reconfigurable architectures such as spatial light modulators (SLMs) and electrically controlled digital‐coding metasurfaces have been demonstrated, they often suffer from high power consumption and limited scalability. Here, we introduce an electrochemically reconfigurable diffractive neural network (ECDNN) based on a PANI‐functionalized Pancharatnam‐Berry (PB) phase metasurface, whose optical response is reversibly controlled through electrochemical redox reactions. Using a simultaneous multi‐objective optimization (SMOO) strategy, different computational tasks can be mapped to distinct state configurations. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate a single‐layer ECDNN capable of performing two classification tasks. The system exhibits response times of 30–40 ms for optical transmission under sub‐volt driving voltages, enabling low‐power operation and facilitating compatibility with low‐voltage driving electronics. Numerical studies further extend the state‐conditioned framework to a two‐layer architecture with four predefined state combinations. This work provides a fast, energy‐efficient, and high‐neuron‐density hardware platform for brain‐inspired optical computing.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Separating thermal and laser intensity effects in plasmonic photocatalysis has proven challenging because the two are frequently intertwined. Higher laser intensities will increase any laser-induced heating, making it difficult to isolate the influence of laser intensity and complicating efforts to disentangle thermal versus nonthermal contributions to plasmonic photocatalysis. Here, we decouple laser intensity and laser heating effects by fabricating plasmonic nanostructures with nearly identical optical properties but divergent thermal properties, allowing us to modulate and even eliminate laser heating while applying the same range of laser intensities. We simultaneously perform upconverting nanoparticle (UCNP)-based microscale thermometry and monitor the photocatalyzed dimerization of 4-nitrothiophenol (4-NTP) to 4,4′-dimercaptoazobenzene (DMAB) with Raman spectroscopy. We show that larger temperature rises enhance the reaction and, even more importantly, the temperature rise alone dictates the degree of 4-NTP to DMAB conversion, independent of the applied laser intensity. These results are consistent across two different plasmonic nanostructures. External heating combined with a threshold laser intensity can also drive the reaction, with the degree of conversion again determined solely by the temperature rise. However, despite the critical influence of the temperature rise, external heating alone fails to catalyze the reaction. Leveraging ultrahigh thermal conductivity diamond substrates, which let us increase the laser intensity without inducing heating, we further demonstrate that higher laser intensities increase the reaction rate yet have no effect on the degree of conversion. Thus, although temperature plays an outsize role, the plasmonic photocatalysis process nonetheless cannot be explained by a purely thermal mechanism.</jats:p>

title: A Reproducible Multi-Target Computational Framework for Prioritizing Plant-Derived Natural Products in Alzheimer’s Disease

affiliation.name: Pharmaceutical Sciences Department, College of Pharmacy, Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah 21955, Saudi Arabia

abstract: <jats:p>Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is biologically heterogeneous, and plant-derived natural products provide chemically diverse starting points for multi-target discovery. Reproducible prioritization is needed to distinguish literature-supported evidence from candidate-specific predictions not yet generated. Our objective was to develop a reproducible, evidence-informed framework for prioritizing plant-derived natural products in AD and define a transparent candidate library and prespecified screening set for subsequent computational and experimental evaluation. Completed work included selection of an AD target panel (AChE/BChE, BACE1, GSK-3β and MAO-B), synthesis of a published target-specific machine-learning (ML) benchmark, curation of a 20-compound candidate library with traceable chemical identities and literature support, and selection of a 13-compound prespecified screening set. Published performance metrics were treated solely as external benchmark evidence. Study-specific model training, prospective ML screening, molecular docking, BBB/drug-likeness and ADMET evaluation, multi-objective ranking, and experimental validation were prespecified as future work and were not performed. The framework links mechanistically justified targets, published ML benchmarks, a chemically diverse 20-compound library, and a 13-compound set for future screening. The library includes evidence-rich reference compounds and comparatively underexplored scaffolds; no candidate-specific computational ranking or selection outcome is reported. This study presents an evidence-informed, multi-target computational framework for prioritizing plant-derived natural products in Alzheimer’s disease. Its methodological contribution lies in integrating a mechanistically defined target panel, published machine-learning benchmarks, a traceable 20-compound candidate library, and a prespecified 13-compound screening set within a transparent prospective evaluation strategy. By distinguishing completed framework-development activities from future computational and experimental analyses, the study establishes a structured foundation for subsequent model validation, multi-objective prioritization, and experimental investigation.</jats:p>

title: Beta Oscillations as a Mechanistic Target for Predictive Processing Deficits in Psychosis

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Predictive processing abnormalities offer a unifying account of perceptual and expressive disturbances in psychosis, yet their cortical implementation remains incompletely understood. Emerging evidence positions beta-band oscillations and their transient burst dynamics as a biologically plausible mechanism through which top-down contextual information may stabilize internal models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Study Design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This narrative review synthesizes evidence from electrophysiology, laminar physiology, computational modelling, language research, and clinical neuroimaging to evaluate beta oscillations as a mechanistic target for predictive processing deficits in psychosis. We integrate data from modified predictive routing frameworks and dendritic computation models to clarify how beta dynamics may prepare cortical pathways for predicted inputs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Study Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across sensory, motor, cognitive, and language domains, schizophrenia features impaired generation, timing, and contextual deployment of beta activity. Psychomotor beta abnormalities provide the strongest direct clinical evidence, while findings related to disorganization and context-dependent cognition provide convergent support. Perceptual and positive symptom associations remain preliminary. Laminar and computational findings indicate that beta bursts can arise from the integration of apical (contextual) and basal (sensory) dendritic inputs in layer 5 pyramidal neurons, providing a mechanistic substrate for top-down predictions. Beta disruptions, therefore, may contribute to disorganization, psychomotor dysfunction, and impaired contextual stabilization. Early neuromodulation, pharmacologic, and neurofeedback studies suggest that beta dynamics are modifiable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Beta oscillations provide a tractable candidate physiological target for linking predictive processing abnormalities to deficits in psychosis. Standardizing burst metrics and developing individualized, closed-loop approaches will be critical for advancing beta-based interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Pressure-enabled thyroid artery embolization: minimizing the risk of non-target embolization
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Thyroid artery embolization (TAE) conventionally involves embolization of both superior thyroid arteries (STAs) and one inferior thyroid artery (ITA), preserving the contralateral ITA to maintain parathyroid perfusion. Selective STA catheterization carries risks of reflux-related non-target embolization and cerebral thromboembolism due to its origin from the carotid arterial system. Pressure-enabled TAE (PED-TAE) is an ITA-first technique that exploits intrathyroidal anastomoses between the STA and ITA to achieve ipsilateral lobar embolization without direct STA catheterization. The technique uses a valved microcatheter with a self-expanding braided nitinol mesh to reduce reflux and facilitate distal embolic delivery through pressure modulation. This technical letter provides a comprehensive, step-by-step guide to PED-TAE, covering preprocedural vascular assessment, arterial access and device selection, optimal microcatheter positioning, cone-beam CT evaluation, embolization technique, procedural endpoints, and peri- and postprocedural medication management. A practical workflow for patient selection and a procedural decision-making algorithm are presented to guide clinical decision-making, address anatomical and technical challenges, and facilitate reproducible application of the technique. Further prospective multicenter studies are warranted to establish the safety, efficacy, and long-term durability of PED-TAE relative to conventional TAE and surgical management.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Uptake of oxidized and other forms of modified low-density lipoprotein (LDL) drives formation of foam cells, a hallmark of atherosclerotic plaques. Experimental studies demonstrating the proinflammatory and cytotoxic properties of oxidized LDL have led to the concept of LDL oxidation as one key factor in both development and destabilization of atherosclerotic plaques. Such data positioned oxidized LDL as a promising target for prevention or mitigation of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Yet the failure of multiple antioxidants to reduce cardiovascular risk in large randomized clinical trials has hampered this prospect. Such null studies have stimulated interest in an alternative approach: the therapeutic potential of antibodies against oxidized LDL. High levels of IgM against oxidized LDL phospholipids are associated with lower cardiovascular risk and these antibodies function primarily through neutralization and stimulation of clearance of modified LDL. IgG antibodies against aldehyde-modified peptide sequences in apolipoprotein B-100, the signature protein component of LDL, are also associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease but experimental studies have shown that these antibodies function by locally forming immune complexes with oxidized LDL that limit the inflammatory activity of certain plaque macrophages. A phase 2 pilot study showed that one such antibody, orticumab, reduces an imaging index of local coronary arterial inflammation in patients with psoriasis. Thus, emerging evidence supports the possibility of using oxidized LDL antibodies to limit atherothrombotic disease.</jats:p>

title: TMET-14 Novel Therapeutic Target for Glioma: PLIN2 Regulates Glioma Metabolism and Ferroptosis

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioma is a primary malignant tumor of the central nervous system, among which glioblastoma has the highest degree of malignancy. Gliomas enhance their survival capacity through metabolic reprogramming. Previous studies have shown that enhanced lipid metabolism promotes the malignant progression of gliomas, indicating that lipid metabolism plays a crucial role in this context. Lipid droplets are organelles responsible for lipid storage. In recent years, researchers have discovered that lipid droplets not only serve as storage compartments for lipids but also participate in cellular energy metabolism, homeostasis regulation, and interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Previous studies have found that the lipid droplet-coating protein PLIN1 affects the malignant biological behavior of gliomas. We investigated another protein of the PLIN family, PLIN2, which is primarily involved in maintaining the stability of cellular lipid droplets. Through analysis of the public database TCGA, we found that high expression of PLIN2 in glioma cohorts is associated with poor prognosis in glioma patients. Subsequently, we constructed PLIN2-overexpressing and PLIN2-knockout cell lines in glioma cell lines U87 and T98G. Our study found that under treatment with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3, U87 cells overexpressing PLIN2 exhibited lower lipid peroxide levels compared to their control counterparts. We then investigated the effect of PLIN2 on ferroptosis in T98G knockout cell lines and found that PLIN2 knockout increased the sensitivity of T98G cells to ferroptosis, making the cells more prone to undergo ferroptosis. We performed EdU proliferation assays and Transwell migration assays on T98G PLIN2 knockout cell lines and found that the proliferation and migration abilities of PLIN2 knockout cells were weaker than those of the control group. Therefore, in glioma cells, PLIN2 is involved in regulating glioma cell metabolism and the ferroptosis process.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most aggressive and treatment-resistant primary brain tumors, with limited therapeutic options and poor patient outcomes. Radiotherapy is a cornerstone of GBM management, and the recent clinical adoption of tile-based radiation therapy (TBRT), in which implantable cesium-131-embedded collagen tiles placed at resection sites, has enabled localized, sustained radiation delivery to the tumor bed. Limited accessibility, poor compatibility, and lack of precise dose control at small scales limit the ability to replicate clinically relevant radiation conditions in controlled lab settings. In addition, studying the effects of these tiles in vitro is important for validating and better understanding their therapeutic potential observed in vivo.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To address this gap, we developed a novel in vitro platform integrating tile-based radiation therapy with organotypic brain slice cultures (OBSC) and standard plate-based cell cultures to study dose-dependent radiation effects in GBM cells. GBM cell lines were cultured within physiologically relevant microenvironments and exposed to localized continuous radiation that closely mimics clinically relevant brachytherapy conditions. This system enables precise modulation of radiation dose and spatial distribution while preserving critical cell-microenvironment interactions.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Our findings demonstrate a robust and quantifiable radiation response in GBM cells following TBRT exposure. Specifically, we observed a marked increase in phosphorylated H2AX (γ-H2AX), a sensitive marker of DNA double-strand breaks, in a time- and dose-dependent manner. This response was consistent across varying radiation doses in various cell lines, both in vitro and on organotypic brain slice cultures.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Importantly, this in vitro TBRT-OBSC model serves as a translational bridge between conventional radiation studies and clinical applications. By incorporating a clinically relevant radiation modality already used in GBM patients, this platform enhances the predictive value of preclinical studies for brachytherapy. Overall, our approach provides a powerful tool for evaluating radiation dose effects to advance precision radiotherapy research in GBM.</jats:p>

title: Memory-window engineering: target specifications for duration, retention through division, and amplitude in immune epigenome editing

affiliation.name: American Heritage School

abstract: <jats:p>Immune activation, tolerance, exhaustion, trained immunity and regulatory stability are held in place by chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, histone modification, and enhancer-promoter wiring. CRISPR-based epigenome editors rewrite these layers without cutting DNA, but most reports address editing efficiency and leave time unanswered. Target duration is a design input to be specified before an editor is chosen; the duration achieved remains an experimental outcome. Memory-window engineering defines a candidate immune edit by three parameters: duration after editor clearance, retention through cell division, and amplitude at single-cell resolution, with target-compartment division rate as an explicit modifier. For passively diluted marks, division rate constrains post-clearance duration; transcriptional and phenotypic persistence may follow different trajectories. Published results from methylation editing at IL1RN, FOXP3 enhancer demethylation, PD-1 enhancer tuning, exhaustion circuits and CRISPRoff programming of primary human T cells are interpreted using their readouts and observation windows; some persistence endpoints remain censored by study duration. Three testable predictions concern CpG density, transcript-versus-mark recovery and division-dependent loss, with competing mechanisms and measurement artefacts considered. Specificity, the nuclease-knockout comparison, and the ethics of durable edits are treated as parts of the same specification. Two design consequences follow. TET-dependent erasure requires oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate; reduced erasure in hypoxic or metabolically inhibitory tumour regions is therefore a hypothesis for edited immune cells. Sustained programming of circulating monocyte output requires an upstream progenitor strategy, whereas long-lived resident myeloid cells are a separate case. A worked CAR T example and five-item reporting minimum distinguish development-stage characterisation from lot-release testing.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a rapidly growing neurological disorder characterized by motor and non-motor symptoms associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Photobiomodulation (PBM) may modulate mitochondrial pathways. This randomized, controlled, single-blind pilot trial investigated intranasal and transpalatal PBM, individually or combined, in 48 individuals with idiopathic PD allocated to TP + IN (intranasal + transpalatal PBM), IN (intranasal PBM), TP (transpalatal PBM), or Sham. Participants underwent 24 sessions over 12 weeks using near-infrared light (808 nm, 100 mW, 60 J, or 120 J per point). Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T1), 1 week after the intervention (T2), and 1-month follow-up (T3) using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS). Forty participants completed the study. IN significantly improved MoCA and MDS-UPDRS scores, with benefits persisting at follow-up. Sham showed a decline in MoCA. These findings suggest that intranasal PBM may be a promising adjunctive therapy for PD; further studies are needed to elucidate mechanisms and optimize treatment protocols.</jats:p>

title: SoccerNet-Guided Domain-Ordered Transfer Learning for Tiny Football Detection with GVRE-Augmented Target Data

affiliation.name: Faculty of Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong

abstract: <jats:p>Detecting a football in broadcast video remains difficult because the object is often only a few pixels wide and is easily obscured by motion blur, compression, or nearby players. This study tests a SoccerNet-guided domain-ordered transfer schedule while holding the target training data constant. The target set contains 298 original images and 257 accepted ball-containing images produced by bounding-box-guided generative visual representation enhancement (GVRE). TargetBaseline trains directly on these 555 images. DomainTransfer first trains on 8,550 SoccerNet-derived frames and then uses the same target set. Three matched You Only Look Once version 8, nano (YOLOv8n) seeds, 1280-pixel inputs, and a validation-first gate define the comparison. On validation, DomainTransfer raises mean Ball Average Precision at Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold 0.50 (AP50) by 0.0548 and fixed-threshold Ball Recall by 0.0741. The single gated test evaluation raises Ball AP50 from 0.5367 to 0.5913 and overall mAP50-95 from 0.6292 to 0.6448. These results support the ordered transfer schedule, although the 25-image test set, target-validation checkpoint selection, and use of one detector scale limit the strength of the conclusion.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hollow‐core anti‐resonant fibers (HC‐ARFs) have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional solid‐core fibers (SCFs) by combining low loss, broad transmission bandwidth, ultra‐low nonlinearity, low dispersion, and reduced latency. This review critically examines advances in HC‐ARFs from structural evolution and guiding physics to applications and deployment. We trace the progression from Kagome and single‐ring designs to nested and double‐nested architectures, and discuss anti‐resonant reflection, inhibited coupling, cladding density of photonic states, major loss mechanisms, and machine‐learning‐assisted prediction and design. We further review applications in ultrafast and nonlinear optics, gas and mid‐infrared lasers, ultraviolet guidance, high‐power delivery and extreme photonics, as well as high‐capacity, ultra‐wideband, long‐haul, quantum, and advanced optical communications. Particular attention is given to fabrication tolerances, reproducibility, bending sensitivity, interconnection, environmental stability, scalability, cost, and system‐level integration. Finally, we identify remaining bottlenecks and prospects for beyond‐fifth‐generation and sixth‐generation networks, artificial‐intelligence data interconnection, next‐generation optical networks, quantum technologies, high‐power laser delivery, and extreme photonics.</jats:p>

title: Propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion for emergency craniotomy following multiple trauma in a resource-limited setting
abstract:
<jats:sec id="st1">
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Target-controlled infusion (TCI) allows intravenous anesthetics to be titrated to model-predicted plasma or effect-site concentrations. In emergency neuroanesthesia, however, its clinical value depends not only on the selected target concentration but also on how these targets are adjusted in response to changing surgical stimulation while maintaining cerebral and systemic physiologic stability. We report the use of propofol TCI with the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI with the Minto model during emergency craniotomy in a patient with severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and major thoracic trauma in Eastern Indonesia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st2">
                    <jats:title>Case Description:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 32-year-old male weighing approximately 80 kg presented with severe TBI after a 5-m fall, accompanied by right hemopneumothorax, multiple rib fractures, and a clavicular fracture. A chest tube was inserted before anesthetic induction. Propofol was administered using the Schnider model with an effect-site target concentration (Ce) of 3–5 µg/mL during induction and 2.5–4 µg/mL during maintenance. Remifentanil was administered using the Minto model at target concentrations of 4–5 ng/mL during induction and 2–3 ng/mL during maintenance, although the anesthesia record did not consistently specify whether plasma or effect-site targeting was used for remifentanil during maintenance. After induction, the targets were reduced and subsequently adjusted according to the stage and intensity of surgical stimulation, hemodynamic response, ventilation, and surgical conditions. During the 4-h procedure, systolic blood pressure remained between 102 and 125 mmHg, oxygen saturation was maintained at 99–100%, and end-tidal carbon dioxide remained between 30 and 35 mmHg. The brain remained relaxed without clinically apparent swelling. This case illustrates how separate hypnotic and opioid targets can be used to guide stepwise titration of propofol and remifentanil during emergency craniotomy when advanced depth-of-anesthesia and intracranial monitoring are not available.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st3">
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Propofol TCI using the Schnider model and remifentanil TCI using the Minto model provided a practical framework for independently titrating the hypnotic and opioid components of anesthesia during emergency craniotomy. In a resource-limited setting, model-predicted concentrations should not be regarded as fixed doses but rather as adjustable targets interpreted in conjunction with surgical stimulation, hemodynamic tolerance, ventilation, brain relaxation, and the limitations of available monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Magnetic reconnection converts magnetic energy into plasma flows and heating. The pressure–strain interaction quantifies the energy conversion between bulk kinetic energy and thermal energy. However, in situ observations of ion pressure–strain interaction during magnetic reconnection are still limited. In this study, we analyze 14 magnetotail reconnection events observed by the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission to investigate the characteristics of ion pressure–strain interaction and energy conversion. Statistical results indicate that the pressure–dilatation term dominates the pressure–strain interaction in the ion flow reversal region of reconnection. At higher ion temperatures, both the ion pressure–strain interaction and convective ion thermal‐energy transport span a wider range of positive and negative values. The magnitude of ion pressure–strain interaction generally exceeds that of electromagnetic work , even when the estimated uncertainties are taken into account. These results provide observational insights into ion pressure–strain interaction and its role in bulk kinetic‐to‐thermal energy conversion during magnetotail magnetic reconnection.</jats:p>

title: Drug Target Interaction Prediction and Anticancer Drug Screening Based on Spatio Temporal Sequence Prediction and Machine Learning

abstract: <jats:p>Cancer treatment has long faced problems such as long drug development cycle, high cost of experimental screening, drug resistance of monotherapy and complex mechanism of combination therapy. Based on the existing introduction, this paper reviews the drug target interaction prediction, drug combination synergy evaluation, spatio-temporal sequence modeling and data-driven anti-cancer drug screening. Firstly, this paper introduces DTI, anti-cancer drug screening process, common databases and collaborative scoring indicators; Secondly, the applications of traditional machine learning, deep learning and ensemble learning methods in DTI and drug combination prediction were compared; Thirdly, the value of spatio-temporal sequence prediction in modeling drug concentration, action time and cell response dynamics was analyzed; Finally, the problems of data heterogeneity, sample imbalance, lack of interpretability of the model and difficulties in clinical transformation faced by the current research are summarized, and it is proposed that in the future, the integration of multi omics, interpretable artificial intelligence and experimental verification closed loop should be strengthened. Research shows that machine learning and spatio-temporal sequence prediction can effectively improve the efficiency of anti-cancer drug screening, and provide important method support for combination drug optimization and precision treatment.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (ATRTs) are malignant, multi-lineage neoplasms of early childhood in the central nervous system. ATRTs are subdivided into TYR, SHH, and MYC groups based on their transcriptional and epigenetic characteristics, and recent histopathological studies revealed that the MYC subtypes harbor mesenchymal features. Patient-derived ATRT cancer cell lines express high levels of vimentin, a marker for EMT. Therefore, we hypothesize that targeting mesenchymal cell state in ATRT is feasible by utilizing FiVe1 and its derivative FMP-502, which lead to hyperphosphorylation of vimentin at the S39, S56, and S83, resulting in multinucleation and mitotic collapse.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We treated three patient-derived ATRT-SHH cell lines (CHLA-02-ATRT, CHLA-04-ATRT, CHLA-05-ATRT), three ATRT-MYC cell lines (CHLA-06-ATRT, CHLA-266, BT-12), and 293T with FiVe1 or FMP-502 and used CellTiter-Glo (CTG) to determine the half-maximal inhibitor concentration (IC50). We confirmed vimentin phosphorylation at S39, S56, and S83 via Western blot. To determine transcription-level changes, we performed RNA-sequencing of CHLA-05-ATRT and CHLA-266 following 24 hours of treatment with FMP-502 at IC75 dose or DMSO.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>IC50 of FiVe1 for ATRT-MYC (1.130-8.621 µM) was significantly lower than that of ATRT-SHH (2.694-55.033 µM). FMP-502 yielded similar results (108.0-317.2 nM for ATRT-MYC and 252.0 nM-1.598 µM for ATRT-SHH). Non-malignant 293T cells demonstrated extremely high IC50 values (18.68 µM for FMP-502). ATRT cells treated with FMP-502 showed significantly increased vimentin phosphorylation at S39, S56, and S83 via Western blot. Differential RNA-sequencing analysis showed that ATRT cells treated with FMP-502 display significant depletion of gene sets relating to DNA repair and replication initiation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our preliminary findings suggest that ATRT-MYC cells are more susceptible to FiVe1 and FMP-502 than ATRT-SHH cells. Furthermore, vimentin hyperphosphorylation in ATRT may disrupt its mesenchymal state by decreasing DNA repair capacity. Our study demonstrates that targeting the mesenchymal state may be a novel approach for ATRT treatment.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Stokes parameters are three real parameters that completely characterize partially coherent light spanned by two modes – whether a pair of polarization or spatial modes – whose use is ubiquitous in optics. Whereas the Stokes parameters are defined through an expansion of the  coherence matrix in terms of Pauli matrices, it has been theorized that the  Gell–Mann matrices – developed in high‐energy particle physics – can serve as a basis for  coherence matrices for three‐mode light. This entails eight Stokes–Gell–Mann (SGM) parameters required for the polarization of non‐paraxial fields (spanned by three polarization modes), and fields comprising three spatial or temporal modes. Here we present the first measurements of the SGM parameters for partially coherent three‐mode light in a photonic integrated platform comprising a hexagonal mesh of Mach–Zehnder interferometers. Measuring the SGM parameters on chip, from which we reconstruct the  coherence matrix, facilitates exploring the full space of iso‐entropy fields that can be inter‐converted into each other unitarily and those that cannot. These results pave the way to utilizing multimode partially coherent light in applications involving optical communications, sensing, and information processing.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mission-oriented innovation policy aims to guide innovation efforts towards addressing societal challenges. Achieving such ambitious goals requires clear directions that mobilize and align resources. Yet, such directions often remain fluid, emerging through both top-down guiding and bottom-up learning involving heterogeneous stakeholders. Currently, we lack insight into how mission direction evolves over time and what this means for its potential to drive change. This study addresses this gap by examining efforts to make the Dutch plastic supply chain more sustainable. Over time, societal and policy priorities shifted from a biobased to a circular economy. We show how some actors responded by framing the mission’s core problem to match their interest, while others reframed their solutions to fit updated mission criteria. Our analysis highlights coexisting search directions, evolving problem–solution framings, and the influence of residual views, offering a nuanced perspective on missions as both guiding forces and outcomes of system directionality.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In industrial production, the real‐time detection of falling small targets in complex scenarios is critical for ensuring both production safety and operational efficiency. Traditional RGB cameras are limited by inherent defects, such as insufficient dynamic range and motion blur, which hinder their ability to meet the demands of high‐speed dynamic scenarios. Event cameras offer significant advantages, owing to their characteristics, such as high temporal resolution (microsecond‐level), low latency and high dynamic range (>120 dB). However, challenges persist, including data sparsity, noise interference, the scarcity of specialised datasets and the demands of real‐time processing. In response to complex industrial scenarios, this paper constructs a specialised dataset, EvFallDet, which contains multiple types of target objects and compound interferences, and proposes a lightweight detection framework, EvFall‐Net. The framework enhances the feature representation capability of small targets through an event encoding strategy, which incorporates spatiotemporal feature decoupling. Experiments demonstrate that this method leads to significant improvements in detection accuracy and robustness when applied to small targets in complex industrial environments.</jats:p>

title: Statin–Ezetimibe Therapy and Incident Myocardial Infarction Across Modified Cardiovascular–Kidney–Metabolic Risk Groups: A Nationwide Target Trial Emulation

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome integrates metabolic risk, kidney dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease. Whether statin-ezetimibe combination therapy is associated with lower subsequent myocardial infarction risk than statin monotherapy among patients across modified cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we emulated separate two-arm landmark target trials within modified early and late cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk groups. Adults aged 30-74 years with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days with statin monotherapy or a fixed-dose statin-ezetimibe combination were eligible. Treatment was assigned at the 180-day landmark. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting and cause-specific Cox regression were used to calculate hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI), with death treated as a competing event for cumulative incidence estimation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 309,371 treated participants, 239,954 had modified early risk and 69,417 had modified late risk. Compared with statin monotherapy, statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower myocardial infarction risk after weighting in both early-risk participants (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81-0.95) and late-risk participants (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.98). 10-year weighted cumulative incidence was 1.97% versus 2.23% in the early-risk group and 3.52% versus 3.94% in the late-risk group. In same-intensity comparisons, the association was most evident with moderate-intensity therapy, particularly in the early CKM group (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.79-0.95).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among adults with dyslipidemia who received prescriptions covering a total of 180 days, statin-ezetimibe combination therapy was associated with a lower subsequent risk of myocardial infarction than statin monotherapy across modified CKM risk groups. The association was most evident in moderate-intensity comparisons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
